وَهَؤُلَاءِ الِاتِّحَادِيَّةُ وَأَمْثَالُهُمْ إنَّمَا أُتُوا مِنْ قِلَّةِ الْعِلْمِ وَالْإِيمَانِ بِصِفَاتِ اللَّهِ الَّتِي يَتَمَيَّزُ بِهَا عَنْ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ وَقِلَّةِ اتِّبَاعِ السُّنَّةِ وَطَرِيقَةِ السَّلَفِ فِي ذَلِكَ بَلْ قَدْ يَعْتَقِدُونَ مِنْ التَّجَهُّمِ مَا يُنَافِي السُّنَّةَ تَلَقِّيًا لِذَلِكَ عَنْ مُتَفَلْسِفٍ أَوْ مُتَكَلِّمٍ فَيَكُونُ ذَلِكَ الِاعْتِقَادُ صَادًّا لَهُمْ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ كُلَّمَا أَرَادَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ أَنْ تَتَقَرَّبَ إلَى رَبِّهَا وَتَسْلُكَ الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ إلَيْهِ وَتَعْبُدَهُ - كَمَا فُطِرُوا عَلَيْهِ وَكَمَا بَلَّغَتْهُمْ الرُّسُلُ مِنْ عُلُوِّهِ وَعَظَمَتِهِ - صَرَفَتْهُمْ تِلْكَ الْعَوَائِقُ الْمُضِلَّةُ عَنْ ذَلِكَ حَتَّى تَجِدَ خَلْقًا مِنْ مُقَلِّدَةِ الْجَهْمِيَّة يُوَافِقُهُمْ بِلِسَانِهِ وَأَمَّا قَلْبُهُ فَعَلَى الْفِطْرَةِ وَالسُّنَّةِ وَأَكْثَرُهُمْ لَا يَفْهَمُونَ مَا النَّفْيُ الَّذِي يَقُولُونَهُ بِأَلْسِنَتِهِمْ؟ بَلْ يَجْعَلُونَهُ تَنْزِيهًا مُطْلَقًا مُجْمَلًا. وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ لَا يَفْهَمُ قَوْلَ الْجَهْمِيَّة. بَلْ يَفْهَمُ مِنْ النَّفْيِ مَعْنًى صَحِيحًا وَيَعْتَقِدُ أَنَّ الْمُثْبِتَ يُثْبِتُ نَقِيضَ ذَلِكَ وَيَسْمَعُ مِنْ بَعْضِ النَّاسِ ذِكْرَ ذَلِكَ.
 مِثْلُ أَنْ يَفْهَمَ مِنْ قَوْلِهِمْ:
 لَيْسَ فِي جِهَةٍ وَلَا لَهُ مَكَانٌ وَلَا هُوَ فِي السَّمَاءِ: أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ فِي جَوْفِ السَّمَوَاتِ وَهَذَا مَعْنًى صَحِيحٌ؛ وَإِيمَانُهُ بِذَلِكَ حَقٌّ وَلَكِنْ
translated_text:
in reports concerning Allah’s attributes—they interpret the hadith to conform to their reason, explicitly give their reason precedence over the hadith, and make it the standard by which the hadith is judged. I would ask: does the law revealed to Muhammad explicitly prescribe giving precedence to this reason of theirs, so that it belongs to the way we are commanded to follow? Or is it the reason of an ignorant, misguided, bewildered innovator who has departed from that way? There is no power nor strength except through Allah.

These Ittihādiyyah (who identify Allah with creation) and others like them have gone astray only because of their deficient knowledge of, and faith in, Allah’s attributes, by which He is distinct from created beings, and their failure to follow the Sunnah and the way of the early generations in this matter. Indeed, they may hold Jahmī beliefs that contradict the Sunnah, having received them from someone given to philosophizing or speculative theology. Those beliefs then obstruct their path to Allah. Whenever their hearts seek to draw near to their Lord, follow the straight path to Him, and worship Him—in accordance with their innate disposition and what the messengers conveyed to them concerning His being on high and His greatness—those misleading obstacles turn them away from this. Thus, you find many who follow the Jahmiyyah uncritically agreeing with them in speech, while their hearts remain true to their innate disposition and the Sunnah. Most of them do not understand the negation they utter; rather, they regard it as an unqualified, general declaration of Allah’s transcendence. Some do not understand the Jahmiyyah’s position at all. Instead, they understand the negation in a sound sense, believe that those who affirm the divine attributes affirm its opposite, and hear some people say so.

For example, they may understand the statement, “He is not in any direction, has no place, and is not in heaven,” to mean that He is not within the heavens. This is a sound meaning, and their belief in it is correct, but

original_text:
يَظُنُّ أَنَّ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا هَذَا النَّفْيَ اقْتَصَرُوا عَلَى ذَلِكَ وَلَيْسَ كَذَلِكَ.
 بَلْ مُرَادُهُمْ:
 أَنَّهُ مَا فَوْقَ الْعَرْشِ شَيْءٌ أَصْلًا وَلَا فَوْقَ السَّمَوَاتِ إلَّا عَدَمٌ مَحْضٌ؛ لَيْسَ هُنَاكَ إلَهٌ يُعْبَدُ وَلَا رَبٌّ يُدْعَى وَيُسْأَلُ وَلَا خَالِقٌ خَلَقَ الْخَلَائِقَ وَلَا عُرِجَ بِالنَّبِيِّ إلَى رَبِّهِ أَصْلًا هَذَا مَقْصُودُهُمْ.
وَهَذَا هُوَ الَّذِي أَوْقَعَ الِاتِّحَادِيَّةَ فِي قَوْلِهِمْ:
 هُوَ نَفْسُ الْمَوْجُودَاتِ؛ إذْ لَمْ تَجِدْ قُلُوبُهُمْ مَوْجُودًا إلَّا هَذِهِ الْمَوْجُودَاتِ؛
 إذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ فَوْقَهَا شَيْءٌ آخَرُ وَهَذَا مِنْ الْمَعَارِفِ الْفِطْرِيَّةِ الشهودية الْوُجُودِيَّةِ:
 أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ إلَّا هَذَا الْوُجُودُ الْمَخْلُوقُ؛ أَوْ وُجُودٌ آخَرُ مُبَايِنٌ لَهُ مُتَمَيِّزٌ عَنْهُ لَا سِيَّمَا إذَا عَلِمُوا أَنَّ الْأَفْلَاكَ مُسْتَدِيرَةٌ وَأَنَّ الْأَعْلَى هُوَ الْمُحِيطُ. فَإِنَّهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ إلَّا هَذَا الْوُجُودُ الْمَخْلُوقُ؛ أَوْ مَوْجُودٌ فَوْقَهُ. فَإِذَا اعْتَقَدُوا مَعَ ذَلِكَ أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ هُنَاكَ وُجُودٌ آخَرُ وَلَا فَوْقَ الْعَالَمِ شَيْءٌ؛
 لَزِمَ أَنْ يَقُولُوا:
 هُوَ هَذَا الْوُجُودُ الْمَخْلُوقُ؛ كَمَا قَالَ الِاتِّحَادِيَّةُ. وَهَذِهِ بِعَيْنِهَا هِيَ حُجَّةُ الِاتِّحَادِيَّةِ.
 وَهَذَا بِعَيْنِهِ هُوَ مَشْرَبُ قُدَمَاءِ الْجَهْمِيَّة وحدثائهم كَمَا يَقُولُونَ:
 هُوَ فِي كُلِّ مَكَانٍ وَلَيْسَ هُوَ فِي مَكَانٍ. وَلَا يَخْتَصُّ بِشَيْءِ. يَجْمَعُونَ دَائِمًا بَيْنَ الْقَوْلَيْنِ الْمُتَنَاقِضَيْنِ لِأَنَّهُمْ يُرِيدُونَ إثْبَاتَ مَوْجُودٍ؛ وَلَيْسَ عِنْدَهُمْ شَيْءٌ فَوْقَ الْعَالَمِ. فَتَعَيَّنَ أَنْ يَكُونَ هُوَ الْعَالَمَ أَوْ يَكُونَ فِيهِ. ثُمَّ يُرِيدُونَ إثْبَاتَ شَيْءٍ غَيْرِ الْمَخْلُوقِ؛

فَيَقُولُونَ:
 لَيْسَ هُوَ فِي الْعَالَمِ كَمَا لَيْسَ خَارِجًا عَنْهُ؛
 أَوْ يَقُولُونَ:
 هُوَ وُجُودُ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ دُونَ أَعْيَانِهَا أَوْ يَقُولُونَ: هُوَ الْوُجُودُ الْمُطْلَقُ فَيُثْبِتُونَهُ فِيمَا يُثْبِتُونَ إذَا كَانَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ مُتَشَابِهَةً فِي النَّفْيِ وَالتَّعْطِيلِ وَهُوَ إنْكَارٌ مَوْجُودٌ حَقِيقِيٌّ مُبَايِنٌ لِلْمَخْلُوقَاتِ عَالٍ عَلَيْهَا.
 وَإِنَّمَا يَفْتَرِقُونَ فِيمَا يُثْبِتُونَهُ وَيُكْرِهُونَ فِطَرَهُمْ وَعُقُولَهُمْ عَلَى قَبُولِ الْمُحَالِ الْمُتَنَاقِضِ فَيَقُولُونَ:
 هُوَ فِي الْعَالَمِ وَلَيْسَ هُوَ فِيهِ أَوْ هُوَ الْعَالَمُ وَلَيْسَ إيَّاهُ أَوْ يُغَلِّبُونَ الْإِثْبَاتَ فَيَقُولُونَ: بَلْ هُوَ نَفْسُ الْوُجُودِ أَوْ النَّفْيِ فَيَقُولُونَ: لَيْسَ فِي الْعَالَمِ وَلَا خَارِجًا عَنْهُ أَوْ يَدِينُونَ بِالْإِثْبَاتِ فِي حَالٍ وَبِالنَّفْيِ فِي حَالٍ إذَا غَلَبَ عَلَى أَحَدِهِمْ عَقْلُهُ غَلَّبَ النَّفْيَ وَهُوَ أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ فِي الْعَالَمِ وَإِذَا غَلَبَ عَلَيْهِ الْوَجْدُ وَالْعِبَادَةُ رَجَّحَ الْإِثْبَاتَ وَهُوَ أَنَّهُ فِي هَذَا الْوُجُودِ أَوْ هُوَ هُوَ لَا تَجِدُ جهميا إلَّا عَلَى أَحَدِ هَذِهِ الْوُجُوهِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ وَإِنْ تَنَوَّعُوا فِيمَا يُثْبِتُونَهُ - كَمَا ذَكَرْته لَك - فَهُمْ مُشْتَرِكُونَ فِي التَّعْطِيلِ. وَقَدْ رَأَيْت مِنْهُمْ وَمِنْ كُتُبِهِمْ؛ وَسَمِعْت مِنْهُمْ وَمِمَّنْ يُخْبِرُ عَنْهُمْ مِنْ ذَلِكَ مَا شَاءَ اللَّهُ. وَكُلُّهُمْ عَلَى هَذِهِ الْأَحْوَالِ ضَالُّونَ عَنْ مَعْبُودِهِمْ وَإِلَهِهِمْ وَخَالِقِهِمْ. ثُمَّ رَأَيْت كَلَامَ السَّلَفِ وَالْأَئِمَّةِ كُلِّهِمْ يَصِفُونَهُمْ بِمِثْلِ ذَلِكَ. فَمَنَّ اللَّهُ عَلَيْنَا بِاتِّبَاعِ سَبِيلِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَآمَنَّا بِاَللَّهِ وَبِرَسُولِهِ. وَكُلُّ هَؤُلَاءِ يَجِدُ نَفْسَهُ مُضْطَرِبَةً فِي هَذَا الِاعْتِقَادِ لِتَنَاقُضِهِ فِي نَفْسِهِ. وَإِنَّمَا يُسَكِّنُ بَعْضَ اضْطِرَابِهِ نَوْعُ تَقْلِيدٍ لِمُعَظَّمِ عِنْدَهُ أَوْ خَوْفُهُ مِنْ مُخَالَفَةِ أَصْحَابِهِ أَوْ زَعْمُهُ أَنَّ هَذَا مِنْ حُكْمِ الْوَهْمِ وَالْخَيَالِ دُونَ الْعَقْلِ.
translated_text:
so they say, “He is not within the world, just as He is not outside it.” Or they say, “He is the existence of created things, not the things themselves.” Or they say, “He is absolute existence.” Thus they affirm Him within whatever they affirm, when their hearts are alike in negation and denial—namely, denying a real being distinct from created things and exalted above them.

They differ only in what they affirm, forcing their innate dispositions and their reason to accept what is impossible and contradictory. They say, “He is within the world, yet He is not within it,” or, “He is the world, yet He is not the world.” Alternatively, they give precedence to affirmation and say, “Rather, He is existence itself”; or to negation and say, “He is neither within the world nor outside it.” Or they adhere to affirmation in one state and negation in another: when reason predominates in one of them, he gives precedence to negation—that He is not within the world; when spiritual feeling and worship predominate, he favors affirmation—that He is within this existence, or is this existence itself. You will find no Jahmī except in one of these four positions. Although they differ in what they affirm—as I have explained to you—they share this denial.

I have seen among them and in their books, and heard from them and from those who report about them, as much of this as Allah has willed. In all these states, they have lost their way concerning the One they worship, their God and their Creator. Then I read the statements of the early Muslim generations and the imams, all of whom describe them in similar terms. Allah has therefore blessed us to follow the path of the believers, and we have believed in Allah and His Messenger.

Every one of these people finds himself unsettled by this belief because it is inherently contradictory. His unease is only partly soothed by some form of unquestioning adherence to someone he reveres, by his fear of disagreeing with his companions, or by his claim that this is a judgment of fancy and imagination rather than reason.

وَهَذَا التَّنَاقُضُ فِي إثْبَاتِ هَذَا الْمَوْجُودِ الَّذِي لَيْسَ بِخَارِجِ عَنْ الْعَالَمِ وَلَا هُوَ الْعَالَمُ الَّذِي تَرُدُّهُ فِطَرُهُمْ وَشُهُودُهُمْ وَعُقُولُهُمْ؛ غَيْرُ مَا فِي الْفِطْرَةِ مِنْ الْإِقْرَارِ بِصَانِعِ فَوْقَ الْعَالَمِ فَإِنَّ هَذَا إقْرَارُ الْفِطْرَةِ بِالْحَقِّ الْمَعْرُوفِ وَذَاكَ إنْكَارُ الْفِطْرَةِ بِالْبَاطِلِ الْمُنْكَرِ.
وَمِنْ هَذَا الْبَابِ:
 مَا ذَكَرَهُ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ طَاهِرٍ المقدسي فِي حِكَايَتِهِ الْمَعْرُوفَةِ: أَنَّ الشَّيْخَ أَبَا جَعْفَرٍ الهمداني حَضَرَ مَرَّةً وَالْأُسْتَاذُ أَبُو الْمَعَالِي يَذْكُرُ عَلَى الْمِنْبَرِ: 
" كَانَ اللَّهُ وَلَا عَرْشَ "
 وَنَفَى الِاسْتِوَاءَ - عَلَى مَا عُرِفَ مِنْ قَوْلِهِ وَإِنْ كَانَ فِي آخِرِ عُمْرِهِ رَجَعَ عَنْ هَذِهِ الْعَقِيدَةِ وَمَاتَ عَلَى دِينِ أُمِّهِ وَعَجَائِزِ نَيْسَابُورَ - قَالَ فَقَالَ الشَّيْخُ أَبُو جَعْفَرٍ 
" يَا أُسْتَاذُ دَعْنَا مِنْ ذِكْرِ الْعَرْشِ - يَعْنِي لِأَنَّ ذَلِكَ إنَّمَا جَاءَ فِي السَّمْعِ -
 أَخْبِرْنَا عَنْ هَذِهِ الضَّرُورَةِ الَّتِي نَجِدُهَا فِي قُلُوبِنَا:
 مَا قَالَ عَارِفٌ قَطُّ "
 يَا اللَّهُ 
" إلَّا وَجَدَ مِنْ قَلْبِهِ مَعْنًى يَطْلُبُ الْعُلُوَّ لَا يَلْتَفِتُ يَمْنَةً وَلَا يَسْرَةً فَكَيْفَ نَدْفَعُ هَذِهِ الضَّرُورَةَ عَنْ قُلُوبِنَا؟ "
. فَصَرَخَ أَبُو الْمَعَالِي وَوَضَعَ يَدَهُ عَلَى رَأْسِهِ وَقَالَ. 
" حَيَّرَنِي الهمداني "
. أَوْ كَمَا قَالَ وَنَزَلَ. فَهَذَا الشَّيْخُ تَكَلَّمَ بِلِسَانِ جَمِيعِ بَنِي آدَمَ فَأَخْبَرَ أَنَّ الْعَرْشَ وَالْعِلْمَ بِاسْتِوَاءِ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ إنَّمَا أُخِذَ مِنْ جِهَةِ الشَّرْعِ وَخَبَرِ الْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ بِخِلَافِ الْإِقْرَارِ بِعُلُوِّ اللَّهِ عَلَى الْخَلْقِ مِنْ غَيْرِ تَعْيِينِ عَرْشٍ وَلَا اسْتِوَاءٍ فَإِنَّ هَذَا أَمْرٌ فِطْرِيٌّ ضَرُورِيٌّ نَجِدُهُ فِي قُلُوبِنَا نَحْنُ وَجَمِيعُ مَنْ يَدْعُو اللَّهَ تَعَالَى فَكَيْفَ نَدْفَعُ هَذِهِ الضَّرُورَةَ عَنْ قُلُوبِنَا.
translated_text:
This contradiction in affirming a being who is neither outside the world nor the world itself—an affirmation rejected by their innate dispositions, direct awareness, and reason—is distinct from the innate acknowledgment of a Maker above the world. The latter is the innate disposition’s acknowledgment of recognized truth; the former is its rejection of manifest falsehood.

An example of this is the well-known account related by Muhammad ibn Tāhir al-Maqdisī. Shaykh Abū Jaʿfar al-Hamdānī once attended a gathering in which the teacher Abū al-Maʿālī was saying from the pulpit, “Allah existed when there was no Throne,” and denying His rising over the Throne—as was well known of his teaching, although toward the end of his life he abandoned this belief and died upon the faith of his mother and the elderly women of Nishapur.

He related that Shaykh Abū Jaʿfar said, “Teacher, let us set aside mention of the Throne”—meaning that knowledge of it comes only through revelation—“and tell us about this inescapable awareness we find in our hearts: no one who knows Allah has ever said, ‘O Allah,’ without finding in his heart an impulse directed upward, turning neither right nor left. How, then, can we remove this inescapable awareness from our hearts?”

Abū al-Maʿālī cried out, placed his hand on his head, and said, “Al-Hamdānī has confounded me!”—or words to that effect—and descended from the pulpit.

This shaykh spoke on behalf of all the children of Adam. He explained that knowledge of the Throne and of Allah’s rising over it comes only through revelation and the reports of the Quran and Sunnah. This differs from acknowledging that Allah is above creation, without specifying a Throne or a rising over it. This is something innate and self-evident that we, and everyone who calls upon Allah Most High, find in our hearts. How, then, can we remove this inescapable awareness from our hearts?

translated_text:
{And the slave woman whom the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, asked, “Where is Allah?” She replied, “In heaven.” He said, “Set her free, for she is a believer.”} was a non-Arab slave woman. Who, do you think, had taught her and informed her of what she said? She was simply expressing the innate disposition upon which Allah Most High had created her. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, affirmed her answer and testified to her faith.

Let anyone endowed with reason reflect on this: he will find that it guides him to know his Lord and acknowledge Him as he should—not the innovations of those given to excessive speculation and pretentious speech, whom Satan has beguiled and lulled with false hopes.

One example is that leading speculative theologians who have mixed theology with philosophy count certain things among carefully guarded secrets and hidden sciences. Yet anyone with even a little reason and religious commitment who examines these things will find such ignorance and error in them that he would never have imagined these men falling into them. Indeed, he may even refuse to believe that such things came from them.

An example is the commentary on the hadith of the Ascension composed by Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī, in which he followed the example of Ibn Sīnā and ʿAyn al-Qudāt al-Hamdānī. He related the hadith of the Ascension in a lengthy narrative, with peculiar names and a sequence found nowhere in the books of the Muslims—not in the authentic, good, or weak hadiths transmitted among the scholars. It was merely fabricated by some beggars and storytellers, some devilish preachers, or some heretics.

He made the Messenger’s Ascension an ascent through thought to the celestial spheres, and identified the prophets he saw with the heavenly bodies: Adam was the moon, Idrīs was the sun, and the four rivers were the four elements. He also held that the Messenger had come to know absolute necessary existence. He then extolled this interpretation, treating it as secret knowledge that must be kept beyond the understanding of believers and their scholars. Indeed, some who had held him in high esteem were utterly astonished when they saw it. One of his partisan defenders continued to deny it until they showed him a copy in the handwriting of a well-known scholar familiar with his circumstances. He had included it in his book entitled “al-Matālib al-ʿĀliya” (The Lofty Pursuits), in which he collected the principal views of the philosophers and speculative theologians.

You also find Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī—who surpassed those men in his knowledge of jurisprudence, Sufism, speculative theology, legal theory, and other fields, as well as in asceticism, worship, sincerity of intention, and mastery of the Islamic sciences—referring in “al-Arbaʿīn” (The Forty) and similar works to his book “al-Madnūn bihi ʿalā Ghayr Ahlihi” (That Which Is Withheld from Those Unqualified for It). If you seek out that book, believing it to contain the secrets of reality and the ultimate objects of inquiry, you will find precisely the teachings of the philosophizing Sabians, with their wording and arrangement altered. Anyone unfamiliar with the true nature of people’s doctrines and those of the various religious communities will believe that this is the secret shared by the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and Abū Bakr, and that it is what is disclosed to those who attain unveiling and apprehend realities through a divine light. translated_text:
Sufis and devout worshippers attain through their spiritual discipline and religious devotion in apprehending realities and having them unveiled to them, to the point that they use this as a standard for judging what the revealed Law has brought. The reason for this was that, through his intelligence and sincere pursuit, he had recognized the inconsistencies in the approach of speculative theologians and philosophizing thinkers. Allah had granted him faith in broad outline—as he himself related—and he began yearning for a detailed understanding of that outline. In the words of the spiritual masters and Sufis, he found something closer to the truth and more firmly grounded than the discourse of philosophers and speculative theologians. His assessment was correct. Yet he had not learned of the prophetic inheritance of knowledge and spiritual states possessed by the foremost members of the Muslim community, or of the knowledge and worship attained by the earliest forerunners, through which they achieved unveilings of knowledge and acts of devotion that those others had not attained.

He therefore came to believe that a detailed understanding of that outline could be attained through that path alone, since he knew no other path. The distinctively Sunni, prophetic path had been closed to him by his limited knowledge of it and by the specious arguments he had adopted from philosophizing thinkers and speculative theologians, who thereby stood between him and that path. For this reason, he frequently condemned these barriers and the path of knowledge. But this concerned only the knowledge he had pursued, which had veiled him from truly following the prophetic message. It is not knowledge at all, but merely philosophical and theological doctrines. As the early Muslim generations said:

“Knowledge of speculative theology is ignorance.”

And as Abū Yūsuf said:

“Whoever seeks knowledge through speculative theology becomes a heretic.”

original_text:
وَلِهَذَا صَارَ طَائِفَةٌ مِمَّنْ يَرَى فَضِيلَتَهُ وَدِيَانَتَهُ يَدْفَعُونَ وُجُودَ هَذِهِ الْكُتُبِ عَنْهُ حَتَّى كَانَ الْفَقِيهُ أَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ بْنُ عَبْدِ السَّلَامِ - فِيمَا عَلَّقَهُ عَنْهُ - يُنْكِرُ أَنْ يَكُونَ

" الْمَضْنُونُ بِهِ عَلَى غَيْرِ أَهْلِهِ "

وَلِهَذَا كَانَ الشَّيْخُ 
" أَبُو عَمْرٍو بْنُ الصَّلَاحِ "
 يَقُولُ - فِيمَا رَأَيْته بِخَطِّهِ -: أَبُو حَامِدٍ كَثُرَ الْقَوْلُ فِيهِ وَمِنْهُ. فَأَمَّا هَذِهِ الْكُتُبُ - يَعْنِي الْمُخَالِفَةَ لِلْحَقِّ - فَلَا يُلْتَفَتُ إلَيْهَا. وَأَمَّا الرَّجُلُ فَيُسْكَتُ عَنْهُ وَيُفَوَّضُ أَمْرُهُ إلَى اللَّهِ.
translated_text:
For this reason, some who recognize his merit and religious devotion have come to deny that these books are his. The jurist Abū Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Salām even denied—in the notes taken from him—that “The Beginning of Guidance” was his work, saying: “It is merely something falsely attributed to him.” Yet the acceptable material in these books exceeds the objectionable material many times over. The objectionable material consists of general statements, and these books contain neither creeds nor the fundamentals of religion.

As for “That Which Is Withheld from Those Unqualified for It,” another group of scholars denied its attribution to him. Those thoroughly familiar with him and his circumstances, however, know that all this is his own discourse, because they know the sources underlying it and recognize the resemblance between its various parts. Nevertheless, he and others like him were—as I have already explained—unsettled, unable to hold consistently to a firm position. Their intelligence and eagerness to learn made them aspire to the path of the foremost among mankind, but it was not decreed for them to follow the path of the foremost members of this community, who inherited knowledge and faith from the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. These are the people who possess the realities of faith and the Quran—as we have already explained—who understand the Book of Allah, know and understand the hadith of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and accompany this knowledge with the corresponding spiritual states and deeds, in accordance with what the prophetic message brought.

For this reason, Shaykh Abū ‘Amr ibn al-Salāh said—in a passage I saw in his own handwriting:

“Much has been said about Abū Hāmid, and he himself has said much. As for these books”—meaning those that contradict the truth—“no heed should be paid to them. As for the man himself, one should remain silent about him and entrust his affair to Allah.”

وَهَذَا بَابٌ وَاسِعٌ فَإِنَّ الْخَارِجِينَ عَنْ طَرِيقَةِ السَّابِقِينَ الْأَوَّلِينَ مِنْ

translated_text:
His meaning is that he should not be spoken of ill, for Allah’s pardon of those who forget or err, and the sinner’s repentance, can efface every sin. Such pardon and repentance are highly likely in his case and in similar cases. Moreover, Allah’s forgiveness through good deeds—his own and those of others—and His expiation of sins through afflictions extend even to cases where sins are established. Thus, one should not presume the absence (*) of such forgiveness in the case of a particular individual without clear insight, especially when he has done much good, possesses sound knowledge, performs righteous deeds, and has good intentions.

He inclined toward philosophy, but presented it in the guise of Sufism and Islamic expressions. For this reason, Muslim scholars refuted him—even his closest associate, Abū Bakr ibn al-‘Arabī, who said:

“Our shaykh Abū Hāmid became deeply immersed in the philosophers’ teachings, then wished to extricate himself, but could not.”

He has also been reported to have espoused doctrines of the Bātiniyya (esoteric sects), and corroboration of these reports can be found in his books. Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Māzarī refuted him in a work devoted specifically to that purpose, as did Abū Bakr al-Turtūshī. His companion Abū al-Hasan al-Marghīnānī refuted his statements in The Niche of Lights and similar works. Shaykh Abū al-Bayān and Shaykh Abū ‘Amr ibn al-Salāh also refuted him. Ibn al-Salāh, Abū Zakariyyā al-Nawawī, and others warned against his statements on these matters. Ibn ‘Aqīl, Ibn al-Jawzī, Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī, and others likewise refuted him.

This is a broad subject, for those who depart from the way of the earliest forerunners among

الْمُهَاجِرِينَ وَالْأَنْصَارِ وَاَلَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوهُمْ بِإِحْسَانِ لَهُمْ فِي كَلَامِ الرَّسُولِ ثَلَاثُ طُرُقٍ:
طَرِيقَةُ التَّخْيِيلِ وَطَرِيقَةُ التَّأْوِيلِ وَطَرِيقَةُ التَّجْهِيلِ.
فَأَهْلُ التَّخْيِيلِ هُمْ الْفَلَاسِفَةُ وَالْبَاطِنِيَّةُ الَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ:

(وَطَرِيقَةُ التَّأْوِيلِ)
 طَرِيقَةُ الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ مَنْ الْجَهْمِيَّة وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَأَتْبَاعِهِمْ يَقُولُونَ: إنَّ مَا قَالَهُ لَهُ تَأْوِيلَاتٌ تُخَالِفُ مَا دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ اللَّفْظُ وَمَا يُفْهَمُ مِنْهُ وَهُوَ - وَإِنْ كَانَ لَمْ يُبَيِّنْ مُرَادَهُ وَلَا بَيَّنَ الْحَقَّ الَّذِي يَجِبُ اعْتِقَادُهُ - فَكَانَ مَقْصُودُهُ أَنَّ هَذَا يَكُونُ سَبَبًا لِلْبَحْثِ بِالْعَقْلِ حَتَّى يَعْلَمَ النَّاسُ الْحَقَّ بِعُقُولِهِمْ وَيَجْتَهِدُوا فِي تَأْوِيلِ أَلْفَاظِهِ إلَى مَا يُوَافِقُ قَوْلَهُمْ لِيُثَابُوا عَلَى ذَلِكَ فَلَمْ يَكُنْ قَصْدُهُ لَهُمْ الْبَيَانَ وَالْهِدَايَةَ وَالْإِرْشَادَ وَالتَّعْلِيمَ بَلْ قَصْدُهُ التَّعْمِيَةُ وَالتَّلْبِيسُ وَلَمْ يُعَرِّفْهُمْ الْحَقَّ حَتَّى يَنَالُوا الْحَقَّ بِعَقْلِهِمْ وَيَعْرِفُوا حِينَئِذٍ أَنَّ كَلَامَهُ لَمْ يُقْصَدْ بِهِ الْبَيَانُ فَيَجْعَلُوا حَالَهُمْ فِي الْعِلْمِ مَعَ عَدَمِهِ خَيْرًا مِنْ حَالِهِمْ مَعَ وُجُودِهِ.
 وَأُولَئِكَ الْمُتَقَدِّمُونَ كَابْنِ سِينَا وَأَمْثَالِهِ يُنْكِرُونَ عَلَى هَؤُلَاءِ وَيَقُولُونَ:
 أَلْفَاظُهُ كَثِيرَةٌ صَرِيحَةٌ لَا تَقْبَلُ التَّأْوِيلَ لَكِنْ كَانَ قَصْدُهُ التَّخْيِيلَ وَأَنْ يَعْتَقِدَ النَّاسُ الْأَمْرَ عَلَى خِلَافِ مَا هُوَ عَلَيْهِ.
وَأَمَّا الصِّنْفُ الثَّالِثُ الَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ:
 إنَّهُمْ أَتْبَاعُ السَّلَفِ فَيَقُولُونَ: إنَّهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ الرَّسُولُ يَعْرِفُ مَعْنَى مَا أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْآيَاتِ وَلَا أَصْحَابُهُ
translated_text:
the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in righteousness, adopt three approaches to the Messenger’s words: imaginative representation, reinterpretation, and attributing ignorance.

Those who adopt imaginative representation are the philosophers and the Bātiniyya. They say that he conjured up images of things that have no underlying reality, and that imaginative representation is the distinctive characteristic of prophethood.

(The approach of reinterpretation)
This is the approach of the speculative theologians among the Jahmiyya, the Muʿtazila, and their followers. They say that his statements have interpretations contrary to what their wording indicates and what is understood from it. Although he did not explain his intended meaning or clarify the truth that must be believed, his purpose, they maintain, was to prompt rational inquiry, so that people would discover the truth through their own reason and strive to reinterpret his words to accord with their own views, thereby earning a reward. Thus, his purpose was not to provide them with clarification, guidance, direction, and instruction, but rather to obscure and confuse. He did not acquaint them with the truth, so that they would arrive at it through their own reason and then recognize that his words were not intended to clarify it. They therefore regard themselves as better off in terms of knowledge without his words than with them.

Those mentioned earlier, such as Ibn Sīnā and others like him, object to this group’s position. They say that his expressions are numerous and explicit, and cannot admit reinterpretation; rather, his intention was imaginative representation and to make people believe things to be otherwise than they actually are.

As for the third group, who claim to be followers of the early generations, they say that the Messenger did not know the meaning of these verses revealed to him, nor did his Companions

original_text:
يَعْلَمُونَ مَعْنَى ذَلِكَ بَلْ لَازِمُ قَوْلِهِمْ:
 أَنَّهُ هُوَ نَفْسُهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ يَعْرِفُ مَعْنَى مَا تَكَلَّمَ بِهِ مِنْ أَحَادِيثِ الصِّفَاتِ بَلْ يَتَكَلَّمُ بِكَلَامِ لَا يَعْرِفُ مَعْنَاهُ وَاَلَّذِينَ يَنْتَحِلُونَ مَذْهَبَ السَّلَفِ يَقُولُونَ: إنَّهُمْ لَمْ يَكُونُوا يَعْرِفُونَ مَعَانِيَ النُّصُوصِ بَلْ يَقُولُونَ ذَلِكَ فِي الرَّسُولِ. وَهَذَا الْقَوْلُ مِنْ أَبْطَلْ الْأَقْوَالِ وَمِمَّا يَعْتَمِدُونَ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ ذَلِكَ مَا فَهِمُوهُ مِنْ قَوْله تَعَالَى 
{وَمَا يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ}

Indeed, their position necessarily implies that he himself did not know the meaning of the hadiths he uttered concerning the divine attributes, but spoke words whose meaning he did not know. Those who claim to follow the way of the early generations say that those generations did not know the meanings of the scriptural texts; indeed, they say this even of the Messenger. This is among the most untenable positions.

Among the things they rely upon is their understanding of the words of Allah Most High:

“And none knows its interpretation except Allah.”

They assume that ta’wīl (interpretation) means what they themselves call reinterpretation: a meaning contrary to the apparent meaning.

These people may then say: “The texts are to be understood according to their apparent meaning, while their ta’wīl is known only to Allah.” Yet by ta’wīl they mean something contrary to the apparent meaning. This is a contradiction on their part. One group understands “the apparent meaning” to refer solely to the wording of the texts. Both groups misunderstand the verse.

This is because the term “ta’wīl” has acquired three meanings through differences in terminological usage.

The first is the reality to which the words ultimately refer, even when this accords with their apparent meaning. This is the sense intended by the term ta’wīl in the Quran and Sunnah, as in the words of Allah Most High:

“Are they waiting for anything but its fulfilment? On the Day its fulfilment comes, those who had forgotten it before will say, ‘The messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth.’”

Another example is the statement of ‘Ā’isha:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would frequently say while bowing and prostrating: ‘Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and to You belongs all praise. O Allah, forgive me,’ thereby putting the Quran into practice.”

translated_text:
The second meaning intended by the term ta’wīl is “explanation,” as it is used by many Quran commentators. Thus Mujāhid, a leading authority in Quran commentary, said that “those firmly grounded in knowledge” know the interpretation of the ambiguous passages. By this he meant explaining them and clarifying their meanings, which those firmly grounded in knowledge do know.

The third meaning intended by ta’wīl is to divert an expression from the apparent meaning it indicates to a contrary meaning, on the basis of separate evidence that requires this. Such interpretation necessarily departs from what the wording indicates and makes clear. Calling this ta’wīl was not the usage of the early generations. Rather, a group of later scholars who delved into jurisprudence, its principles, and speculative theology restricted the term ta’wīl to this meaning. They assumed that this was what Allah Most High intended by His words:

“And none knows its interpretation except Allah.”

They then followed two approaches regarding this interpretation: one group said that none knows it except Allah, while another said that those firmly grounded in knowledge know it. Both groups are mistaken.

For in many instances—or in most, indeed the vast majority of them—this interpretation amounts to distorting words from their proper places, like the interpretations of the Qarāmitah and the Bātiniyyah. This is the interpretation that the early generations of this community and its leading scholars unanimously condemned. They denounced its adherents from every corner of the earth, and meteors were hurled in their wake.

the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah concerning the Ambiguous Passages of the Quran about Which They Entertained Doubts and Which They Interpreted Contrary to Their True Meaning.” Ahmad thus reproached them for explaining the Quran in ways contrary to its meaning.

Neither Ahmad nor any of the leading scholars said that the Messenger did not know the meanings of the verses and hadiths concerning the divine attributes. Nor did they say that the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness did not know the explanation and meanings of the Quran. How could they, when Allah commanded reflection upon His Book? He Most High said:

“This is a blessed Book which We have revealed to you, that they may reflect upon its verses.”

He did not say, “some of its verses.” He also said:

“Then do they not reflect upon the Quran?”

And He said:

“Then have they not reflected upon the word?”

There are other such texts which make clear that Allah loves people to reflect upon the entire Quran, and that He has made it a light and guidance for His servants. It is impossible for something whose meaning cannot be understood to serve that purpose.

Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī said: “Those who used to teach us the Quran—‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān and ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd—told us: ‘Whenever we learned ten verses from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, we would not move beyond them until we had learned the knowledge and practice they contained.’ They said: ‘Thus we learned the Quran, knowledge, and practice together.’” These matters are discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is this: if what someone says about the Messenger and his explanations to people belongs to the teachings of the heretics, what can his position concerning the early generations be, that he should claim to follow them? Even by his own reckoning and that of his group, he is at odds with the Messenger and the early generations. For he has openly proclaimed teachings of the deniers which, in his view, the Messenger considered best left undisclosed because they would corrupt people. But this is not so in the judgment of those possessed of knowledge and faith.

Rather, he died leaving us upon a clear, bright path, whose night is like its day; none deviates from it except one who is doomed to perish.

He informed us that:

“Every new matter introduced after him is an innovation, and every innovation is misguidance.”

Some practitioners of speculative theology may recite this verse by Majnūn of Banū ‘Āmir:

“Each claims a bond with Laylā,
Yet Laylā acknowledges none of their claims.”

If someone composes poetry containing wisdom, or quotes a verse to illustrate something he has recognized as true, he is close to the mark. But if he seeks to establish a claim merely through words arranged in verse or otherwise, he should be told: “You must demonstrate that the early generations do not acknowledge those with whom you claim affiliation.”

This is evident in what he and others have mentioned: they attribute to the early generations statements they never made, and which no one knowledgeable about them and upright in his reporting has transmitted from them. For a transmitter must possess both knowledge and integrity.

If we suppose that someone has reported the position of the early generations as he describes it, then either he has little knowledge of their transmitted accounts—like Abū al-Ma‘ālī, Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī, Ibn al-Khatīb, and others like them. Their knowledge of hadith was insufficient for them to be counted even among ordinary practitioners of that discipline, let alone its specialists. Each of these men knew al-Bukhārī, Muslim, and their hadiths only by hearsay, much as ordinary people speak of them. They do not distinguish between authentic, mass-transmitted hadith

Then he said: ‘Whoever has undergone an experience like mine will have come to know what I know.’”

He would often recite:

“Reason’s bold advance ends in fetters,
And most of mankind’s striving goes astray.
Our souls feel estranged within our bodies;
Our worldly life yields only harm and misery.
From a lifetime of inquiry we have gained
Nothing but a collection of ‘he said’ and ‘they said.’”

Here, too, is Imām al-Haramayn, who abandoned the views he had espoused and defended, and chose the way of the early generations. He would say:

“My companions, do not occupy yourselves with speculative theology. Had I known that it would bring me to this, I would never have pursued it.”

At his death, he said:

“I plunged into the vast sea, leaving behind the people of Islam and their sciences, and ventured into what they had forbidden me to pursue. Now, unless my Lord comes to my aid with His mercy, woe to Ibn al-Juwaynī! Here I am, dying upon my mother’s creed”—or he said, “the creed of the elderly women of Nishapur.”

Likewise, Abū ‘Abd Allāh Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Karīm al-Shahrastānī stated:

“He reported that he had found among the philosophers and speculative theologians nothing but bewilderment and regret.”

He would recite:

“By my life, I have travelled through all the seats of learning,
And cast my gaze among their landmarks;
Yet I saw only a bewildered man, his hand upon his chin,
Or a regretful man, gnashing his teeth.”

It gained wide currency, and people of the time went to great lengths in praising it and esteeming the doctrine that Creator and creation are one which it contains—recited as death approached him:

“If what I have suffered marks my rank in love with you,
Then I have wasted my days.
A wish my soul attained for a time—
Today I deem it a jumble of dreams.”

Among the foundations of faith is that Allah makes His servant steadfast through the firm word in this worldly life and in the Hereafter, as the Most High says:

“Have you not seen how Allah sets forth a parable: a good word is like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and whose branches reach into the sky?”

“It yields its fruit at all times by its Lord’s permission. And Allah sets forth parables for people so that they may take heed.”

“And a bad word is like a bad tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, with no stability.”

“Allah makes those who believe steadfast through the firm word in this worldly life and in the Hereafter. And Allah leads the wrongdoers astray, and Allah does whatever He wills.”

The word is the foundation of belief, for belief is the word that a person holds to be true. The best of words and beliefs is the declaration of Allah’s oneness and the belief that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah. The worst of words and beliefs is the declaration of associating partners with Allah, which means taking another deity alongside Allah. This is false and has no reality. Hence He, glorified be He, says:

“With no stability.”

Thus, the more a researcher investigates and a person acts upon these corrupt words and beliefs, the more he increases only in misguidance, distance from the truth, and knowledge of their falsity. As the Most High says:

“Or like layers of darkness in a deep sea, covered by waves, above which are waves, above which are clouds—darkness upon darkness. When one stretches out his hand, he can hardly see it. And whoever Allah does not grant light has no light.”

He, glorified be He, thus sets forth two parables:

The first is the parable of disbelief and compound ignorance, which the person possessing it thinks has substance, whereas in reality it is an illusion with no existence, like a mirage. The heart thirsts for truth just as the body thirsts for water. When he seeks what he thought was water, he finds it to be a mirage, and he finds Allah there, who pays him his account in full; and Allah is swift in reckoning. This is how you will find most of those who depart from the Sunnah and the community.

The second is the parable of disbelief and simple ignorance, in which a person neither discerns any truth nor sees any guidance. Compound disbelief necessarily entails simple disbelief, and every instance of disbelief must involve compound ignorance. Allah, glorified be He, set forth these two parables to illustrate the condition of holding a false belief and the condition of not knowing the truth—which resembles the condition of those who have incurred wrath and those who are astray—the condition of one who obstinately clings to falsehood until punishment befalls him, and the condition of a person astray who cannot see the path of guidance.

We therefore ask Allah the Almighty to make us steadfast through the firm word in this worldly life and in the Hereafter, and to enable us to hold fast to the Book and the Sunnah.

translated_text:
What many followers of shaykhs and Sufis attribute to truthful shaykhs may, for example, be lies and impossibilities. Or it may consist of ambiguous statements of theirs that these followers have misinterpreted; mistakes and lapses made by some shaykhs; or their sins and errors, such as the many religious innovations and immoral acts that some commit on the basis of a defensible interpretation or on an unjustifiable basis. The person may be pardoned for this, repent of it, have good deeds through which he is forgiven, or suffer afflictions through which his sins are expiated. Alternatively, such statements may come from people who imitate Allah’s allies through ascetic practices, acts of worship, and spiritual attainments, yet are not among Allah’s God-fearing allies. Rather, they are among the ignorant, the unjust, the transgressors, the hypocrites, or the disbelievers.

This is widespread and has filled the world. You find every group claiming exclusive access to secrets and realities that even the messengers do not claim, asserting that these are possessed by its select few and must be met only with unquestioning acceptance. They support these claims with fabricated hadiths and false interpretations. One example is the statement they attribute to ‘Umar:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and Abū Bakr used to converse, while I was like a black African between them.”

Thus they portray ‘Umar, in the company of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his friend, as being like a black African, although he was present and listening to their words.

Then one of them claims to have acquired this knowledge through something cast into his heart, and each claims that the lies and falsehood he himself utters constitute that knowledge. Were I to enumerate the various kinds of false claims in this matter, the discussion would be lengthy.

Some of them ascribe poems to the shaykh, calling them “the Quran’s Companion.” These poems stir him more deeply, and their contents bring him greater joy, than the Quran does, although they contain various lies and errors.

translated_text:
Others compose poems for him proclaiming union with God, asserting that he is the creator of all creation, that he created the heavens and the earth, and that they prostrate before him and worship him.

Others describe their Lord in their poems using accounts transmitted in fabricated reports that liken Him to created beings, claim to describe how He is, and ascribe a body to Him. These are fabricated lies and outright disbelief: sharing meals and drinks with Him, walking alongside Him, embracing Him, His descending to the earth and sitting in one of its gardens, and the like. Each of them treats these things as hidden secrets and closely guarded knowledge reserved for the elect among Allah’s God-fearing allies.

One example is what you find among the Rāfidah, adherents of Shiism, and those who have learned from them: claims to knowledge of secrets and realities supposedly received from the Prophet’s household, concerning either religious knowledge or knowledge of events. They regard these as among the most exalted matters, which they must urge one another to conceal, while believing whatever of them they do not truly understand. Yet all of it is fabricated lies and invented falsehood. This group—the “Rāfidah”—is among those most given to lying and claiming possession of concealed knowledge. This is why the Bātiniyyah and the Qarāmitah have affiliated themselves with them.

The first of these people appeared in the time of the Commander of the Faithful, ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him. They began claiming that he had been singled out to receive secret knowledge and a special bequest. His closest companions would therefore ask him about this, and he would deny it. When word reached him that such claims were being made, he would address the people and deny that this was true of him.

 فَمِنْ أَكْبَرِ الْأَشْيَاءِ كَذِبًا حَتَّى يُقَالَ: مَا كُذِبَ عَلَى أَحَدٍ مَا كُذِبَ عَلَى جَعْفَرٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ. وَمِنْ هَذِهِ الْأُمُورِ الْمُضَافَةِ كِتَابُ " الْجَفْرِ " الَّذِي يَدَّعُونَ أَنَّهُ كَتَبَ فِيهِ
translated_text:
The compilers of the authentic hadith collections have transmitted these words of ‘Alī through several routes. For example, one authentic report relates that Abū Juhayfah said:

“I asked ‘Alī, ‘Do you have anything that is not in the Quran?’ He replied, ‘No, by Him who splits the grain and creates the soul! We have nothing except what is in the Quran, apart from an understanding of His Book that Allah grants a man, and what is in this document.’ I asked, ‘What is in the document?’ He replied, ‘Blood money, the release of captives, and that a Muslim is not to be killed for killing a disbeliever.’”

Al-Bukhārī’s wording is:

“‘Do you have any revelation other than what is in Allah’s Book?’ He replied, ‘No, by Him who splits the grain and creates the soul! I know of nothing except an understanding of the Quran that Allah grants a man.’”

The two authentic hadith collections also relate, through Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, from his father—and this is one of the soundest chains of transmission on earth—that ‘Alī said:

“We have nothing except Allah’s Book and this document from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: ‘Medina is a sanctuary between ‘Ayr and Thawr.’”

In a narration recorded by Muslim:

“‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib addressed us, saying: ‘Whoever claims that we have a book that we read, other than Allah’s Book and what is in this document’—the narrator said, ‘His document was hanging in the sheath of his sword’—‘has lied. It contains the ages of camels and certain matters concerning wounds, and in it the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “Medina is a sanctuary.”’” The hadith continues.

As for the lies and secrets they claim to have received from Ja‘far al-Sādiq, these are among the greatest fabrications. It is even said that no one has had as many lies attributed to him as Ja‘far, may Allah be pleased with him. Among these works attributed to him is the book al-Jafr, in which they claim he wrote

The same applies to the book “al-Bitāqa” (The Card), which Ibn al-Hillī and others like him from the Maghrib claim, and to works such as “al-Jadwal” (The Table), concerning the crescent moon, “al-Haft,” attributed to Ja‘far, and much Quran commentary and other material.

Another example is the “Epistles of the Brethren of Purity,” compiled by a group in Baghdad under Buyid rule. They were Sabian adherents of philosophy who professed adherence to the upright monotheistic faith. They claimed to have combined the religion of the Sabians who had altered their religion with the upright monotheistic faith, bringing together philosophical discourse and elements of the Sharia. The work contains much disbelief and ignorance. Nevertheless, some people—including certain prominent judges in the provinces—claim that it consists of the words of Ja‘far al-Sādiq. This is a heretic’s assertion and an ignorant man’s slander.

[Another example is what some ordinary people recount of the predictions of future battles attributed to “Ibn Ghandab.” They claim that he taught al-Hasan and al-Husayn. The scholars agree that no such thing ever existed. These predictions attributed to “Ibn Ghandab” were merely composed by certain ignorant people during the reign of Nūr al-Dīn or thereabouts. They are defective verse that reveals their composer’s ignorance.]

Likewise, most of these predictions of future battles transmitted in verse and similar forms are lies. In our own time, judges and shaykhs have fabricated more than one such work. Falsehood concerning events in the world is more prevalent than falsehood concerning religious matters, because those who give worldly interests precedence over religion are more eager for such knowledge. Although religious people also have an interest in it, their interest in religion is stronger. The former do not possess the same light for distinguishing truth from falsehood as religious people do. Hence liars have proliferated in this field, many of their falsehoods have gained currency, vast sums have been wrongfully acquired through them, and many people aspiring to kingship and similar ambitions have been killed as a result.

For this reason, they employ various methods of deception in this field and deliberately lie about it. Sometimes they appeal to physical movements and configurations brought about by Allah, such as the movements of the celestial spheres and heavenly bodies, meteors, thunder, lightning, winds, and other such phenomena. At other times, they rely on movements and configurations that they themselves produce, such as divining with sand, pebbles, and barley, drawing lots by hand, and similar practices belonging to the same category as divination by arrows. They seek knowledge of events through this practice of divination, whether using arrows, pebbles, or other objects mentioned by scholars of Quranic exegesis.

translated_text:
please the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is when a person sets out trusting in Allah and hears a good word:

“He liked good omens and disliked taking ill omens.”

A good omen reinforces what a person has undertaken with Allah’s permission and in reliance upon Him, whereas taking an ill omen runs counter to this. It is therefore disliked for a person to take ill omens. Such omens harm only those who heed them, because they have harmed themselves; they do not harm those who rely upon Allah. The purpose here is not to discuss these matters or explain why they sometimes prove correct and repeatedly prove wrong.

Rather, the point is that people deliberately tell many lies concerning these practices, even when the practices have given no indication of what they claim. Likewise, many people deliberately lie about dreams, although these include righteous dreams, which constitute one of the forty-six parts of prophethood. Similarly, the jinn would mix a hundred lies with a word they heard from heaven and then convey it to the soothsayers. Thus, it is established in Sahīh Muslim:

“Mu‘āwiyah ibn al-Hakam al-Sulamī reported: I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, I have only recently left the time of ignorance, and Allah has brought Islam. Some men among us visit soothsayers.’

“He replied, ‘Do not visit them.’

“I said, ‘Some men among us take ill omens.’

“He replied, ‘That is something they feel in their hearts, but it must not deter them.’

“I said, ‘Some men among us draw lines.’

“He replied, ‘One of the prophets used to draw lines; whoever matches his lines is right.’”

If abundant lies may be deliberately introduced even into things that are parts of prophethood or reports from the angels, what, then, of something inherently inconsistent, with no firm foundation? This is why you find that most people whose religion is corrupt engage in falsehoods concerning events in the world, such as those who hold that the Creator and creation are one. For Ibn ‘Arabī, in his book “‘Anqā’ Mughrib” and elsewhere, foretold many future events

most of which were false. The same applies to Ibn Sab‘īn, and likewise to those who calculated how long this Muslim community would endure through the numerical values of alphabetic letters—a method inherited from the Jews—and through the movements of the heavenly bodies—a method inherited from the Sabians. This was done by Abū Nasr al-Kindī and other philosophers, by some followers of al-Rāzī who wrote on Quranic interpretation, and by some with Shiite leanings who interpreted the experiences of ascetics.

I have encountered groups among their followers who claim that these matters belong to hidden secrets and closely guarded knowledge. I discussed this with several groups of them, swearing to them that it was fabricated falsehood and that none of these things would come to pass. I challenged some of them to join me in invoking Allah’s curse upon whichever of us was lying, because the matter concerned the foundations of religion. They belonged to those who hold that the Creator and creation are one, whose claims would take a long time to describe.

They claimed that their shaykh, whom they regarded as the foremost spiritual knower and ascetic of his age, was the Messiah who would descend. They claimed that this meant the descent of the spiritual essence of Jesus, peace be upon him; that his mother was named Mary; that he would unite the three religions; and that he would appear in a manifestation more perfect than that of Muhammad and the other messengers. They hold views that rank among the gravest abominations, whose enumeration and description would take a long time.

Another astonishing thing is that these theologians, who claim to know the realities of matters of knowledge and religion while opposing the Sunnah and the Muslim community, each cite as evidence whatever hadith they happen to encounter

that is fabricated or too ambiguous for its meaning to be understood. Whenever one of them finds a report containing ambiguity, he interprets it according to his own opinion. Some of them thus cite fabrications, such as the statement falsely attributed to ‘Umar, “I was like a Zanj man (a black African),” or what they narrate about “the secret of the Ascension,” or their account that:

“The people of the Suffah heard the intimate discourse without the Messenger being aware of it. When the Messenger descended, they informed him. He asked, ‘From where did you hear it?’ They replied, ‘We were listening to the address.’”

Indeed, when I explained to a group who had assumed the role of shaykhs and become examples for people to follow that this was a lie, and that Allah had never caused any such thing to happen, I said: “What makes this clear to you is that the Ascension took place in Mecca, according to the explicit text of the Quran and the consensus of the Muslims, whereas the Suffah existed only in Medina. How, then, could there have been people of the Suffah in Mecca?”

Likewise, they cite the claim that the people of the Suffah fought against the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions alongside the polytheists when the latter prevailed, claiming that they were with Allah. They use this to justify following whatever actually happens, whether it constitutes obedience to Allah or disobedience, and to equate whatever happens with what His religion prescribes. This resembles the words of those who associated partners with Allah:

“If Allah had willed, we would not have associated partners with Him, nor would our fathers.”

There are many fabrications of this kind.

As for ambiguous reports, an example is their appeal to certain Companions’ prohibition against disclosing some obscure matters of knowledge, such as the statement of ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him:

“Speak to people about what they understand, and leave aside what they cannot comprehend. Would you like Allah and His Messenger to be disbelieved?”

And the statement of ‘Abdullāh ibn Mas‘ūd:

translated_text:
“No man relates to a people an account beyond their understanding without its becoming a trial for some of them.”

And the statement of ‘Abdullāh ibn ‘Abbās concerning the interpretation of the verses:

“What assurance do you have that, if I explained them to you, you would not disbelieve? Your disbelief in them would consist in denying them.”

These reports are true. Yet each of them identifies what was left unspoken with his own claims of secrets and realities which, when disclosed, prove to be falsehood, disbelief, and hypocrisy. Even Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī, in “Minhāj al-Qāsidīn” (The Path of the Seekers) and elsewhere, and others like him, cited these lines attributed to ‘Alī ibn al-Husayn:

“How many a jewel of knowledge, were I to disclose it,
Would bring the charge: ‘You are an idol-worshipper!’
And Muslim men would deem my blood lawful to shed,
Regarding their foulest deed as something good.”

If, then, such are the methods of those who claim a depth of understanding and knowledge of secrets that has led them outside the Sunnah and the Muslim community—who allege that this knowledge concerning religion or the created world belongs exclusively to them, believe its general and ambiguous statements, and claim to have been granted an understanding of the realities of worship and purity of religious devotion that was not granted to the earliest generation, the guardians of Islam and luminaries of the faith, yet do not dare reject or deny these claims, despite their falsehood sometimes being apparent and sometimes hidden—then it is evident that reason and religion require us to recognize that prophethood and messengership have the stronger claim to all deep understanding, knowledge, insight, and comprehensive understanding of the secrets of things and their inner realities. No believer disputes this. We are now addressing those whose hearts contain faith.

Since this is so, those who know these matters best are those most closely connected with the Messenger: those who know best his words and deeds, his movements and stillness, his comings and goings, his inward and outward life; those most knowledgeable about his Companions, his life and its events; those most diligent in studying all this and those who transmitted it; and those most devoted to following him and taking him as their example.

These are the people of the Sunnah and hadith. They preserve his hadith, distinguish its sound reports from its unsound ones, comprehend it, and possess an understanding of its meanings that Allah grants them. They believe and affirm it, obey and submit, and follow his example. Alongside this, they possess powerful intellects, sound analogical reasoning and discernment, and profound spiritual unveilings and communications. Their reflection, reasoning and judgment are the soundest, and their dreams and unveilings the truest.

Does not anyone with even the slightest reason and religious commitment know that these people have a stronger claim to truthfulness, knowledge, faith and sound understanding than those who oppose them? That they possess knowledge which the ignorant and the religious innovator deny? That what they possess is the manifest truth, whereas those who are ignorant of their ways and oppose them are themselves burdened with empty verbiage and misguidance?

This is a subject that would require a lengthy explanation. For human souls produce words and deeds that none but the Lord of Majesty can fully encompass. Utterances include informative statements and performative expressions, such as commands and prohibitions. The finest and truest discourse is the Book of Allah: its reports are the truest reports, its exposition the clearest exposition, and its commands the wisest commands.

“Then in what statement after Allah and His verses will they believe?”

And everyone

 وَوَجْهُ الْحَصْرِ:
 أَنَّهُ إمَّا أَنْ يَحْذِفَ الْفَاعِلَ أَوْ يَذْكُرَهُ وَإِذَا ذَكَرَهُ فَإِمَّا أَنْ يَجْعَلَهُ مِنْ قَوْلِ اللَّهِ أَوْ مِنْ قَوْلِ نَفْسِهِ.
 فَإِنَّهُ إذَا جَعَلَهُ مِنْ كَلَامِ الشَّيَاطِينِ لَمْ يُقْبَلْ مِنْهُ وَمَا جَعَلَهُ مِنْ كَلَامِ الْمَلَائِكَةِ فَهُوَ دَاخِلٌ فِيمَا يُضِيفُهُ إلَى اللَّهِ وَفِيمَا حُذِفَ فَاعِلُهُ فَقَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ مِمَّنِ افْتَرَى عَلَى اللَّهِ كَذِبًا أَوْ قَالَ أُوحِيَ إلَيَّ وَلَمْ يُوحَ إلَيْهِ شَيْءٌ وَمَنْ قَالَ سَأُنْزِلُ مِثْلَ مَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ}
 . وَتَدَبَّرْ كَيْفَ جَعَلَ الْأَوَّلِينَ فِي حَيِّزِ الَّذِي جَعَلَهُ وَحْيًا مِنْ اللَّهِ وَلَمْ يُسَمِّ الْمُوحِي؟
 فَإِنَّهُمَا مِنْ جِنْسٍ وَاحِدٍ فِي ادِّعَاءِ جِنْسِ الْإِنْبَاءِ وَجَعَلَ الْآخَرَ فِي حَيِّزِ الَّذِي ادَّعَى أَنْ يَأْتِيَ بِمِثْلِهِ وَلِهَذَا قَالَ:
 
{مِمَّنِ افْتَرَى عَلَى اللَّهِ كَذِبًا}
 ثُمَّ قَالَ: 
{وَمَنْ قَالَ سَأُنْزِلُ مِثْلَ مَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ}
 فَالْمُفْتَرِي لِلْكَذِبِ وَالْقَائِلُ: أُوحِيَ إلَيَّ وَلَمْ يُوحَ إلَيْهِ شَيْءٌ: مِنْ جُمْلَةِ الِاسْمِ الْأَوَّلِ وَقَدْ قُرِنَ بِهِ الِاسْمُ الْآخَرُ فَهَؤُلَاءِ الثَّلَاثَةُ الْمُدَّعُونَ لِشِبْهِ النُّبُوَّةِ. وَقَدْ تَقَدَّمَ قَبْلَهُمْ الْمُكَذِّبُ لِلنُّبُوَّةِ.
translated_text:
who follows discourse or an utterance put forward in opposition to the Quran—of which it is said that its speaker receives it through inspiration and revelation, or that he composes and originates it—is among the gravest wrongdoers. Thus, when Allah, glorified be He, mentioned the statement of those who failed to give Him His due esteem by denying that revelation was sent down to human beings, He mentioned the three categories of those who imitate him and claim to match him.

For someone claiming to match him either says, “Allah has revealed to me”; or says, “It was revealed to me,” “It was imparted to me,” or “I was told,” without naming the speaker; or attributes it to himself and states that he himself composed it.

These possibilities exhaust the alternatives because he either leaves the agent unnamed or names him. If he names him, he presents it either as Allah’s speech or as his own. If he presents it as the speech of devils, it will not be accepted from him. Whatever he presents as the speech of angels falls within what he attributes to Allah or what he expresses without naming its agent. Allah Most High therefore said:

“Who does greater wrong than someone who fabricates a lie against Allah, or says, ‘Revelation has come to me,’ when nothing has been revealed to him, or says, ‘I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down’?”

Reflect on how He grouped the first two within the category of someone who presents it as revelation from Allah without naming the revealer. Both belong to the same class in claiming to receive communications, whereas He placed the other in the category of someone who claims to produce its like. Thus He said:

“Someone who fabricates a lie against Allah,”

then said:

“Or says, ‘I will send down the like of what Allah has sent down.’”

The fabricator of lies and the person who says, “Revelation has come to me,” when nothing has been revealed to him, both fall under the first designation, to which the other designation is conjoined. These, then, are the three who lay claim to a semblance of prophethood. Before them, the denier of prophethood had already been mentioned.

فَهَذَا يَعُمُّ جَمِيعَ أُصُولِ الْكُفْرِ الَّتِي هِيَ تَكْذِيبُ الرُّسُلِ أَوْ مُضَاهَاتُهُمْ كمسيلمة الْكَذَّابِ وَأَمْثَالِهِ. وَهَذِهِ هِيَ

 الَّتِي نَرُدُّهَا نَحْنُ فِي هَذَا الْمَقَامِ لِأَنَّ الْمُخَالِفَ لِلسُّنَّةِ يَرُدُّ بَعْضَ مَا جَاءَ بِهِ الرَّسُولُ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَوْ يُعَارِضُ قَوْلَ الرَّسُولِ بِمَا يَجْعَلُهُ نَظِيرًا لَهُ: مِنْ رَأْيٍ أَوْ كَشْفٍ أَوْ نَحْوِ ذَلِكَ.
فَقَدْ تَبَيَّنَ أَنَّ الَّذِينَ يُسَمُّونَ هَؤُلَاءِ وَأَئِمَّتَهُمْ حَشْوِيَّةً هُمْ أَحَقُّ بِكُلِّ وَصْفٍ مَذْمُومٍ يَذْكُرُونَهُ وَأَئِمَّةُ هَؤُلَاءِ أَحَقُّ بِكُلِّ عِلْمٍ نَافِعٍ وَتَحْقِيقٍ وَكَشْفِ حَقَائِقَ وَاخْتِصَاصٍ بِعُلُومِ لَمْ يَقِفْ عَلَيْهَا هَؤُلَاءِ الْجُهَّالُ الْمُنْكِرُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ الْمُكَذِّبُونَ لِلَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ.

translated_text:
Thus, this encompasses all the foundations of disbelief: denying the messengers or seeking to rival them, as did Musaylimah the Liar and others like him. These are the “foundations of innovation” that we refute here, for whoever opposes the Sunnah rejects some of what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought, or counters the Messenger’s words with something he treats as their equal: an opinion, an unveiling, or the like.

It has therefore become clear that those who call these people and their leaders Hashwiyyah are themselves more deserving of every blameworthy description they mention. The leaders of those they disparage have a stronger claim to every form of beneficial knowledge, rigorous scholarship, the uncovering of truths, and specialized knowledge unknown to these ignorant detractors who deny Allah and His Messenger.

If they disparage them as Hashwiyyah because they narrate hadiths without discrimination, then their opponents are the foremost purveyors of worthless opinions and discourse whose soundness is unknown—indeed, whose falsity is known. If it is because they include ordinary people who lack discernment, then every one of those sects has among its followers some of the most ignorant and unbelieving people. Yet the ordinary followers of those they disparage are the ones who frequent the mosques for prayer, remember Allah and supplicate to Him, perform pilgrimage to the Ancient House, strive in Allah’s cause, and embody honesty, trustworthiness, and every kind of good in the world.

It has thus become clear to you that their opponents are more deserving of these grounds for censure, while these people are further removed from them. People must therefore turn to them concerning the prophetic inheritance with which Allah has singled them out, and which is found only among them.

وَأَيْضًا فَيَنْبَغِي النَّظَرُ فِي الْمَوْسُومِينَ بِهَذَا الِاسْمِ وَفِي الْوَاسِمِينَ لَهُمْ بِهِ:

translated_text:
Moreover, we should consider both those given this label and those who apply it to them: which of the two is more deserving of it? It is well known that this label became prevalent among those who deny the divine attributes and are suspected of heresy. Scholars such as Abū Hātim and others have stated that a hallmark of heretics is their calling the people of hadith Hashwiyyah.

We shall use terms whose application is not disputed, such as “affirmation” and “negation.” We therefore say: it is well known that some people apply this label to the people of hadith who accept hadith according to its apparent meaning. The further someone is removed from hadith, the more vehemently he disparages its adherents with this label: the Qarmatians, then the philosophers, then the Muʿtazilah. They use it to disparage the speculative theologians who affirm the divine attributes—among the Kullābiyyah, Karrāmiyyah, and Ashʿariyyah—as well as jurists, Sufis, and others.

They apply this label to anyone who follows and accepts the scriptural texts. Those who affirm attributes established through reason, such as knowledge and power, but not those known through revelation, and others of similar views, call those who affirm the attributes known through revelation Hashwiyyah. Such is the practice of Abū al-Maʿālī al-Juwaynī, Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī, and others like them.

Abū Muhammad followed Abū al-Maʿālī’s approach in jurisprudence and speculative theology. Yet Abū Muhammad was more knowledgeable about hadith and more faithful to it than Abū al-Maʿālī, and better versed in the schools of jurisprudence. Abū al-Maʿālī adhered more closely to speculative theology, while the two were comparable in their command of Arabic.

original_text:
الْحَشْوِ:
 لِأَنَّهَا مَسَائِلُ عِلْمِيَّةٌ وَالْحَدِيثُ لَا يُفِيدُ ذَلِكَ؛ لِأَنَّ اتِّبَاعَ النُّصُوصِ مُطْلَقًا فِي الْمَبَاحِثِ الْأُصُولِيَّةِ الْكَلَامِيَّةِ حَشْوٌ؛ لِأَنَّ النُّصُوصَ لَا تَفِي بِذَلِكَ؛

translated_text:
the Hashwiyyah, because these are matters requiring certain knowledge, which hadith does not provide; following scriptural texts as a general principle in foundational inquiries of speculative theology is mere filler, because those texts do not suffice for that purpose.

The issue thus comes down to one of two things: doubt concerning either the chain of transmission or the text. Either they attribute to the Messenger something he is not known to have said—as with solitary reports—and maintain that these reports yield certain knowledge; or they regard their understanding of the wording as certain knowledge when it is not, given the possible interpretations of textual evidence.

There is no doubt that this is the mainstay of every heretic and hypocrite: it nullifies knowledge of the message with which Allah sent His Messenger. Sometimes he says, “We do not know that they said this,” and sometimes, “We do not know what they meant by these words.” Once knowledge of their statements or their meaning is denied, no knowledge can be gained from them. He can then advance whatever doctrines he wishes, secure against being challenged with reports from the prophets, for he has entrusted that frontier to those two guards, who repel the Messenger’s troops from him and assail anyone who invokes those reports as evidence.

This very position constitutes an attack on prophethood itself, even if he professes reverence for the prophets and acknowledges their perfection: his is the acknowledgment of someone who receives no knowledge from them. In his eyes, the Messenger is thus like a caliph accorded recognition on coins and in sermons—merely in form and wording, in writing and speech—without any command or prohibition of his being obeyed. He possesses the outward form of leadership through the coinage and sermons assigned to him, but not its reality.

translated_text:
discharge the duties of rule, such as jihad and governance, as many governors’ deputies act when those who appointed them are weak and incapable, so that sound administration results from combining the precedence of the man of office and noble lineage with his deputy’s strength; or even if a ruler does this out of personal desire and ambition for leadership for himself and his faction, excluding someone more entitled to it than he is, and follows the path of those who seize power through aggression—it is well known that a believer in Allah and His Messenger cannot deem it permissible to say of the prophetic message that it is incapable of establishing and explaining knowledge, such that acknowledging it while obtaining knowledge of divine matters elsewhere would ensure the soundness of religion. Nor can he deem it permissible to transgress against it by putting himself forward before Allah and His Messenger, placing his own knowledge and statements above the Messenger’s knowledge and statements. Nor can he deem it permissible to subject it to rational reinterpretations and claim that this perfects the religion, and that the religion cannot be complete without it.

At best, he claims that the Messenger knew that what he conveyed had interpretations and explanations other than what the apparent sense and understood meaning of his words indicated; that he left these unexplained only because he could not explain them among those Bedouins and others like them; and that he entrusted this task to the intellects of later generations. This is indeed what they do.

For the adherents of philosophy say that the messengers were unable to explain the truths because disclosing them would corrupt people, whose minds could not bear them. They may then say that the messengers knew these truths. Some of them may instead say, “They did not know them,” or, “I know them better than they did.” They then explain these truths themselves through the methods of inference at their disposal.

Yet they have failed to understand that if knowledge of these truths is possible, then it is possible for the messengers, just as they claim it is possible for themselves. Otherwise, by their own admission, they have no way of knowing them. The same applies to expressing

and explaining knowledge through speech and writing. If that is impossible, then neither can you do it—yet you speak and record your knowledge in books. If it is possible, then your claim that “the messengers were unable to do so” cannot be valid.

If you say, “These truths can be communicated to a select few, but not to people at large”—which is indeed what they say—then it is well known that the messengers’ knowledge would be possessed by their closest followers, just as your knowledge is possessed by yours. It is also well known that the more thoroughly someone knows a leader’s words, circumstances, and affairs, both private and public, and the more faithfully he upholds them, the stronger his claim to a close association with that leader.

There is no doubt that the people of hadith are the most knowledgeable members of the Muslim community and the most intimately acquainted with the knowledge of the Messenger and his closest followers: the Rightly Guided Caliphs and the rest of the Ten; Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, Muʿādh ibn Jabal, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, Salmān al-Fārisī, Abū al-Dardāʾ, ʿUbādah ibn al-Sāmit, Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, and Hudhayfah ibn al-Yamān; and Saʿd ibn Muʿādh, Usayd ibn Hudayr, Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah, ʿAbbād ibn Bishr, Sālim, the freedman of Abū Hudhayfah, and others. These were among those closest to the Messenger, most knowledgeable about his private affairs, and most faithful in following his example in them.

The scholars of hadith know these people and their private affairs better than anyone else and follow their example most faithfully.  وَهَؤُلَاءِ هُمْ الَّذِينَ جَمَعُوا بَيْنَ الْبَصِيرَةِ فِي الدِّينِ وَالْقُوَّةِ عَلَى الدَّعْوَةِ وَلِذَلِكَ كَانُوا وَرَثَةَ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ الَّذِينَ قَالَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى فِيهِمْ:
 
{وَاذْكُرْ عِبَادَنَا إبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ أُولِي الْأَيْدِي وَالْأَبْصَارِ}
translated_text:
their leaders, and the closest followers of the speculative theologians possess the knowledge of their leaders, as do the closest followers of the Qarmatians and the Bātiniyyah. The same applies to the leading scholars of Islam: those closest to each imam know his private affairs best. Take Mālik ibn Anas, for example.

Since Ibn al-Qāsim was the closest to him and knew his private affairs best, Mālik’s followers relied on his transmission. Indeed, even the “private questions” transmitted by Ibn Abī al-Ghamr are accepted on his authority, although some have challenged them. The same applies to Abū Hanīfah: Abū Yūsuf, Muhammad, and Zufar knew him best. Likewise with other imams. A scholar may write a book or make a statement, and someone who did not hear it directly from him may understand his intent better than someone who did. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Someone to whom a message is conveyed may understand it better than someone who heard it directly.”

In any case, however, the transmitter must be among the close associates who know the circumstances of the person from whom he transmits. Similarly, among the followers of the imams are those who understand their texts better than some of their direct companions.

It is firmly established in the minds of Muslims that the heirs of the messengers and the successors of the prophets are those who uphold the religion through knowledge, action, and calling people to Allah and the Messenger. These are the Messenger’s true followers. They are like a tract of good, fertile land that receives water and produces abundant pasture and grass: it flourishes in itself, and through it people flourish.

These are the people who combine insight into the religion with the strength to call others to it. For this reason, they are the heirs of the prophets, concerning whom Allah Most High said:

“And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, possessors of strength and vision.”

original_text:
فَالْأَيْدِي الْقُوَّةُ فِي أَمْرِ اللَّهِ وَالْأَبْصَارُ الْبَصَائِرُ فِي دِينِ اللَّهِ فَبِالْبَصَائِرِ يُدْرَكُ الْحَقُّ وَيُعْرَفُ وَبِالْقُوَّةِ يَتَمَكَّنُ مِنْ تَبْلِيغِهِ وَتَنْفِيذِهِ وَالدَّعْوَةِ إلَيْهِ. فَهَذِهِ الطَّبَقَةُ كَانَ لَهَا قُوَّةُ الْحِفْظِ وَالْفَهْمِ وَالْفِقْهِ فِي الدِّينِ وَالْبَصَرِ وَالتَّأْوِيلِ؛

 " هَلْ خَصَّكُمْ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِشَيْءِ دُونَ النَّاسِ؟

 لَا؛ وَاَلَّذِي فَلَقَ الْحَبَّةَ وَبَرَأَ النَّسَمَةَ؛ إلَّا فَهْمًا يُؤْتِيهِ اللَّهُ عَبْدًا فِي كِتَابِهِ. فَهَذَا الْفَهْمُ هُوَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الْكَلَأِ وَالْعُشْبِ الَّذِي أَنْبَتَتْهُ الْأَرْضُ الطَّيِّبَةُ. وَهُوَ الَّذِي تَمَيَّزَتْ بِهِ هَذِهِ الطَّبَقَةُ عَنْ الطَّبَقَةِ الثَّانِيَةِ؛ وَهِيَ الَّتِي حَفِظَتْ النُّصُوصَ فَكَانَ هَمُّهَا حِفْظَهَا وَضَبْطَهَا؛ فَوَرَدَهَا النَّاسُ وَتَلَقَّوْهَا بِالْقَبُولِ؛ وَاسْتَنْبَطُوا مِنْهَا وَاسْتَخْرَجُوا كُنُوزَهَا وَاتَّجَرُوا فِيهَا؛ وَبَذَرُوهَا فِي أَرْضٍ قَابِلَةٍ لِلزَّرْعِ وَالنَّبَاتِ؛ وَرَوَوْهَا كُلٌّ بِحَسَبِهِ. 
{قَدْ عَلِمَ كُلُّ أُنَاسٍ مَشْرَبَهُمْ}
 . وَهَؤُلَاءِ الَّذِينَ قَالَ فِيهِمْ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{نَضَّرَ اللَّهُ امْرَأً سَمِعَ مَقَالَتِي فَوَعَاهَا؛ ثُمَّ أَدَّاهَا كَمَا سَمِعَهَا؛ فَرُبَّ حَامِلِ فِقْهٍ وَلَيْسَ بِفَقِيهِ؛ وَرُبَّ حَامِلِ فِقْهٍ إلَى مَنْ هُوَ أَفْقَهُ مِنْهُ}
 . وَهَذَا عَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ عَبَّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا حَبْرُ الْأُمَّةِ؛ وَتُرْجُمَانُ الْقُرْآنِ. مِقْدَارُ مَا سَمِعَهُ مِنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَا يَبْلُغُ نَحْوَ الْعِشْرِينَ حَدِيثًا الَّذِي
translated_text:
Thus, “strength” means strength in carrying out Allah’s command, and “vision” means insight into Allah’s religion. Through insight, the truth is grasped and recognized; through strength, one is able to convey it, put it into practice, and call others to it. This group possessed powers of memorization and understanding, deep knowledge of religion, discernment, and interpretation.

They caused rivers of knowledge to flow from the revealed texts, unearthed their treasures, and were granted a special understanding of them. Thus, when the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked, “Did the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, give you anything exclusively, to the exclusion of others?” he replied:

“No, by Him who splits the grain and creates the soul, except for an understanding of His Book that Allah grants a servant.”

This understanding is like the pasture and grass produced by fertile land. It is what distinguishes this group from the second group: those who preserved the texts and devoted their attention to memorizing and accurately retaining them. People came to them and accepted these texts, drew inferences from them, extracted their treasures, put them to profitable use, sowed them in soil suited to cultivation and growth, and watered them, each according to his capacity.

“Each group knew its own drinking place.”

These are the people concerning whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“May Allah make radiant the person who hears my words, retains them, and then conveys them just as he heard them. For many a bearer of religious knowledge has no deep understanding of it, and many a bearer of religious knowledge conveys it to someone with greater understanding than his own.”

Consider ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, the great scholar of this community and interpreter of the Quran. What he heard from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, amounts to fewer than twenty or so hadiths in which he

{قُلْ إنْ كُنْتُمْ تُحِبُّونَ اللَّهَ فَاتَّبِعُونِي يُحْبِبْكُمُ اللَّهُ}

translated_text:
says, “I heard and saw.” He also heard much from the Companions, and his understanding and ability to draw inferences were blessed, until he filled the world with knowledge and religious understanding. Abū Muhammad ibn Hazm said that his fatwas were collected in seven large volumes. Yet this collection contained only what had reached its compiler; otherwise, Ibn ʿAbbās’s knowledge was like an ocean. His religious understanding, his deductions, and his understanding of the Quran were of such a calibre that he surpassed others, although they had heard what he heard and memorized the Quran just as he had. His soil, however, was among the richest and most receptive to cultivation. He sowed the revealed texts in it, and it brought forth every noble kind of growth. That is Allah’s bounty, which He grants to whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.

What comparison is there between Ibn ʿAbbās’s fatwas, his interpretation, and his deductions, and the fatwas and interpretation of Abū Hurayra? Yet Abū Hurayra had a stronger memory than he did; indeed, he was the foremost memorizer of hadith in the entire community. He conveyed hadith just as he had heard it and diligently reviewed it at night. His efforts were devoted to memorizing and conveying what he had memorized exactly as he had heard it. Ibn ʿAbbās’s efforts, by contrast, were devoted to gaining deep understanding, drawing inferences, opening up the wellsprings of the revealed texts, making rivers flow from them, and extracting their treasures.

So too did their heirs after them: in their religion, they relied on drawing inferences from the revealed texts, not on philosophical imaginings, analogical opinion, or other innovated views. Inevitably, victory, true praise, and reward both now and hereafter belonged to the heirs of the prophets, who follow them in this world and the Hereafter. For a person follows the religion of his close friend.

“Say, ‘If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you.’”
