translated_text:
In any case, they are the most knowledgeable people in the community about the Messenger’s hadith, his life, his purposes, and his circumstances.

By the people of hadith, we do not mean those who confine themselves to hearing, writing down, or transmitting it. Rather, we mean all those best qualified in memorizing it, knowing it, understanding it outwardly and inwardly, and following it inwardly and outwardly. The same applies to the people of the Quran.

The least of their qualities is their love for the Quran and hadith, their study of both and their meanings, and their practice of what they know both require. Thus, their jurists know the Messenger better than other jurists; their Sufis follow the Messenger more closely than other Sufis; their rulers are better qualified than others to govern according to the Prophet’s example; and their ordinary people are more faithful in their allegiance to the Messenger than others.

It is well known that those who exalt philosophy and speculative theology and believe in their teachings are further removed than these people from knowing hadith and following it. This is an observable fact. Indeed, if you examine their circumstances, you will find them among the most ignorant people concerning the sayings of the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—his circumstances, and the inward and outward aspects of his affairs. You will even find many ordinary people more knowledgeable about these matters than they are. You will find that they do not distinguish between what the Messenger said and what he did not say. They may not even distinguish between a mass-transmitted hadith from him and a fabricated hadith falsely attributed to him.

In seeking agreement with him, they rely only on whatever accords with their own views, whether fabricated or not. They therefore turn away from hadiths which those intimately acquainted with the Messenger know with certain, self-evident knowledge to be his words, in favour of hadiths which those same people know with certain, self-evident knowledge to have been falsely attributed to him, while they

How, then, can someone who has neither memorized the Quran nor understood its meanings, and who knows neither hadith nor its meanings, know the truths learned from the Messenger? A verse may be mentioned in someone’s presence, and he will say, “We do not accept that this hadith is authentic.” Or he may say, “Because he—peace be upon him—said such-and-such,” when the words are actually a verse from the Book of Allah. Astonishing examples of this have reached us, and those that have not reached us are more numerous still.

A trustworthy man told me that one of the leading speculative theologians, a man called Shams al-Dīn al-Asbahānī, the teacher of al-Aykī, took charge of the school at the shrine of al-Husayn in Egypt. They handed him a volume from a multivolume Quran, and he read, “In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful,” pronouncing the letters alif, lām, mīm and sād as a word, until someone told him, “Alif, lām, mīm, sād.”

Reflect on this fair judgment, so that it becomes clear to you that those who disparage the people of hadith and turn away from their way are undoubtedly ignorant heretics and hypocrites. Thus, when Imam Ahmad learned that the people of hadith had been mentioned in Mecca in the presence of Ibn Abī Qutayla, who said, “They are evil people,” Imam Ahmad stood up, shaking out his garment and saying, “A heretic! The people of knowledge, however, used to say that they are the “abdāl” (substitutes), because they take the place of the prophets and truly stand in their stead. They are not among those lacking substance, whose reality is unknown. Each of them stands in the prophets’ place within the sphere in which he represents them: one in knowledge and exposition, another in worship and spiritual state, and another in both.

They also used to say that they are the victorious group who will prevail, upholding the truth, until the Hour comes. For with them are the guidance and the religion of truth with which Allah sent His messengers. It is this religion that Allah has promised to make prevail over all other religions, and Allah is sufficient as a witness.

وَكُلُّ عُقَلَاءِ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ مُتَّفِقُونَ عَلَى أَنَّهُ أَكْمَلُ وَأَفْضَلُ النَّوْعِ الْبَشَرِيِّ وَأَنَّ جِنْسَ الرُّسُلِ أَفْضَلُ مِنْ جِنْسِ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ الْمَشَاهِيرِ ثُمَّ قَدْ يَزْعُمُونَ أَنَّ الرُّسُلَ وَالْأَنْبِيَاءَ حُكَمَاءُ كِبَارُ وَأَنَّ الْفَلَاسِفَةَ الْحُكَمَاءَ أَنْبِيَاءُ صِغَارٌ وَقَدْ يَجْعَلُونَهُمْ صِنْفَيْنِ. وَلَيْسَ هَذَا مَوْضِعَ شَرْحِ ذَلِكَ. فَقَدْ تَكَلَّمْنَا عَلَيْهِ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ.
 وَإِنَّمَا الْغَرَضُ:
 أَنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ الْأَسَاطِينَ مِنْ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ وَالْمُتَكَلِّمِين غَايَةُ
translated_text:
and matters of knowledge alike. Others, however, do not deny the outward practices established through mass transmission, though they may regard them as intended for the general public rather than the elite, just as they do with matters conveyed in revealed reports.

Their discourse revolves around the claim that the prophetic message serves the welfare of the general public in knowledge and practice, but not that of the elite. This is the central premise of the authors of “Rasā’il Ikhwān al-Safā” (Epistles of the Brethren of Purity) and the other distinguished proponents of philosophy. Some of them nevertheless hold that compliance with the practical prescriptions of religious law is obligatory. Such people are numerous among their jurists, Sufis, and judicious philosophers. This was the extent of Ibn Sīnā’s understanding when he repented and committed himself to fulfilling the obligations prescribed by religious law. The ancient philosophers held that the laws laid down by the foremost sages of their lands had to be followed; all the more reason, then, for them to require adherence to the laws of the messengers. For, as Ibn Sīnā said:

“The philosophers of the world agree that no law superior to this law of Muhammad has ever come into the world.”

All judicious philosophers agree that he is the most perfect and excellent member of the human race, and that the messengers as a class are superior to the celebrated philosophers as a class. They may then claim that the messengers and prophets are great sages, while the philosopher-sages are lesser prophets; or they may regard them as two distinct classes. This is not the place to explain that, for we have discussed it elsewhere.

The point is simply that the furthest these leading philosophers and speculative theologians go

translated_text:
is to make this claim. We have presented the matter through an exhaustive rational classification, leaving no category out, to show that whoever opposes the hadith scholars in knowledge and practice is either ignorant or a hypocrite. A hypocrite is ignorant and worse besides, as we shall explain, if Allah wills. The ignorant person in question has an element of hypocrisy, even if he is unaware of it. Thus, whoever denies this is both ignorant and a hypocrite.

We therefore said: Whoever claims that he and the leading figures of his group know realities better than the messengers and explain them more clearly is a heretic and a hypocrite if he outwardly professes faith in them, by the agreement of the believers. We shall address him later.

If, however, he says, “The messengers possessed greater knowledge and clarity of exposition, but these realities cannot be known, or cannot be explained at all, or both are possible only for the elite,” we reply: “Then you cannot attain the knowledge and clarity of exposition that the messengers were unable to attain.”

If you say, “These realities cannot be known,” we reply: “Then you and your leading figures are all the more incapable of knowing them.”

If you say, “The messengers cannot explain them,” we reply: “Then neither you nor your leading figures can explain them.”

If you say, “That is possible for the elite, but not for the general public,” we reply: “Then it is possible for the messengers to convey that to the elite, though not to the general public.”

translated_text:
If they claim that none of the elite among the messengers’ companions could understand these realities, they place the first and foremost believers below later generations in knowledge and faith. This is one of the claims of the heretics, for it ranks certain ancient peoples—the Greeks, Indians, and others—as superior to this community in intellect and in their understanding of divine matters and matters of worship. Such are the claims of hypocritical heretics, since Muslims agree that this community is the best and most accomplished of all communities, and that its best and most accomplished members are its earliest believers.

Once this is conceded, those who know these earliest believers best and follow them most closely are the scholars of hadith and the adherents of the sunnah. Hence Imam Ahmad said in the epistle of ‘Abdūs ibn Mālik:

“The fundamental principles of the sunnah, according to us, are to hold firmly to the way of the companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to follow their example, and to abandon religious innovations. Every religious innovation is misguidance. The sunnah, according to us, consists of the reports from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

The sunnah explains the Quran and provides evidence concerning it—that is, indications of its meaning.

For this reason, scholars have stated that the Rāfidī doctrine is the foundation of heresy, and that the first person to introduce it was a hypocritical heretic, ‘Abd Allāh ibn Saba’. For whoever impugns the first and foremost believers thereby impugns their transmission of the message, their understanding of it, or their adherence to it. The Rāfidīs sometimes impugn their knowledge of the message and sometimes their adherence to it—and attribute these instead to the Prophet’s household and to an infallible figure who has no existence whatsoever.

The heretics among the philosophers, the Nusayrīs, and others sometimes impugn the transmission of the message; this is

the view of their ignorant members. At other times, they impugn the understanding of the message. This is the position of their more adept members, including the leading philosophers, the Ittihādiyya, and others like them.

Once, when al-Tilimsānī was ill, a man visited him accompanied by some students of hadith. Al-Tilimsānī began explaining his principle concerning thought: that it is a veil, and that everything hinges on unveiling. What he meant was the unveiling of absolute existence. One of those students asked, “What, then, does Umm al-Dardā’s statement mean: ‘Abū al-Dardā’s finest deed was reflection’?”

Annoyed that someone like this had been admitted to his presence, he said to the man who had brought him, “How can someone like this be allowed to visit me?” Then he said:

“Do you know, my son, what Abū al-Dardā and others like him resemble? They resemble people who heard certain words and preserved them for us, so that we would be the ones to understand them and know what their speaker intended. They also resemble a courier who carried a letter from the ruler to his deputy.”

Or he said something to that effect, for it has been a long time since I heard this account. The man who visited him related it to me; he is trustworthy and knows what he is talking about in this matter. He had explored these fields extensively.

Likewise, Ibn Sīnā and others express disparagement of the Companions inherited from his father and his Qarmatian associates. Thus, when they discuss humanity’s need for the imamate toward the end of their treatment of philosophy, you find them alluding to the views of the misguided Rāfidīs. The Rāfidīs, however, are more explicit in their vilification than these philosophers.

For this reason, you find an association and resemblance between the “Rāfidīs,” the “Qarmatians,” and the “Ittihādiyya.” Several things unite them. Among these are attacks on the best members of this community, on what the adherents of the sunnah and the community uphold, and on what

is firmly established among the fundamental tenets of the faith and the foundations of religion. They also claim to possess something esoteric that distinguishes them from everyone else and is exclusive to them. Yet they curse one another, hate one another, and disagree with one another. I have seen and heard countless instances of this, just as Allah said concerning the Christians:

“And from those who say, ‘We are Christians,’ We took their covenant, but they forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of. So We stirred up enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Resurrection.”

And He said concerning the Jews:

“And We cast enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Resurrection. Whenever they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it.”

The same applies to the theologians who muddle together different positions. At times they side with the Muslims—even if they are innovators—and at times with the Sabian philosophers. At other times they side with the polytheistic unbelievers. Sometimes they weigh the different factions against one another and wait to see which side will prevail; sometimes they remain bewildered between them. This last group has become numerous among those who profess Islam, including scholars, rulers, and others, especially when the polytheistic Turks gained ascendancy over the lands of Islam in the East during the seventh century AH.

Many of those who professed Islam harbored such hypocrisy and apostasy that the polytheists and the People of the Book were given power over Muslim lands. Thus, you find Abū Abd Allāh al-Rāzī questioning whether proofs expressed in words establish certainty and whether transmitted reports yield knowledge. These are the two premises underlying heresy, as we explained earlier.

Then, in those matters of Islam that he does affirm, he relies on what is necessarily known to belong to the religion of Islam, such as acts of worship and manifest prohibitions. Likewise, regarding the affirmation of bodily resurrection—after examining Quran commentaries and hadiths—he regards knowledge of it as derived from many sources. Thus he does not engage in negation in the manner of

His position concerning “the Companions” is similar. Although he acknowledges their integrity in what they transmitted and their knowledge in general, he claims in some places that they did not know the philosophers’ specious arguments or the matters they explored, because he found no transmitted account of the Companions speaking in the philosophers’ terminology. He uses this as an argument in refuting those who claimed . . . (1).

Likewise, such assertions concerning “the Companions” are found only among the most ignorant and unjust of those who speak on scholarly matters: these speculative theologians, would-be philosophers, Shia partisans, and the Ittihādiyya. These assertions resemble the words of many scholars and rulers: “I am braver than they were. They did not fight an enemy like the one we fought, nor engage directly in warfare as we have, nor govern as we have.” Such talk is found only among the most ignorant and unjust kings.

If he means that the Companions did not know the philosophers’ particular expressions and the means by which they explain their intended meanings, this does not detract from them. Messengers and their companions are not required to know the languages of other nations; they are required to know only what is indispensable to conveying the message. The interpreters who mediate between them know each party’s expressions and their meanings. If the two meanings are identical—as with words denoting the sun and the moon—they convey the shared meaning; otherwise, they know where the two meanings coincide and differ, and convey to each party what the other intends. In doing so, they explain the concepts and clarify the identity, similarity, and closeness between the two meanings.

translated_text:
Thus, the Companions knew what the Messenger had brought. What he brought contained a demonstration of the falsity of every unbeliever’s disbelief, establishing this through sound reasoning that was more valid and clearer in its exposition than those unbelievers’ arguments. As Allah Most High says:

“And they do not come to you with an argument except that We bring you the truth and the best explanation.”

He, glorified be He, informs us that whenever the unbelievers present the Messenger with a rational argument supporting their falsehood, Allah brings him the truth, together with explanations, evidence, and examples that explain, reveal, and clarify the truth better than their reasoning does. Every judgment or argument advanced by the Sabians, the would-be philosophers, and other unbelievers falls within the scope of what the Companions knew.

Allah Most High mentions this verse after His words:

“And the Messenger said, ‘My Lord, indeed my people have abandoned this Quran.’”

“And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals. But sufficient is your Lord as a guide and a helper.”

He thus makes clear that whoever abandons the Quran is among the Messenger’s enemies, and that this enmity is inevitable and inescapable. Do you not consider His words, Most High:

“And on the Day the wrongdoer bites his hands, he will say, ‘Oh, I wish I had taken a path with the Messenger!

“‘Woe to me! I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend!

“‘He led me away from the Reminder after it had come to me.’ And Satan always forsakes man.”

Allah Most High sent His Prophet Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to all the worlds, and set forth examples for them all in the message with which He sent him. As He Most High says:

“And We have certainly set forth for people in this Quran every kind of example, so that they may take heed.”

He thus informs us that He has set forth every kind of example in this Quran for all people.

There is no doubt that the language used in addressing people varies according to need, just as weapons do in warfare. If the Muslims’ enemies differ in their fortifications and armaments from the Persians and Byzantines, then fighting them must accord with what the Sharia requires. Its foundation is to seek what best fulfils obedience to Allah and most benefits His servant—what is best in this world and the Hereafter.

Someone familiar with their warfare may be better able to fight them than someone who is not, not because he possesses greater strength or courage, but because of his affinity with them. Likewise, a non-Arab who emulates the Arabs—such people being the best of the non-Arabs—knows better how to address his own non-Arab people than an Arab does. And an Arab who emulates non-Arabs—such people being the lowest among the Arabs—knows better how to address Arabs than a non-Arab does. It is reported in a hadith:

“The best of your non-Arabs are those who emulate your Arabs, and the worst of your Arabs are those who emulate your non-Arabs.”

Thus, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, besieged Tā’if, he bombarded its people with a catapult. He fought them in a manner unlike that in which he fought others in direct battle, as at Badr and elsewhere. Likewise, when the Muslims were besieged in the year of the Trench, they dug a trench, something they had not needed outside a siege. It is said that Salmān advised them to do this, and they accepted his advice because it was a means of carrying out what Allah and His Messenger had commanded.

translated_text:
Allah and His Messenger—that is, anything not commanded as either obligatory or recommended.

As for anything commanded as obligatory or recommended, where that command is established by evidence from the Sharia, it belongs to the religion Allah has prescribed, even if those in authority disagree over some of these matters. This applies whether or not it was practised during the lifetime of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Whatever was done after his death at his command—such as fighting the apostates, the renegade Kharijites, the Persians, the Byzantines and the Turks, expelling the Jews and Christians from the Arabian Peninsula, and other such acts—is part of his Sunnah.

For this reason, ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Azīz used to say:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, established practices whose observance affirms the Book of Allah, brings obedience to Allah to completion, and strengthens adherence to Allah’s religion. No one may change them or entertain the opinion of anyone who opposes them. Whoever follows their guidance is rightly guided; whoever seeks victory through them is granted victory. Whoever opposes them and follows a path other than that of the believers, Allah will leave him to what he has chosen and cause him to enter Hell—an evil destination.”

The Sunnah of his rightly guided caliphs is therefore among the things commanded by Allah and His Messenger. There is detailed evidence from the Sharia for this, which is not appropriate to discuss here.

Thus, just as Allah has explained in His Book how to address the People of the Book and establish the proof against them through the signs He has made clear of Muhammad’s messengership, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; through what their own scriptures contain concerning this and what they have distorted and altered in their religion; and through confirmation of what the messengers before him brought—so that, when a learned and fair-minded person from the People of the Book hears this, he finds it all among the clearest arguments and soundest proofs.

translated_text:
And debate and argument are beneficial only when accompanied by justice and fairness. Otherwise, an unjust person either denies the truth he knows—as do the sophist and the one who distorts revelation through esoteric interpretation—or refuses to listen and examine the means of attaining knowledge, turning away from reflection and reasoning. Just as outward sensory perception is not attained by one who turns away, and carries no weight with one who denies it, so inward perception is not attained by one who turns away from reflection and inquiry. Rather, the seeker of knowledge strives to acquire it through its proper avenues.

For this reason, he is called a diligent striver, just as someone who strives diligently in worship or other pursuits is given that description. As one of the early generations said:

“One who strives diligently among you is but as one at play among them.”

Ubayy ibn Ka‘b and Ibn Mas‘ūd said:

“Moderation in following the Sunnah is better than strenuous effort in religious innovation.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When a judge strives to reach the correct ruling and succeeds, he has two rewards; when he strives but errs, he has one reward.”

Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal said—this is also narrated as a statement traced back to the Prophet, though it is preserved as a statement of Mu‘ādh:

“Devote yourselves to knowledge. Teaching it is a good deed; seeking it is worship; discussing it is glorification of Allah; investigating it is striving in His cause; teaching it to someone who does not know it is charity; and imparting it to those suited to receive it is a means of drawing near to Allah.”

Thus, one who investigates knowledge is described as striving in Allah’s cause.

Since argument is beneficial only when accompanied by justice, Allah Most High said:

“And do not argue with the People of the Scripture except in a way that is best, except for those who commit injustice among them.”

We are therefore not obliged to argue in the best manner with someone who acts unjustly. When knowledge is obtained from those among the People of the Book who have embraced Islam, who know what they possess in their own language and translate it for us into Arabic, it is useful in debating with them and addressing them, as was the practice of ‘Abd Allāh ibn Salām

Hebrew words bear some resemblance to Arabic words, just as words resemble one another through derivation based on phonetically related consonants. I have heard the Torah’s wording in Hebrew from people of the Book who embraced Islam, and found the two languages so remarkably close that I came to understand much of their Hebrew speech merely through my knowledge of Arabic. Its sound meanings are either close to those of the Quran, like them, or identical with them, although the Quran possesses exceptional qualities of expression and meaning.

If someone among them engaged in argument wishes to challenge the Quran on the basis of transmitted evidence or reason—for example, by citing something attributed to the prophets in their scriptures that contradicts what Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought, or something contrary to what Allah has stated in their scriptures, as when they claimed before the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that Allah had commanded them to blacken the adulterer’s face with charcoal rather than stone him—then the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the believers could request the Torah and trustworthy interpreters to read it in Arabic and translate it, such as ‘Abd Allāh ibn Salām and others like him. Likewise, one may read a copy translated into Arabic by trustworthy translators, using Arabic script and wording. Corresponding in their script and conversing in their language are activities of the same kind. Although they may occur together, either may also occur independently of the other—for example, writing Arabic words in Hebrew script or other non-Arabic scripts, or writing non-Arabic words in Arabic script. It has also been said that this suffices.

For this reason, Allah, glorified be He, said:

“All food was lawful for the Children of Israel, except what Israel had forbidden himself before the Torah was revealed. Say, ‘Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful.’”

He thus mentioned that abrogation depends on the divine will and that the later command may be more beneficial and conducive to good. His words, “He guides whom He wills to a straight path,” explain what is more beneficial and conducive to good, while “whom He wills” refers the matter back to His will.

All the speculative theologians rely on some aspect of this verse when they say that religious obligations depend either on divine will alone, as some maintain, or on benefit, as others maintain. On either view, abrogation is possible.

Then He, glorified be He, demonstrated that abrogation had occurred through the Torah’s prohibition of things previously lawful: He had made certain things lawful for Israel, then prohibited them in the Torah. This permission had been established by divine law through a pronouncement. They had not merely deemed those things permissible by retaining their original status, such that withdrawing that permission would not constitute abrogation, as some of them claim. He commanded that the Torah be brought concerning this matter. This is indeed what we have found in it, as converts to Islam from among the People of the Book have related to us on more than one occasion.

The same applies to debating Sabian philosophers, polytheists, and others like them. other than those originally found in them, and the like—then, if he discusses matters unrelated to religion, such as questions of “medicine” and pure “arithmetic” treated in their works, and those who learned from them—such as Muhammad ibn Zakariyyā al-Rāzī, Ibn Sīnā, and other heretical physicians—write material that amounts merely to benefiting from the works of unbelievers and hypocrites in worldly affairs, this is permissible.

This is just as it is permissible to live in their houses, wear their clothes and bear their weapons, or enter into agreements with them to cultivate land, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, did with the Jews of Khaybar. Likewise, when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and Abū Bakr left Mecca as emigrants, they hired “Ibn Urayqit”—a man from Banū al-Dīl—as an expert guide, meaning someone skilled in finding the way. They entrusted him with their lives and their mounts, and arranged to meet him at the cave of Thawr on the third morning. Khuzāʿah, both its Muslims and its unbelievers, were trusted confidants and sincere advisers to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and he accepted their advice. All this is reported in the two Sahīh collections. Abū Tālib also supported and defended the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, despite his polytheism. Such examples are numerous.

Among the polytheists and the People of the Book are trustworthy individuals, as Allah Most High said:

“Among the People of the Book are some who, if you entrust them with a great amount of wealth, will return it to you; and among them are some who, if you entrust them with a single dinar, will not return it to you unless you keep standing over them.”

For this reason, it is permissible to entrust one of them with property, and a Muslim may seek treatment from an unbeliever if he is trustworthy. The leading scholars, including Ahmad and others, expressly stated this, since it involves accepting their accounts of worldly matters within their knowledge and trusting them in those matters. This is permissible provided it does not entail an overriding harm, such as his exercising authority over Muslims, gaining ascendancy over them, or the like. Thus, acquiring medical knowledge from their books is like relying on an unbeliever to find the way or seeking medical treatment from him.

translated_text:
Indeed, this is even better, for they did not write their books for any particular Muslim, such that betrayal might enter into them. There is no need here to rely on any of them and risk betrayal; rather, this is simply benefiting from what they have produced, like clothing, dwellings, farmland, weapons, and the like.

If they discuss matters concerning “religion,” then, if they transmit them from the prophets, they are like the People of the Book in this respect, but worse off. If they make knowledge of these matters dependent on rational inference, then whatever agrees with the Quran is true. Whatever contradicts it, however, is shown to be false by the examples set forth in the Quran, as Allah Most High says:

“They do not bring you any argument but We bring you the truth and the best explanation.”

Thus, the Quran contains both the truth and clear reasoning that demonstrates the invalidity of the reasoning they present. If their statements are undifferentiated but contain truth—as is generally the case with the Sabians who altered their religion, such as “Aristotle” and his followers, and with others who followed them—then the truth is to be accepted and falsehood rejected. Yet even the truth they contain is not set forth as clearly as the truth is in the Quran. This matter therefore depends on knowing the Quran, its meanings, its explanation, and its translation.

Translation and explanation have “three levels”:

The first is translating the wording alone, such as replacing an expression with a synonymous expression. In this kind of translation, you seek to establish that what one group means by its expression is precisely what another group means by theirs. This is useful knowledge, for many people tie a meaning to a particular expression and do not consider it independently of both expressions.

The second is translating and explaining the meaning by giving the listener a clear conception of it. Making the meaning clear to him and enabling him to understand it goes beyond translating the wording. This is like explaining an Arabic book to an Arabic speaker who has heard its Arabic words but has neither grasped nor understood their meanings. A meaning can be made clear by describing the thing itself or something comparable to it: attributes are combined from individual concepts that the listener understands, and this combination represents the meaning, either precisely or approximately.

(The third level is demonstrating its truth and establishing it by mentioning the night and the reasoning that establishes that meaning, either through evidence alone or through evidence that explains the cause of its existence. Here, examples and comparisons may be needed to enable him to accept that meaning as true, just as, at the “second level,” examples are needed to give him a clear conception of it. Merely conceiving it may itself yield knowledge of its truth. If understanding its meaning suffices to accept it as true, no analogy, example, or further evidence is needed.

Once a person knows the Quran in this way, the statements of the People of the Book, the Sabians, and the polytheists—whether they agree with it or contradict it—must likewise be translated in both wording and meaning.

The Quran contains a detailed explanation of everything, as Allah Most High says:

“It is not a fabricated account, but a confirmation of what came before it and a detailed explanation of everything.”

And He says:

“We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of everything.”

It is well known that the Muslim community is commanded to convey the Quran, both its wording and its meaning, just as this was enjoined upon

Translation may require examples to give a clear conception of the meanings, and these then form part of a complete translation.

If, as is well known, most Muslims—indeed, most of those among them who claim scholarly learning—do not carry out the translation, interpretation, and explanation of the Quran, then others are all the more likely to be unable to translate and explain what they possess. For Muslims have a more complete understanding, their Book is more upright in its statements and finer in its discourse, and their language is more expansive. This is especially so when those meanings are not established as true, but contain much falsehood. Translating false meanings and giving a clear conception of them is difficult, because nothing true corresponds to them in every respect.

Thus, if we are asked about something they say, “Is it true or false? And how can the truth and falsehood within it be discerned?” we give a verbal reply supported by argument and evidence, just as the polytheists and the People of the Book used to ask the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about various questions or debate with him, and just as nations used to dispute with their messengers. For many people claim that the revealed Law agrees with philosophy.

An example of this is when they mention “the ten intellects” and “the nine souls,” and say that the first intellect is the first emanation from the Being whose existence is necessary in itself; that it is a necessary consequence of His essence and an effect caused by Him; that the second likewise emanates from the first; and that every celestial sphere has an intellect and a soul.

It is said in reply: Your expression “intellect and soul” belongs to your own terminology and must therefore be translated. Even if the words are Arabic, their meaning must still be translated.

They then say: “Intellect” is the spirit abstracted from matter—that is, the body—and its attachments. They call it an intellect, and also call it “separate.” They call such spirits “entities separate from matter” because they are separate from bodies, just as the human spirit, when it leaves the body, becomes separate from the matter that is the body. “Soul” is the spirit that governs the body, like the human soul while it is in the body. So long as it is in the body, it moves it. When it leaves the body, it becomes pure intellect: that is, it apprehends knowledge without moving any body. These, then, are the intellects and souls.

The account we have given is among the best translations of what is meant by intellect and soul, yet most of them do not grasp this.

They say: We have established a soul for every celestial sphere because its motion is voluntary, and voluntary motion can only proceed from a soul. We have also established an intellect for every soul because the intellect is perfect and has no need of motion, whereas that which moves seeks perfection. There must therefore be something above it on which it is modeled, and something that is its cause.

The references in the Quran and Sunnah to the angels and their multitude are beyond enumeration. Indeed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The heaven creaks, and rightly should it creak: there is not a space four fingers wide in it without an angel standing, sitting, bowing, or prostrating.”

Allah, Most High, says:

“The heavens almost break apart from above them, while the angels glorify their Lord with praise and seek forgiveness for those on earth. Indeed, Allah is the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful.”

Whoever limits their number to ten or nineteen, or claims that the nineteen appointed over Saqar are the intellects and souls, does so out of ignorance of what has come from Allah and His Messenger.

His error in this is evident if the names do not agree in the attributes or magnitude of what they designate, as synonymous terms do. The two things designated agree only in that each is a spirit connected with the heavens. This is merely one of the attributes of the angels of the heavens. Thus, what they have affirmed is only some of

the attributes of some angels. Compared with the angels—their attributes, their magnitude, and their numbers—what they have affirmed is exceedingly little: an even smaller proportion than the prophets acknowledged by the Samaritans represent among all the prophets, for they believe in no prophet after Moses and Joshua. How could it be otherwise, when the only attributes they have affirmed for the angels are what they know from their own selves: mere knowledge for the intellects and voluntary motion for the souls?

It is well known that the angels possess knowledge, states, wills, and deeds that none but the Lord of Majesty can enumerate. The Quran’s descriptions of their glorification and worship of Allah are too numerous to mention here, as in His account of addressing the angels and commanding them to prostrate to Adam. In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah has angels who roam, free of other duties, seeking gatherings of remembrance. When they find a gathering in which Allah is remembered, they sit with those present and surround one another with their wings until they fill the space between themselves and the lowest heaven. “They say, ‘We have come from servants of Yours on earth who glorify You, proclaim Your greatness, declare that none has the right to be worshipped but You, praise You, and ask of You.’

“He says, ‘What do they ask of Me?’

“They say, ‘They ask You for Your Paradise.’

“He says, ‘Have they seen My Paradise?’

“They say, ‘No, O Lord.’

“He says, ‘What would it be like if they saw My Paradise?’

“They say, ‘They also seek Your protection.’

“He says, ‘From what do they seek My protection?’

“They say, ‘From Your Fire.’

“He says, ‘Have they seen My Fire?’

“They say, ‘O Lord, no.’

“He says, ‘What would it be like if they saw My Fire?’

“They say, ‘They also ask Your forgiveness.’

“He then says, ‘I have forgiven them, granted them what they asked for, and protected them from what they sought protection against.’

“They say, ‘O Lord, among them is so-and-so, a servant who frequently sins. He was merely passing by and sat with them.’

“He says, ‘I have forgiven him too. They are people whose companion will not be wretched.’”

In the two Sahīh collections, ‘Urwa reports that ‘Ā’isha told him that she asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “Have you ever experienced a day more difficult than the day of Uhud?”

He replied:

“I have suffered much at the hands of your people. I went on my way, weighed down by sorrow, and did not come to myself until I reached Qarn al-Tha‘ālib. I raised my head and saw a cloud shading me. When I looked, I saw Gabriel within it. “The angel of the mountains called to me and greeted me with peace. Then he said, ‘O Muhammad, it is as you wish. If you wish, I will crush them between al-Akhshabayn, the two mountains.’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Rather, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their descendants people who worship Allah alone, associating nothing with Him.”

In the Sahīh, Anas reports:

“It is as though I can still see the dust rising in the lane of Banū Ghunm from Gabriel’s procession.”

In the two Sahīh collections, ‘Ā’isha reports that al-Hārith ibn Hishām asked, “O Messenger of Allah, how does revelation come to you?”

He replied:

“Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and this is the most difficult form for me. Then it ceases, and I have retained what he said. At other times, the angel appears to me in the form of a man and speaks to me, and I retain what he says.”

The accounts of Gabriel coming to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—sometimes in the form of a Bedouin and sometimes in the form of Dihya al-Kalbī—and repeatedly speaking to him and teaching him to recite are too numerous to recount here.

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Angels take turns among you by night and by day, and they gather at the dawn and afternoon prayers. Then those who spent the night among you ascend, and their Lord asks them—though He knows better than they do—‘In what state did you leave My servants?’ They reply, ‘We left them praying, and we came to them while they were praying.’”

In the two Sahīh collections, ‘Ā’isha reports:

“I stuffed a pillow bearing images for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; it resembled a cushion. He came and stood there, and the expression on his face began to change. I asked, ‘What is the matter, O Messenger of Allah?’

“He said, ‘What is this pillow?’

“I replied, ‘It is a pillow I made for you to recline on.’

“He said, ‘Did you not know that the angels do not enter a house containing an image? Those who make images will be punished on the Day of Resurrection and told, “Give life to what you have created.”’”

And in the two Sahīh collections,

Ibn ‘Abbās reports:

“I heard Abū Talha say, ‘I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say, “Angels do not enter a house containing a dog or an image depicting figures.”’”

Likewise, in the two Sahīh collections, ‘Abd Allah ibn ‘Umar reports:

“Gabriel made a promise to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said, ‘We do not enter a house containing a dog or an image.’”

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The angels pray for each of you as long as he remains in the place where he prayed, saying, ‘O Allah, forgive him; O Allah, have mercy on him,’ provided he does not invalidate his ablution.”

These and similar texts describe the categories of angels, their attributes, and their actions in ways that rule out their being the “intellects and souls” these people describe, or Gabriel being the “active intellect,” or the angels associated with human beings being good faculties and the devils being corrupt faculties, as these people claim.

Moreover, their claim that the intellects and souls—which they identify as angels—are effects caused by Allah, emanating from His Essence as an effect proceeds from its cause, amounts to saying that they are begotten of Allah and that Allah has begotten the angels.

This is something Allah has rejected and declared Himself free of. He has declared its proponent a liar and exposed the falsehood of this claim through His words:

“He neither begets nor was begotten, and there is none comparable to Him.”

The Most High also says:

“Indeed, it is out of their falsehood that they say, ‘Allah has begotten,’ and they are surely liars. Has He chosen daughters over sons? What is the matter with you? How do you judge? Will you not take heed? Or do you have clear authority? Then bring your scripture, if you are truthful.”

And through His words: “And they have assigned partners to Allah

—the jinn—although He created them. And without knowledge they have falsely attributed sons and daughters to Him. Glory be to Him! He is exalted above what they describe.”

And the words of the Most High:

“They say, ‘The Most Merciful has taken a child.’ Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honored servants. They do not speak before He speaks, and they act at His command. He knows what is before them and what is behind them. They intercede only for those with whom He is pleased, and they stand in awe of Him.”

The Most High also says:

“The Messiah would never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels brought near to Him.”

And the Most High says:

“They say, ‘The Most Merciful has taken a child.’ You have indeed uttered something monstrous! The heavens almost rupture at it, the earth splits apart, and the mountains collapse in ruins, because they attribute a child to the Most Merciful. It is not fitting for the Most Merciful to take a child. Everyone in the heavens and the earth will come to the Most Merciful as a servant. He has accounted for them and counted them precisely. Each of them will come to Him alone on the Day of Resurrection.”

He thus declares that they are subjected to Him—that is, subdued, directed, held in servitude, and subjugated. They are not like an effect generated by necessity, whose condition cannot conceivably change. He also declares that they are servants of Allah, not to be likened to Him as an effect is likened to its cause or a child to its parent, as these Sabians claim.

The Most High says:

“They say, ‘Allah has taken a child.’ Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are obedient to Him. He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

He thus declares that He brings about everything by His word “Be,” not through an effect being generated from Him.

Likewise, He says, glorified is He:

“They have assigned partners to Allah—the jinn—although He created them. And without knowledge they have falsely attributed sons and daughters to Him. Glory be to Him! He is exalted above what they describe. He is the Originator of the heavens and the earth. How could He have a child when He has no consort? He created all things, and He has knowledge of all things.”

He thus declares that generation occurs only from two sources, just as a conclusion follows from two premises. The same applies to all other known effects: an effect arises only through the conjunction of whatever completes its cause. No single thing by itself can ever be a cause or a parent. Nothing in this world arises except from two sources, even if these are the agent and that which receives its action, as with fire and wood, or the sun and the earth. From one thing alone, however, nothing proceeds or is generated. The Quran thus makes clear that they have erred in their analogical reasoning concerning causation and generation, in holding that the world proceeds from Him through causation and generation.

Likewise, He says:

“And of all things We created pairs, so that you may take heed”?

This contradicts their assertion that only one thing proceeds from Him.

This fulfills what Allah Most High declares in His words:

“They never bring you an argument without Our bringing you the truth and the best explanation.”

For He has undertaken to do this regarding everyone who departs from following the Messenger. The Most High says:

“Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion to His servant, so that he may be a warner to the worlds.”

(He thus mentions) divine oneness and messengership, continuing up to His words:

“On the Day when the wrongdoer will bite his hands, saying, ‘If only I had taken a path with the Messenger! Woe to me! If only I had not taken so-and-so as a close friend! He led me away from the Reminder after it had come to me.’ And Satan ever forsakes man.”

Everyone who departs from following the Messenger is therefore a wrongdoer to that extent. One who introduces religious innovations is a wrongdoer to the extent that he departs from the Messenger’s sunnah.

“They never bring you an argument without Our bringing you the truth and the best explanation.”

These Sabians have indeed brought an argument, namely their assertion:

“From one, only one can proceed and be generated. The Lord is one, so only one can proceed from Him and be generated from Him.”

Allah therefore brought the truth and the best explanation. He made clear that nothing at all proceeds from or is generated from a single thing, and that nothing has been generated from Him or proceeded from Him. Rather, He created everything, and He created two of every kind, forming a pair. Hence Mujāhid said regarding the even and the odd—as al-Bukhārī records in his Sahīh:

“The even is creation, for every created thing has a counterpart; the odd is Allah, who has no likeness.”

Thus He said:

“How could He have a son when He has no consort?”

For effects proceeding from causes, and things generated among existing beings, necessarily involve two things: one acts like the father, and the other like the receptive mother. They may call these the agent and the recipient, as with the sun and the earth, or fire and wood. As for a single thing proceeding from a single thing, this has no existence whatsoever in reality. Their analogy with rays in relation to the sun, and with sound—such as ringing—in relation to motion and striking, likewise constitutes an argument against them in support of Allah, His Messenger, and the believers.

 فَذَلِكَ لَا بُدَّ فِيهِ مِنْ شَيْئَيْنِ وَهُمَا الشَّمْسُ الَّتِي تَجْرِي مَجْرَى الْأَبِ الْفَاعِلِ وَالْأَرْضِ الَّتِي تَجْرِي مَجْرَى الْأُمِّ الْقَابِلَةِ. وَهِيَ الصَّاحِبَةُ لِلشَّمْسِ. وَكَذَلِكَ الصَّوْتُ لَا يَتَوَلَّدُ إلَّا عَنْ جِسْمَيْنِ يَقْرَعُ أَحَدُهُمَا الْآخَرَ أَوْ يُقْلِعُ عَنْهُ فَيَتَوَلَّدُ الصَّوْتُ الْمَوْجُودُ فِي أَجْسَامِ الْعَالَمِ عَنْ أَصْلَيْنِ يَقْرَعُ أَحَدُهُمَا الْآخَرَ أَوْ يُقْلِعُ عَنْهُ. فَمَهْمَا احْتَجُّوا بِهِ مِنْ الْقِيَاسِ فَاَلَّذِي جَاءَ اللَّهُ بِهِ هُوَ الْحَقُّ وَأَحْسَنُ تَفْسِيرًا وَأَحْسَنُ بَيَانًا وَإِيضَاحًا لِلْحَقِّ وَكَشْفًا لَهُ. وَأَيْضًا فَجَعَلَهَا عِلَّةً تَامَّةً لِمَا تَحْتَهَا وَمُؤَكِّدَةً لَهُ وَمُوجِبَةً لَهُ حَتَّى يَجْعَلُونَهَا مَبَادِئَنَا وَيَجْعَلُونَهَا لَنَا كَالْآبَاءِ وَالْأُمَّهَاتِ وَرُبَّمَا جَعَلُوا الْعَقْلَ هُوَ الْأَبُ وَالنَّفْسُ هِيَ الْأُمُّ.
 وَرُبَّمَا قَالَ بَعْضُهُمْ:
 
" الْوَالِدَانِ "
 الْعَقْلُ وَالطَّبِيعَةُ كَمَا قَالَ صَاحِبُ الْفُصُوصِ فِي قَوْلِ نُوحٍ 
{اغْفِرْ لِي وَلِوَالِدَيَّ}
 أَيْ مَنْ كُنْت نَتِيجَةً عَنْهُمَا وَهُمَا الْعَقْلُ وَالطَّبِيعَةُ. وَحَتَّى يُسَمُّونَهَا الْأَرْبَابَ وَالْآلِهَةَ الصُّغْرَى وَيَعْبُدُونَهَا. وَهُوَ كُفْرٌ مُخَالِفٌ لِمَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ الرُّسُلُ.

If, however, the rays are understood to mean what is reflected onto the earth, then this necessarily involves two things: the sun, which acts as the active father, and the earth, which acts as the receptive mother. The earth is thus the sun’s consort. Likewise, sound is generated only from two bodies, one striking the other or pulling away from it. Thus, the sound found in the bodies of this world is generated from two sources, one striking the other or pulling away from it. Whatever analogy they invoke as evidence, what Allah has brought is the truth and the best explanation—the clearest and most illuminating exposition of the truth.

Moreover, they regard them as a complete cause of what lies beneath them, reinforcing and necessitating it. They even regard them as our originating principles and as our fathers and mothers. Sometimes they make the intellect the father and the soul the mother.

Some of them sometimes say that “the two parents” are the intellect and nature, as the author of al-Fusūs (The Bezels) said concerning Noah’s words:

“Forgive me and my parents.”

That is, those of whom I was the product, namely the intellect and nature. They even call them lesser lords and gods and worship them. This is disbelief, contrary to what the messengers brought.

It was in this sense that some of the early generations described the Sabians as worshipping angels. Likewise, the Arabic translations of their ancient authorities’ writings state that they called them lesser gods and lords, just as they also worshipped the stars. The Quran denies that they are lords or gods, or that they possess anything beyond what belongs to a messenger who acts only upon the command of the one who sent him and intercedes only after being granted permission to intercede.

Allah refuted those among the Arabs, Romans, and other nations who made such claims. He, Most High, said:

“Nor would he command you to take the angels and prophets as lords. Would he command you to disbelieve after you have submitted to Allah?”

And He, Most High, said:

“They say, ‘The Most Merciful has taken a son.’ Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honoured servants.”

“They do not speak before He speaks, and they act by His command.”

And He, Most High, said:

“Say, ‘Call upon those whom you claim to be gods besides Allah. They do not possess even an atom’s weight in the heavens or on earth, nor do they have any share in either, nor does He have any helper among them.’”

“Intercession is of no benefit with Him except for one whom He permits. Then, when fear is lifted from their hearts, they say, ‘What did your Lord say?’ They reply, ‘The truth. And He is the Most High, the Most Great.’”

Some hadiths have already been cited concerning the angels falling unconscious when Allah issues a decree concerning creation or a religious revelation.

And He, Most High, said:

“How many angels there are in the heavens whose intercession avails nothing, except after Allah has given permission for whom He wills and is pleased with.”

And He, Most High, said:

“Rather, they are honoured servants”—and the rest of the verse.

translated_text:
And He, Most High, said:

“We descend only by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs whatever is before us, whatever is behind us, and whatever lies between. Your Lord is never forgetful.”

And He, Most High, said:

“Say, ‘Call upon those whom you claim besides Him. They have no power to remove harm from you or to shift it elsewhere.’”

“Those whom they invoke seek a means of approach to their Lord—which of them will be nearest—and hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, your Lord’s punishment is to be feared.”

The verse was revealed concerning those who invoke angels and prophets. This is not the place for an exhaustive discussion of that matter. For Allah, glorified be He, sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “with concise, comprehensive speech.” The expressions in the Quran are comprehensive and all-encompassing, conveying in universal and general terms what is scattered throughout the speech of others. Moreover, He names each thing in a way that indicates the attribute relevant to the stated and explained judgment, and makes clear how that designation conveys its meaning.

His declaring Himself free of offspring, begetting, and taking a child is more comprehensive and sounder than expressing the denial through the term ʿilla (cause). The original sense of ʿilla concerns change, as with an illness that alters the body’s healthy condition; ʿalīl (ill) is the opposite of healthy.

It has been said that “maʿlūl” is used only in connection with drinking. One says, “He drank water ʿallan baʿda nahalin (a second time after the first),” and ʿallaltuhu means that you gave him a second drink.

As for using the term “ʿilla” for something that necessitates or entails another thing, this belongs to the conventional usage of the scholars of speculative theology. Although these two senses are related to the ordinary linguistic meaning of ʿilla through the notion of change, that relationship is more evident in the term “tawallud” (generation). Hence, it is more common in ordinary speech. People say:

{تَبَارَكَ الَّذِي نَزَّلَ الْفُرْقَانَ عَلَى عَبْدِهِ لِيَكُونَ لِلْعَالَمِينَ نَذِيرًا}
 {الَّذِي لَهُ مُلْكُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ
translated_text:
“Such-and-such results from this matter”; “This generates such-and-such”; and “This or that has resulted from that matter”—speaking of any cause that produces an effect in speech and action. Even natural philosophers speak of “the elements and generated things,” meaning the minerals, plants, and animals generated from the four basic elements: earth, water, air, and fire.

Thus, His denial—glorified be He—that He begets anything entails that nothing is generated from Him. His denial that He takes a child entails that He has not done so with any of His creatures as a mark of honour, and that it is not fitting for Him to accord any of His servants the status of a child.

This refutes the claims of those who assert such things concerning the Messiah and others, those who say:

“We are the children of Allah,”

and those who say, “Philosophy is becoming like God.” A child is of the same kind as its parent and is its counterpart, even though it is an offshoot of it. Hence, those who affirm these ideas are among the most extreme of all people in asserting resemblance and equivalence to Him, assigning Him rivals, and equating others with Him and placing them on a par with Him.

Thus, the philosophers who maintain that intellects and souls emanate from Him through generation and causation make them His rivals and take them as gods and lords. Indeed, they may worship only them and invoke none besides them, regarding them as the originators of everything else beneath them.

So praise be to Allah, who has not taken a child and has no partner in His dominion. And:

“Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion to His servant, so that he may be a warner to all the worlds.”

“He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth

original_footnote: (١) بهامش الأصل هنا متروك محل خمسة أسطر. قال في المسودة: يتلوه الوريقة، ولم نجدها
translated_text:
and who has taken no child and has no partner in His dominion, and who created everything and determined it precisely.” (1).

For these people have made the jinn partners with Allah, although He created them, and have falsely attributed sons and daughters to Him without knowledge. It has been said that the term “jinn” includes the angels, as has been said concerning His words:

“They have established a kinship between Him and the jinn.”

Although it has been said, in explaining this, that some Arab polytheists claimed that Allah had entered into marriage ties with the jinn, who then bore the angels, they also worshipped the angels, just as the Sabaean philosophers worshipped them. As the Exalted says:

“They have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, female. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned.”

And the Exalted says:

“And on the Day when He gathers them all together, He will then say to the angels, ‘Was it you that these people used to worship?’”

“They will say, ‘Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not they. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them believed in them.’”

This means that the angels did not command them to do so. Rather, the jinn commanded them to do so, so that they would worship the devils that appear to them in visible forms, just as idols have devils associated with them.

Likewise, devils descend upon some of those who worship the celestial bodies and observe them until an apparition descends upon one of them and speaks to him. It is, in fact, one of the devils.

For this reason, the Exalted says:

“Did I not enjoin upon you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan? Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you.”

“And that you should worship Me? This is a straight path.”

“And he has indeed led astray great multitudes among you

“Will you then take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me, while they are enemies to you? What an evil substitute for the wrongdoers!”

Although they do not intend to worship Satan or ally themselves with him, in reality they worship him and ally themselves with him. It has thus become clear that these Sabaean philosophers, who are proponents of religious innovation, believe in only a little of what the messengers brought concerning the angels—their attributes and their stature.

This is because these people pursued only the path of reasoning from the motions of the celestial spheres and drawing analogies with their own souls, while denying and remaining ignorant of aspects of Allah’s creation and His bringing things into existence.

The reason for this is what a number of those who compiled accounts of them have mentioned: their early leading figures, such as Pythagoras, Socrates and Plato, used to travel to the land of the prophets in Syria and receive teachings from Luqmān the Wise and, after him, from the companions of David and Solomon. Aristotle, however, did not travel to the land of the prophets, nor did he possess the knowledge of the surviving prophetic teachings that his predecessors possessed. He had only a small measure of sound Sabaean belief, so he invented these syllogistic teachings for them. They became a framework followed by his adherents. At times, he happened to speak correctly about the natures of bodies or the form of logic.

“As for the earlier thinkers,” they are not known to have had a complete, innovated doctrinal system comparable to those of the proponents of innovation among Muslim speculative theologians, such as Abū al-Hudhayl, Hishām ibn al-Hakam and others like them who devised a doctrinal system

For the leading scholars of the Muslims—such as Mālik, Hammād ibn Zayd, al-Thawrī and others like them—spoke only of what the revealed message brought, wherein lie guidance and healing. Those who have no knowledge of the Muslims’ path substitute the teachings of these people for it. This is what causes religious innovations to emerge in every community: the ways of the messengers become obscured among them, and destruction ensues.

For this reason, they used to say: Holding firmly to the Sunnah is salvation. Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

“The Sunnah is like Noah’s Ark: whoever boards it is saved, and whoever stays behind perishes.”

This is true. Only those who believed the messengers and followed them boarded Noah’s Ark, while those who did not board it had rejected the messengers. Following the Sunnah means following the message that came from Allah. Thus, one who follows it is, inwardly and outwardly, like one who boarded the Ark with Noah. Whoever fails to follow the message is like one who failed to follow Noah, peace be upon him, and board the Ark with him.

Likewise, when a knowledgeable believer reflects on the various doctrines containing error and disbelief held by philosophers and other peoples, he finds that the Quran and Sunnah reveal their true condition, clarify whatever truth they contain, and distinguish their truth from their falsehood.

The Companions were the most knowledgeable of all people concerning this, just as they were the most steadfast in waging jihad against the disbelievers and hypocrites. As Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd said of them:

“Whoever among you wishes to follow an example should follow those who have died, for no living person can be considered safe from trials. This combination is rare among later generations, as reflected in the saying, “Among the rarities are a jurist who is a Sufi and a scholar who is an ascetic,” and similar remarks. Those whose hearts are righteous, whose intentions are good, and whose aims are sound are praised because their hearts are free of blameworthy desires. Yet they often lack knowledge and an understanding of people’s actual circumstances—an understanding that calls for condemning evil, forbidding it, and waging jihad in Allah’s cause. Those who delve deeply into the sciences, on the other hand, may acquire such knowledge of evils and specious arguments that it leads them into various forms of error and misguidance. The Companions of Muhammad, however, had the most righteous hearts and the deepest knowledge of all people.

Moreover, among most of those in later generations who delve deeply into knowledge, whether speculative theologians or devotees, this depth is accompanied by blameworthy affectation: speaking and acting without knowledge, and pursuing what cannot be attained. The Companions of Muhammad, despite being the most accomplished of all people in beneficial knowledge and righteous deeds, were the least given to affectation. One of them would utter a word or two of wisdom or insight through which Allah would guide an entire community. This is among Allah’s favors to this community. Others, by contrast, fill pages with contrived statements and extravagant utterances that rank among the worst needless innovations and invented opinions. Their only precedent in this was the follies of the soul inherited from those whose intentions in religion were corrupt.

 مَنْ يَعْمَلْ لِي إلَى غُرُوبِ الشَّمْسِ عَلَى قِيرَاطَيْنِ قِيرَاطَيْنِ؟ فَعَمِلَتْ الْمُسْلِمُونَ. فَغَضِبَتْ الْيَهُودُ وَالنَّصَارَى.
 وَقَالُوا:
 نَحْنُ أَكْثَرُ عَمَلًا وَأَقَلُّ أَجْرًا؟
 قَالَ:
 فَهَلْ ظَلَمْتُكُمْ مِنْ حَقِّكُمْ شَيْئًا؟
 قَالُوا:
 لَا قَالَ: فَهُوَ فَضْلِي أوتيه مَنْ أَشَاءُ}
 . فَدَلَّ الْكِتَابُ وَالسُّنَّةُ عَلَى أَنَّ اللَّهَ يُؤْتِي أَتْبَاعَ هَذَا الرَّسُولِ مِنْ فَضْلِهِ مَا لَمْ يُؤْتِهِ لِأَهْلِ الْكِتَابَيْنِ قَبْلَهُمْ فَكَيْفَ بِمَنْ هُوَ دُونَهُمْ مِنْ الصَّابِئَةِ؟ دَعْ مُبْتَدِعَةَ الصَّابِئَةِ مِنْ الْمُتَفَلْسِفَةِ وَنَحْوِهِمْ.
translated_text:
It is related that Allah, glorified be He, said to the Messiah:

“I shall create a community that I shall favor above every other community, though it has neither knowledge nor forbearance.” The Messiah said, “My Lord, how will You favor them above all other communities when they have neither knowledge nor forbearance?” He said, “I shall bestow upon them from My knowledge and My forbearance.”

This is among the distinctive blessings of following the Messenger. The more closely a person follows him, the more fully he attains this blessing. As Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger. He will grant you a double portion of His mercy, provide you with a light by which you may walk, and forgive you. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

“So that the People of the Scripture may know that they have no control over any of Allah’s bounty, and that bounty is in Allah’s hand: He grants it to whom He wills. And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.”

Likewise, the two Sahīh collections contain the reports narrated by Abū Mūsā and ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar:

“The parable of us and the nations before us is that of a man who hired workers. He said, ‘Who will work for me until midday for one qīrāt each?’ The Jews worked. Then he said, ‘Who will work for me until the afternoon prayer for one qīrāt each?’ The Christians worked. Then he said, ‘Who will work for me until sunset for two qīrāts each?’ The Muslims worked. The Jews and Christians became angry and said, ‘We have done more work for less pay!’ He said, ‘Have I withheld anything that was your due?’ They said, ‘No.’ He said, ‘Then this is my bounty, which I grant to whom I will.’”

Thus, the Quran and the Sunnah show that Allah grants the followers of this Messenger bounty that He did not grant the adherents of the two Scriptures before them. What, then, of those among the Sabians who rank below them, let alone the innovators among the Sabians—the philosophizers and their like?

original_text:
وَمِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ:
 أَنَّ أَهْلَ الْحَدِيثِ وَالسُّنَّةِ أَخَصُّ بِالرَّسُولِ وَأَتْبَاعِهِ.
 فَلَهُمْ مِنْ فَضْلِ اللَّهِ وَتَخْصِيصِهِ إيَّاهُمْ بِالْعِلْمِ وَالْحِلْمِ وَتَضْعِيفِ الْأَجْرِ مَا لَيْسَ لِغَيْرِهِمْ كَمَا قَالَ بَعْضُ السَّلَفِ:
 
" أَهْلُ السُّنَّةِ فِي الْإِسْلَامِ كَأَهْلِ الْإِسْلَامِ فِي الْمِلَلِ "
. فَهَذَا الْكَلَامُ تَنْبِيهٌ عَلَى مَا يَظُنُّهُ أَهْلُ الْجَهَالَةِ وَالضَّلَالَةِ مِنْ نَقْصِ الصَّحَابَةِ فِي الْعِلْمِ وَالْبَيَانِ أَوْ الْيَدِ وَالسِّنَانِ. وَبَسْطُ هَذَا لَا يَتَحَمَّلُهُ هَذَا الْمَقَامُ.
 وَالْمَقْصُودُ:
 التَّنْبِيهُ عَلَى أَنَّ كُلَّ مَنْ زَعَمَ بِلِسَانِ حَالِهِ أَوْ مَقَالِهِ: أَنَّ طَائِفَةً غَيْرَ أَهْلِ الْحَدِيثِ أَدْرَكُوا مِنْ حَقَائِقِ الْأُمُورِ الْبَاطِنَةِ الْغَيْبِيَّةِ فِي أَمْرِ الْخَلْقِ وَالْبَعْثِ وَالْمَبْدَأِ وَالْمَعَادِ وَأَمْرِ الْإِيمَانِ بِاَللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ وَتَعَرُّفِ وَاجِبِ الْوُجُودِ وَالنَّفْسِ النَّاطِقَةِ وَالْعُلُومِ وَالْأَخْلَاقِ الَّتِي تَزْكُو بِهَا النُّفُوسُ وَتَصْلُحُ وَتَكْمُلُ دُونَ أَهْلِ الْحَدِيثِ فَهُوَ - إنْ كَانَ مِنْ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ بِالرُّسُلِ - فَهُوَ جَاهِلٌ فِيهِ شُعْبَةٌ قَوِيَّةٌ مِنْ شُعَبِ النِّفَاقِ وَإِلَّا فَهُوَ مُنَافِقٌ خَالِصٌ مِنْ الَّذِينَ 
{وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمْ آمِنُوا كَمَا آمَنَ النَّاسُ قَالُوا أَنُؤْمِنُ كَمَا آمَنَ السُّفَهَاءُ أَلَا إنَّهُمْ هُمُ السُّفَهَاءُ وَلَكِنْ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ}
 وَقَدْ يَكُونُ مِنْ 
{الَّذِينَ يُجَادِلُونَ فِي آيَاتِ اللَّهِ بِغَيْرِ سُلْطَانٍ أَتَاهُمْ}
 وَمِنْ 
{وَالَّذِينَ يُحَاجُّونَ فِي اللَّهِ مِنْ بَعْدِ مَا اسْتُجِيبَ لَهُ حُجَّتُهُمْ دَاحِضَةٌ عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ وَعَلَيْهِمْ غَضَبٌ وَلَهُمْ عَذَابٌ شَدِيدٌ}
 . وَقَدْ يَبِينُ ذَلِكَ بِالْقِيَاسِ الْعَقْلِيِّ الصَّحِيحِ الَّذِي لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ - وَإِنْ كَانَ ذَلِكَ ظَاهِرًا بِالْفِطْرَةِ لِكُلِّ سَلِيمِ الْفِطْرَةِ - فَإِنَّهُ مَتَى كَانَ الرَّسُولُ أَكْمَلَ الْخَلْقِ وَأَعْلَمَهُمْ
translated_text:
It is well known that the people of hadith and the Sunnah have the closest ties to the Messenger and his followers. They therefore enjoy Allah’s favor, His singling them out for knowledge and forbearance, and multiplied rewards in a measure not granted to others. As one of the early generations said:

“The people of the Sunnah stand within Islam as the people of Islam stand among the religions.”

These remarks draw attention to what ignorant and misguided people imagine to be the Companions’ shortcomings in knowledge and exposition, or in strength and prowess in battle. This is not the place for a detailed treatment of the matter.

The point is to emphasize that anyone who claims, through his conduct or his words, that a group other than the people of hadith has grasped hidden, unseen realities that the people of hadith have not—concerning creation and resurrection, the beginning and the final return, faith in Allah and the Last Day, knowledge of the Necessary Existent and the rational soul, and the knowledge and moral qualities through which souls are purified, reformed, and perfected—is, if he believes in the messengers, an ignorant person with a pronounced trait of hypocrisy. Otherwise, he is an outright hypocrite, among those described in the words:

“When it is said to them, ‘Believe as the people have believed,’ they say, ‘Should we believe as the foolish have believed?’ Indeed, it is they who are the foolish, but they do not know.”

He may also be among “those who dispute concerning Allah’s signs without any authority having come to them,” and among those described in the words:

“As for those who argue concerning Allah after He has been acknowledged, their argument is invalid before their Lord; wrath is upon them, and a severe punishment awaits them.”

This can also be demonstrated through sound rational reasoning that admits of no doubt—even though it is evident by natural disposition to everyone whose disposition is sound. For if the Messenger is the most perfect of all creation and the most knowledgeable

original_text:
بِالْحَقَائِقِ وَأَقْوَمَهُمْ قَوْلًا وَحَالًا:
 لَزِمَ أَنْ يَكُونَ أَعْلَمُ النَّاسِ بِهِ أَعْلَمَ الْخَلْقِ بِذَلِكَ وَأَنْ يَكُونَ أَعْظَمُهُمْ مُوَافَقَةً لَهُ وَاقْتِدَاءً بِهِ أَفْضَلَ الْخَلْقِ.
 وَلَا يُقَالُ:
 هَذِهِ الْفِطْرَةُ يُغَيِّرُهَا مَا يُوجَدُ فِي الْمُنْتَسِبِينَ إلَى السُّنَّةِ وَالْحَدِيثِ مِنْ تَفْرِيطٍ وَعُدْوَانٍ لِأَنَّهُ يُقَالُ: إنَّ ذَلِكَ فِي غَيْرِهِمْ أَكْثَرُ وَالْوَاجِبُ مُقَابَلَةُ الْجُمْلَةِ بِالْجُمْلَةِ فِي الْمَحْمُودِ وَالْمَذْمُومِ هَذِهِ هِيَ الْمُقَابَلَةُ الْعَادِلَةُ. وَإِنَّمَا غَيْرُ الْفِطْرَةِ قِلَّةُ الْمَعْرِفَةِ بِالْحَدِيثِ وَالسُّنَّةِ وَاتِّبَاعِ ذَلِكَ مَعَ مَا يُوجَدُ فِي الْمُخَالِفِينَ لَهَا مِنْ نَوْعِ تَحْقِيقٍ لِبَعْضِ الْعِلْمِ وَإِحْسَانٍ لِبَعْضِ الْعَمَلِ. فَيَكُونُ ذَلِكَ شُبْهَةً فِي قَبُولِ غَيْرِهِ وَتَرْجِيحِ صَاحِبِهِ. وَلَا غَرَضَ لَنَا فِي ذِكْرِ الْأَشْخَاصِ. وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ أَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ بْنُ قُتَيْبَةَ فِي أَوَّلِ كِتَابِ 
" مُخْتَلِفِ الْحَدِيثِ "
 وَغَيْرُهُ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ مَا لَا يُحْصَى مِنْ الْأُمُورِ الْمُبَيِّنَةِ لِمَا ذَكَرْنَاهُ.
 وَإِنَّمَا الْمَقْصُودُ:
 ذِكْرُ نَفْسِ الطَّرِيقَةِ الْعِلْمِيَّةِ وَالْعَمَلِيَّةِ الَّتِي تُعْرَفُ بِحَقَائِقِ الْأُمُورِ الْخَبَرِيَّةِ النَّظَرِيَّةِ وَتُوَصِّلُ إلَى حَقَائِقِ الْأُمُورِ الْإِرَادِيَّةِ الْعَمَلِيَّةِ. فَمَتَى كَانَ غَيْرُ الرَّسُولِ قَادِرًا عَلَى عِلْمٍ بِذَلِكَ أَوْ بَيَانٍ لَهُ أَوْ مَحَبَّةٍ لِإِفَادَةِ ذَلِكَ؟ فَالرَّسُولُ أَعْلَمُ بِذَلِكَ وَأَحْرَصُ عَلَى الْهُدَى وَأَقْدَرُ عَلَى بَيَانِهِ مِنْهُ. وَكَذَلِكَ أَصْحَابُهُ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ وَأَتْبَاعُهُمْ.
 وَهَذِهِ صِفَاتُ الْكَمَالِ وَالْعِلْمِ وَالْإِرَادَةِ وَالْإِحْسَانِ وَالْقُدْرَةِ عَلَيْهِ كَمَا قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي دُعَاءِ الِاسْتِخَارَةِ:
translated_text:
of realities and the most upright in speech and conduct, it follows that those who know him best are the most knowledgeable of all creation concerning those realities, and that those who conform most closely to him and follow his example are the best of all creation.

One should not object: “This natural disposition is altered by the negligence and transgression found among those who identify with the Sunnah and hadith.” The answer is that these failings are more prevalent among others. What is required is to compare each group as a whole with the other, considering both praiseworthy and blameworthy qualities. This is the just comparison. What alters this natural disposition is limited knowledge of hadith and the Sunnah and insufficient adherence to them, coupled with the degree of rigor in certain areas of knowledge and excellence in certain actions found among those who oppose them. These merits then become a misleading basis for accepting a person’s other views and giving him preference. We have no interest in naming individuals. Abū Muhammad ibn Qutaybah, at the beginning of his book Mukhtalif al-Hadīth (Conflicting Hadith Reports), and other scholars have mentioned countless matters in this connection that illustrate what we have said.

The aim is simply to describe the method of knowledge and action itself: the method by which the realities of matters addressed through reports and theoretical inquiry are understood, and the realities of matters involving will and action are attained. Whenever someone other than the Messenger possesses knowledge of these matters, the ability to explain them, or a desire to impart that knowledge, the Messenger knows more about them, is more eager to provide guidance, and is better able to explain them than that person. The same applies to his Companions after him and to their followers.

These are the qualities of perfection: knowledge, will, doing good, and the ability to do so, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the supplication for seeking Allah’s guidance in making a choice:

original_text:
{اللَّهُمَّ إنِّي أَسْتَخِيرُك بِعِلْمِك وَأَسْتَقْدِرُك بِقُدْرَتِك وَأَسْأَلُك مِنْ فَضْلِك الْعَظِيمِ. فَإِنَّك تَقْدِرُ وَلَا أَقْدِرُ وَتَعْلَمُ وَلَا أَعْلَمُ وَأَنْتَ عَلَّامُ الْغُيُوبِ}
 . فَعَلَّمَنَا صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنْ نَسْتَخِيرَ اللَّهَ بِعِلْمِهِ فَيُعَلِّمَنَا مَنْ عِلْمِهِ مَا نَعْلَمُ بِهِ الْخَيْرَ وَنَسْتَقْدِرَهُ بِقُدْرَتِهِ فَيَجْعَلَنَا قَادِرِينَ.
 إذْ الِاسْتِفْعَالُ هُوَ طَلَبُ الْفِعْلِ كَمَا قَالَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ الصَّحِيحِ:
 يَقُولُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى: 
{يَا عِبَادِي كُلُّكُمْ جَائِعٌ إلَّا مَنْ أَطْعَمْته فَاسْتَطْعِمُونِي أُطْعِمْكُمْ يَا عِبَادِي: كُلُّكُمْ ضَالٌّ إلَّا مَنْ هَدَيْته فَاسْتَهْدُونِي أَهْدِكُمْ}
 . فَاسْتِهْدَاءُ اللَّهِ طَلَبُ أَنْ يَهْدِيَنَا وَاسْتِطْعَامُهُ طَلَبُ أَنْ يُطْعِمَنَا هَذَا قُوتُ الْقُلُوبِ وَهَذَا قُوتُ الْأَجْسَامِ وَكَذَلِكَ اسْتِخَارَتُهُ بِعِلْمِهِ وَاسْتِقْدَارُهُ بِقُدْرَتِهِ.
 ثُمَّ قَالَ:
 
{وَأَسْأَلُك مِنْ فَضْلِك الْعَظِيمِ}
 فَهَذَا السُّؤَالُ مِنْ جُودِهِ وَمَنِّهِ وَعَطَائِهِ وَإِحْسَانِهِ الَّذِي يَكُونُ بِمَشِيئَتِهِ وَرَحْمَتِهِ وَحَنَانِهِ.
 وَلِهَذَا قَالَ:
 
{فَإِنَّك تَقْدِرُ وَلَا أَقْدِرُ وَتَعْلَمُ وَلَا أَعْلَمُ}
 وَلَمْ يَقُلْ: إنِّي لَا أَرْحَمُ نَفْسِي؛ لِأَنَّهُ فِي مَقَامِ الِاسْتِخَارَةِ يُرِيدُ الْخَيْرَ لِنَفْسِهِ وَيَطْلُبُ ذَلِكَ. لَكِنَّهُ لَا يَعْلَمُهُ وَلَا يَقْدِرُ عَلَيْهِ إنْ لَمْ يُعْلِمْهُ اللَّهُ إيَّاهُ وَيُقَدِّرْهُ عَلَيْهِ.
 فَإِذَا كَانَ الرَّسُولُ أَعْلَمُ الْخَلْقِ بِالْحَقَائِقِ الْخَبَرِيَّةِ وَالطَّلَبِيَّةِ وَأَحَبَّ الْخَلْقِ لِلتَّعْلِيمِ وَالْهِدَايَةِ وَالْإِفَادَةِ وَأَقْدَرَ الْخَلْقِ عَلَى الْبَيَانِ وَالْعِبَارَةِ:
 امْتَنَعَ أَنْ يَكُونَ مَنْ هُوَ دُونَهُ أَفَادَ خَوَاصَّهُ مَعْرِفَةَ الْحَقَائِقِ أَعْظَمَ مِمَّا أَفَادَهَا الرَّسُولُ لِخَوَاصِّهِ؛
translated_text:
“O Allah, I seek Your guidance in making a choice by Your knowledge, and I seek ability from You by Your power, and I ask You of Your immense bounty. For You have power and I do not; You know and I do not; and You are the Knower of all that is unseen.”

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus taught us to seek Allah’s guidance by His knowledge, so that He teaches us from His knowledge what enables us to recognize what is good, and to seek ability from Him by His power, so that He makes us able.

The Arabic form istif‘āl expresses a request for an action, as in the authentic hadith in which Allah Most High says:

“O My servants, all of you are hungry except those whom I have fed. So ask Me to feed you, and I shall feed you. O My servants, all of you are astray except those whom I have guided. So ask Me for guidance, and I shall guide you.”

Seeking Allah’s guidance means asking Him to guide us, and seeking food from Him means asking Him to feed us. The former is nourishment for the hearts, and the latter nourishment for the bodies. The same applies to seeking His guidance in making a choice by His knowledge and seeking ability from Him by His power.

Then he said:

“And I ask You of Your immense bounty.”

This is a request for His generosity, favor, gifts, and kindness, which He bestows through His will, mercy, and compassion.

That is why he said:

“For You have power and I do not; You know and I do not.”

He did not say, “I have no compassion for myself,” because a person seeking guidance in making a choice desires good for himself and asks for it. Yet he neither knows what that good is nor has the ability to attain it unless Allah makes it known to him and enables him to attain it.

If, then, the Messenger is the most knowledgeable of all creation about realities pertaining to what is reported and what is sought, the most eager of all creation to teach, guide, and impart knowledge, and the most capable of all creation in explanation and expression, then it is impossible that anyone below him should have imparted to his own close followers a greater knowledge of these realities than the Messenger imparted to his own close followers;
