Section

As for the statement, “The Hashwiyya are of two kinds: one does not shrink from hashw, likening Allah to creation, or ascribing a body to Him; the other conceals itself behind the way of the early generations. Yet the way of the early generations consists only of affirming Allah’s oneness and declaring Him free of imperfection, not likening Him to creation or ascribing a body to Him”—all proponents of innovation likewise claim this for themselves. As the poet said:

Each claims a bond of love with Laylā,
Yet Laylā acknowledges none of their claims.

This statement contains both truth and falsehood. Among its true elements is the condemnation of those who liken Allah to His creatures and regard His attributes as being of the same kind as theirs.

Allah Most High has said:

“There is nothing like Him.”

And He Most High has said:

“Nor is there to Him any equivalent.”

And He has said:

“Do you know of any equal to Him?”

We have discussed this at length and presented the rational proofs indicated by the Book of Allah that negate such likeness. We have explained aspects of this that the deniers of the divine attributes, who present themselves as upholding Allah’s freedom from imperfection, have not mentioned—arguments neither found in their books nor heard from their leading authorities. Indeed, most of the arguments they offer are weak, because they seek to establish both truth and falsehood; no consistently valid proof can therefore be established for that

—a proof free of flaws—unlike the case of someone who is measured in what he says and strives to speak rightly. Allah will set his deeds right, as He Most High says:

“O you who have believed, fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice.”

“He will amend for you your deeds and forgive you your sins.”

Another element of truth in his statement is its indication that those who claim to follow the way of the early generations should be refuted when they are ignorant of their teachings or depart from them through additions or omissions. Likening Allah to His creation and falsely attributing statements to the early generations are reprehensible, whether or not this is called hashw. This applies to many extremists among those who affirm the divine attributes and transmit fabricated hadiths concerning them, such as the report about “the sweat of horses”; “His descent late on the day of ‘Arafah upon a dark-grey camel, to shake hands with those on foot and embrace those riding”; “His manifesting Himself to His Prophet on earth”; “his seeing Him on a chair between heaven and earth”; “his seeing Him during circumambulation”; or “in some of the lanes of Medina”—and other fabricated hadiths of this kind.

I have seen examples of this that rank among the gravest abominations and acts of disbelief. Several people have brought me booklets and books containing such fabrications against Allah and His Messenger. Chains of transmission have been fabricated for these hadiths. Indeed, one of them took a book written by Shaykh Abū al-Faraj al-Maqdisī concerning the criteria by which a follower of the Sunnah is distinguished from an adherent of innovation, and presented it as something Allah had revealed to His Prophet on the night of the Ascension, commanding him to test people by it: whoever accepted it was a follower of the Sunnah, and whoever did not was an adherent of innovation. They also added to it things that Shaykh Abū al-Faraj had never said, nor would any rational person say.

The point is that his words contain some truth, but also several falsehoods.

First: His statement, “He does not shy away from hashw and corporealism,” condemns people using labels for which Allah has revealed no authority. The One whose praise confers honor and whose condemnation brings disgrace is Allah. Labels that carry religious praise or blame must be those for which Allah has revealed His authority and which are established by the Quran, the Sunnah, or scholarly consensus, such as believer and disbeliever, learned and ignorant, moderate and deviant.

As for these “three expressions,” they occur neither in Allah’s Book nor in any hadith from Allah’s Messenger. Nor did any of the early generations of this community or its leading scholars use them, whether to deny or affirm them. The first to introduce their use as terms of condemnation were the “Muʿtazilah,” who parted from the main body of Muslims. Following the path of the Muʿtazilah rather than that of the community’s early generations means abandoning the upright speech required in religion and following the path of misguided innovators.

Of these expressions, the only one whose condemnation is reported from some of the early generations is “likening Allah to His creation.” Had he confined himself to that expression, he would have had a precedent among the righteous early generations. Had he mentioned the descriptions that Allah negates in the Quran, such as “equal, rival, and namesake,” and said, “Some of them do not shy away from asserting a likeness between Allah and His creation, or the like,” he would have condemned a statement that Allah negates in His Book and whose proponent the Quran shows to be blameworthy. It would then remain to consider whether the person making that statement actually deserves the blame attributed to him.

If you condemn all those who affirm the attributes, including your predecessors and others, you are left with none but the Jahmiyya: the Muʿtazila and those among the later Ashʿarīs and others who agree with them in denying the scripturally attested attributes. Yet you have offered no argument that can be relied upon. If, however, you do not include those who affirm the scripturally attested attributes under the label “al-Hashwiyya,” this statement does not help you. Indeed, you yourself have espoused this position elsewhere. If a person’s words leave him no alternative but to condemn either himself or his predecessors—whose standing as leading scholars he acknowledges, and whom he recognizes as superior to their followers—then, in either case, this condemnation falls upon him.

He would also share something of the character of the Khawārij, to the first of whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“You would indeed be ruined and at a loss if I did not act justly.”

That is to say: if you acknowledge that I am Allah’s Messenger, yet claim that I act unjustly, then you are ruined and at a loss. Likewise, anyone who condemns those whom he acknowledges to be the finest and best members of the Muslim community, and from whom his own group received its knowledge and faith, is ruined and at a loss through this condemnation. Such is the condition of the Rāfida in their condemnation of the Companions.

translated_text:
The third point concerns his statement:

“The other hides behind the doctrine of the early generations.”

If by “hiding” you mean concealing adherence to the doctrine of the early generations, the response is this: that doctrine is kept concealed only in lands dominated by people of religious innovation, such as the lands of the Rāfida and the Khawārij. An oppressed believer there may conceal his faith and his adherence to the Sunnah, just as the believer from Pharaoh’s household concealed his faith, and as many believers concealed theirs while living in the territory of war. If these people are in a land where you wield authority, and they have concealed their adherence to the doctrine of the early generations, then you have condemned yourself, since you belong to a group among whom that doctrine must be concealed. If you yourself are among the oppressed who conceal their adherence to it, there is no sense in condemning yourself. If you belong neither to them nor to the ruling elite, there is no justification for condemning people by describing them as “hiding.”

If, however, by “hiding” you mean that they use it as a shield, protect themselves from others through it, and openly profess it, so that when one of them is addressed, he says, “I follow the doctrine of the early generations”—and this is what he intended, and Allah knows best—then the response to him is this:

There is no fault in someone openly professing the doctrine of the early generations, identifying with it, and declaring his allegiance to it. Rather, by unanimous agreement, this must be accepted from him, for the doctrine of the early generations can only be true.

If he conforms to it both inwardly and outwardly, he is like the believer who follows the truth both inwardly and outwardly. If he conforms to it only outwardly, but not inwardly, he is like the hypocrite: his outward profession is accepted, and his inner state is left to Allah. We have not been commanded to probe people’s hearts or cut open their bellies.

 وَأَمَّا التَّوْحِيدُ الَّذِي بَعَثَ اللَّهُ بِهِ الرُّسُلَ وَأَنْزَلَ بِهِ الْكُتُبَ:
 فَلَيْسَ هُوَ مُتَضَمِّنًا شَيْئًا مِنْ هَذِهِ الِاصْطِلَاحَاتِ بَلْ أَمَرَ اللَّهُ عِبَادَهُ أَنْ يَعْبُدُوهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا يُشْرِكُوا
translated_text:
As for his statement:

“The doctrine of the early generations consists solely of affirming divine oneness and transcendence, not attributing a body to Allah or likening Him to creation.”

The response to him is this: the terms “divine oneness,” “divine transcendence,” “likening Allah to creation,” and “attributing a body to Allah” have acquired multiple meanings because dialectical theologians and others use different technical conventions. Each group means something by these terms that others do not.

The Jahmiyya among the Mu'tazila and other groups mean by “divine oneness and transcendence” the denial of all attributes, and by “attributing a body to Allah and likening Him to creation” the affirmation of any of them. Thus, anyone who says, “Allah sees,” or “He possesses knowledge,” is, in their view, someone who likens Allah to creation and attributes a body to Him.

Many dialectical theologians who affirm the divine attributes mean by divine oneness and transcendence the denial of all or some of the attributes known from scriptural reports, and by attributing a body to Allah and likening Him to creation the affirmation of all or some of those attributes.

The philosophers mean by divine oneness what the Mu'tazila mean, and more besides. They even say that He has only an attribute of negation, an attribute of relation, or one combining the two.

The Ittihādiyya (proponents of the unity of existence) mean by divine oneness that He is absolute existence. Others have still other technical usages for this term.

As for the divine oneness with which Allah sent the messengers and revealed the scriptures, it includes none of these technical usages. Rather, Allah commanded His servants to worship Him alone and associate no partners

 وَأَمَّا أَهْلُ الْحَدِيثِ:

translated_text:
with Him whatsoever. Thus, no one besides Him may have any share in the worship and its attendant acts that belong exclusively to Him. This concerns deeds. As for words, it consists in believing in the attributes with which He has described Himself and with which His Messenger has described Him.

If you mean that the doctrine of the early generations is divine oneness in the sense conveyed by the Quran and Sunnah, then this is true. Those who affirm the divine attributes known from scriptural reports do not disagree with this.

But if you mean that the doctrine of the early generations is divine oneness and transcendence as certain groups understand them, then anyone who examines the reliably transmitted statements of the early generations, preserved in collections of their reports, knows this to be false. Not a single statement from any of the early generations agrees with the distinctive positions of these groups, nor does a single statement deny the divine attributes known from scriptural reports.

It is well known that if the doctrine of the early generations is to be established through transmission from them, then one must refer to the reports transmitted from them. But if it is to be established solely through inference, whereby anyone who considers a view correct says:

“This is the view of the early generations, because the early generations say only what is correct, and this is correct,”

then this is precisely what emboldens each of the proponents of religious innovation to claim that he follows the doctrine of the early generations. Whoever makes this statement has exposed his own fault: he has claimed adherence to their doctrine without transmitting anything from them, relying instead on his assertion that his own view is the truth.

As for the scholars of hadith, they describe the doctrine of the early generations only through mass-transmitted reports

translated_text:
, citing the Muslim scholars who transmitted their doctrine, and at other times relating their actual words on this subject, as we did in our response to the request for a fatwa.

When we sought to explain the doctrine of the early generations, we presented two methods:

First, we cited as many of their statements as were available, identifying the scholars who transmitted them through accepted chains of transmission.

Second, we identified those who transmitted the doctrine of the early generations from all the various Muslim groups: the four schools of jurisprudence, the scholars of hadith, the Sufis, and the speculative theologians, such as al-Ashʿarī and others. Thus, the doctrine of the early generations was transmitted unanimously by these groups and through mass transmission. We did not establish it merely by claiming that we were right and our opponents were wrong, as the proponents of religious innovation do.

Furthermore, the term “tajsīm” (corporealism) does not occur in the statements of any of the early generations, whether in denial or affirmation. How, then, can it be permissible to say that the doctrine of the early generations consists in denying or affirming corporealism, when neither this term nor its meaning has been reported from them?

Likewise, the term “divine oneness,” in the sense of denying any of the attributes, does not occur in the statements of any of the early generations. Nor does the term “transcendence,” in the sense of denying any of the divine attributes known from scriptural reports, occur in the statements of any of the early generations.

(الْوَجْهُ الرَّابِعُ)
 أَنَّ هَذَا الِاسْمَ لَيْسَ لَهُ ذِكْرٌ فِي كِتَابِ اللَّهِ وَلَا سُنَّةِ رَسُولِهِ وَلَا كَلَامِ أَحَدٍ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَالتَّابِعِينَ وَلَا مِنْ أَئِمَّةِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَلَا شَيْخٍ أَوْ عَالِمٍ
translated_text:
The term “likening” does, however, occur in the statements of some of them, together with their explanation of it, as we have recorded from them. By “likening,” they meant likening Allah to His creation, not denying the attributes found in the Quran and hadith. Furthermore, even if this statement were true in itself, it would still lack any supporting proof that ought to be followed. It is merely an assertion made in the course of a dispute—something easily offered by anyone who considers it permissible and commendable to speak without knowledge or justice.

It also reveals little familiarity with the views of either the people of the Sunnah or the proponents of religious innovation, for he said:

“Likewise, all proponents of religious innovation claim that they follow the doctrine of the early generations.”

This is not the case. Rather, groups notorious for religious innovation, such as the Kharijites and the Rafidites, do not claim to follow the doctrine of the early generations. Indeed, they declare most of the early generations to be disbelievers. The Rafidites disparage Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, the majority of the earliest pioneers among the Emigrants and the Helpers, those who followed them in righteousness, and the other leading scholars of Islam. How, then, can they claim to follow the doctrine of the early generations? Instead, they falsely and slanderously claim adherence to the doctrine of the Prophet’s household. Likewise, the Kharijites declared ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, and the majority of Muslims among the Companions and their successors to be disbelievers. How, then, can they claim to follow the doctrine of the early generations?

(The fourth point)

This designation is not mentioned in the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger, or the statements of any of the Companions, their successors, the leading scholars of Islam, or any shaykh or scholar

Since that is not the case, condemning people by this designation has no basis in a scriptural text, scholarly consensus, or any authority whom laypeople may legitimately follow. When such condemnation has no foundation for either scholars exercising independent judgment or those who follow scholarly authority generally, it is utterly unsound and unjust. Even if someone whom certain laypeople could legitimately follow were to condemn others by this designation, that would not constitute proof, since another layperson following an authority whom he may legitimately follow cannot be condemned on that basis. Moreover, Abū Muhammad and others like him did not consider it permissible to pronounce on many subsidiary questions of jurisprudence merely by following scholarly authority. How, then, could he permissibly pronounce on the fundamentals of religion on that basis?

The crux of the matter is this:

Anyone who condemns others by this designation is either exercising independent scholarly judgment or following scholarly authority. The former must have a scriptural text, scholarly consensus, or evidence derived from either, for condemnation and praise are judgments governed by the revealed law. We have already explained this and stated that praise and condemnation, love and hatred, promises of reward and threats of punishment, allegiance and enmity, and similar religious judgments are valid only when based on designations for which Allah has revealed authority. Making such judgments dependent on invented designations is impermissible; indeed, it amounts to instituting a religion for which Allah has given no permission. We also explained that one must know the limits of what Allah has revealed to His Messenger.

The Muʿtazilites likewise declare groups among the Companions and their successors to be sinners. They disparage many of them and the hadiths they transmitted that contradict their views and desires. Indeed, they also declare to be disbelievers those among the earlier and later generations who oppose the principles they have adopted. Thus, their disparagement extends to the scholars of

Professing adherence to the doctrine of the early generations is not one of their distinguishing marks, even though they affirm the caliphate of the four caliphs. They also revere leading scholars of Islam, and the majority of them, in a way that those other groups do not. Yet their disparagement of many of these scholars is beyond the scope of this discussion.

“As for al-Nazzām,” his disparagement of the Companions is likewise beyond the scope of this discussion.

Even if these proponents of religious innovation disparaged the early generations partly because of shortcomings and transgressions among those claiming adherence to them, and because some of them exercised independent scholarly judgment in matters where the correct view lay elsewhere, such occurrences became a trial for their opponents, leading them far astray.

The point here is that the groups commonly known among the people of the Sunnah and the community for religious innovation do not profess adherence to the early generations. Indeed, the group most notorious for religious innovation is the Rafidites, to the extent that ordinary people recognize no distinguishing mark of religious innovation other than Rafidism. In their usage, a Sunni is anyone who is not a Rafidite. This is because, more than any other group, the Rafidites oppose the Prophetic hadiths and the meanings of the Quran, disparage the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars, and attack the majority of the community. Since they are furthest from following the early generations, they are the most notorious for religious innovation.

Thus, it is clear that the distinguishing mark of the proponents of religious innovation is their failure to profess adherence to the way of the early generations. Hence Imam Ahmad said in the epistle transmitted by ‘Abdūs ibn Mālik:

“The foundations of the Sunnah, according to us, are to adhere to the way of the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

translated_text:
As for the dialectical theologians who affirm the divine attributes—the Kullābīs, Karrāmīs, and Ashʿarīs—along with the jurists, Sufis, and hadith scholars, these generally do not disparage the early generations. Indeed, they may agree with them on most of the broad outlines of their teachings. Yet the more knowledgeable any of them is about hadith, the better he understands the doctrine of the early generations and the more closely he follows it. Each group’s reverence for the early generations is proportionate to its adherence to the Sunnah and the scarcity of religious innovation within it.

As for the claim that professing adherence to the early generations is a distinguishing mark of the proponents of religious innovation, this is categorically false. Such a situation is possible only where ignorance is widespread and knowledge scarce.

This is illustrated by the fact that many of Abū Muhammad’s associates among the followers of Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī explicitly acknowledge their disagreement with the early generations—for example, concerning faith and the reinterpretation of Quranic verses and hadiths. They say:

“The doctrine of the early generations is that faith consists of speech and action, and that it increases and decreases. As for the dialectical theologians among our associates, their doctrine is such-and-such.”

Likewise, they say:

“The doctrine of the early generations is that these verses and hadiths concerning the divine attributes are not to be reinterpreted. The dialectical theologians, however, advocate reinterpreting them, regarding this as either obligatory or permissible.”

They mention the disagreement between the early generations and their associates who practise dialectical theology. This is what their tongues declare and their books record. Is there no discerning person who will take heed, no deluded person who will desist?

That position is established as belonging to the early generations, even by the explicit admission of their opponents. Then a doctrine arises that departs from their position. Does this not explicitly imply that the early generations had gone astray concerning monotheism and Allah’s freedom from imperfection, while later generations came to understand these matters? This is necessarily false in light of sound knowledge and firmly grounded religion.

translated_text:
Moreover, dialectical theologians sometimes defend the positions of the early generations and sometimes those of the dialectical theologians, as several of them do, including Abū al-Maʿālī al-Juwaynī, Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī, al-Rāzī, and others. Yet whichever doctrine they defend on a given occasion is, by implication, the one to be relied upon. Thus, they do not remain steadfast upon a single religious position, and doubts overwhelm them. This is Allah’s customary way with those who turn away from the Quran and Sunnah.

At other times, they regard their later brethren as more adept and knowledgeable than the early generations, saying:

“The way of the early generations is safer, but the way of these later scholars is more knowledgeable and wiser.”

They thus credit their brethren with superiority in knowledge, exposition, rigorous inquiry, and understanding, while attributing to the early generations deficiency and shortcomings in these matters, or error and ignorance. The most they will do for the early generations is offer excuses for their shortcomings and neglect.

There is no doubt that this is a form of Rāfidī rejectionism. Although it does not amount to declaring the early generations unbelievers—as some of the Rāfidīs and Khārijites do—or declaring them morally corrupt—as some of the Muʿtazilīs, Zaydīs, and others do—it does amount to declaring them ignorant, mistaken, and misguided, and attributing sins and acts of disobedience to them. Even if this falls short of imputing moral corruption, it still amounts to claiming that the people of generations deemed inferior by the revealed Law are more knowledgeable and virtuous than those of the generations deemed superior.

For anyone who reflects upon the Quran and Sunnah and upon the consensus of all the groups belonging to Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah, it is necessarily known that the best generation of this community—in deeds, words, beliefs, and every other virtue—is the first generation, then

translated_text:
those who follow them, then those who follow them—as has been established through multiple reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and that they surpass the later generations in every virtue: knowledge, deeds, faith, intellect, religion, exposition, and worship, and are better qualified to explain every difficult matter. No one denies this except someone who obstinately disputes what is necessarily known to be part of Islam and whom Allah has led astray with knowledge. As Abdullāh ibn Masūd, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“Whoever among you wishes to follow an example should follow those who have died, for the living are not safe from trials. Those are the Companions of Muhammad: those of this community with the most righteous hearts, the deepest knowledge, and the least affectation. They are people whom Allah chose to accompany His Prophet and establish His religion. So recognize their due and hold fast to their guidance, for they followed upright guidance.”

Another said:

“Adhere to what has been handed down from those who came before, for they brought what suffices and heals. No hidden good unknown to them has emerged since their time.”

Moreover, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No time comes but that the one after it is worse, until you meet your Lord.”

How, then, could an age come upon us that is better with regard to the greatest object of knowledge—namely, knowledge of Allah Most High? This can never happen.

How well al-Shāfiī, may Allah have mercy on him, expressed it in his Epistle:

“They surpass us in all knowledge, intellect, religion, virtue, and every means by which knowledge is attained or guidance grasped. Their judgments for us are better than our own judgments for ourselves.”

Furthermore, these Jahmī Kullābīs—such as Abū Muhammad, the author of this statement, and others like him—may be asked: How can you abandon the way of the early generations when the highest attainment of the early generations is to be

in agreement with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace?

Indeed, most of the knowledge and faith possessed by the early generations came from their Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through whom Allah brought them out of darkness into the light and guided them to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy. Concerning him, Allah said:

“It is He who sends down clear verses upon His servant to bring you out of darkness into the light.”

And He Most High said:

“O you who believe, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger. He will grant you a double portion of His mercy, provide you with a light by which to walk, and forgive you. Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

“So that the People of the Book may know that they have no power over any of Allah’s bounty.”

And He Most High said:

“Allah has certainly bestowed a favor upon the believers by sending among them a Messenger from among themselves, reciting His verses to them, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, although before that they were clearly astray.”

And He Most High said:

“And thus We have revealed to you a spirit by Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was, but We have made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. Indeed, you guide to a straight path.”

“The path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth.”

Abū Muhammad and others like him have followed the path of the heretics who say that the Messenger did not explain the truth concerning monotheism, nor explain to people how things truly are. Rather, he presented to people the opposite of the truth; as for the truth itself, he either concealed it or did not know it.

For these heretics among the philosophers, and those who follow their path in opposing what the Messenger brought concerning matters of knowledge—such as monotheism, the Hereafter, and the like—say that the Messenger perfected practical matters relating to ethics and to household and civic governance

translated_text:
to Alexander, son of Philip of Macedon, from whom the Jews and Christians reckon the Roman era. He lived about three hundred years before Christ. They may suppose that he was “Dhū al-Qarnayn” (the Two-Horned One) mentioned in the Quran, and that Aristotle was a minister to the Dhū al-Qarnayn mentioned in the Quran. This is ignorance. For this Alexander, son of Philip, did not reach the lands of the Turks or build the barrier; he reached only the lands of the Persians.

Dhū al-Qarnayn, who is mentioned in the Quran, reached the eastern and western reaches of the earth and lived before this Alexander. It is said that his name was Alexander, son of Dārā. He was a believer who worshipped Allah alone, whereas the other was a polytheist: he and his people worshipped the stars and idols and practised sorcery. Likewise, Aristotle and his fellow Greeks were polytheists who worshipped idols and practised sorcery. They wrote works on these subjects; the accounts of them are well known, and the traces they left plainly attest to this. What comparison can there be between the two?

The purpose here is to explain what these esoteric philosophers say about what the Messenger brought.

And (the second group among them say that the Messenger knew the actual truth concerning divine oneness and the resurrection. They say he knew that the Lord has no affirmative attribute, that He is not seen and does not speak; that the celestial spheres are eternal and beginningless, having always existed and continuing forever; that bodies will not rise again; and that Allah has no angels who are living, speaking beings descending with revelation

For, if these beliefs were made known, their minds and hearts would not accept them; instead, they would reject them and recoil from them. He therefore presented them with imagery and similitudes that would benefit them in their religion, even though this involved misleading them, keeping them ignorant, and causing them to believe things contrary to their actual reality, because of the benefit this would bring them.

They take as imams the leaders of the esoteric sects, such as the descendants of Ubayd ibn Maymūn al-Qaddāh, who claimed descent from Muhammad ibn Ismā‘īl ibn Ja‘far. They were not his descendants; rather, their ancestor was a Jew who was the stepson of a Magian, and they professed Shiism outwardly. In reality, they did not adhere to the creed of any Shia group: neither the Imāmīs nor the Zaydīs, nor even the extremists who believe in Alī’s divinity or prophethood. Rather, they were worse than all these groups. Hence Muslim scholars wrote numerous works exposing their secrets and tearing away their veils, and Muslims undertook many military campaigns against them. Their history is well known. Ibn Sīnā and his household were followers of these people during the reign of their Egyptian ruler. This was why Ibn Sīnā embraced philosophy.

These people regard Muhammad ibn Ismā‘īl as the concealed imam and maintain that he abrogated the religious law of Muhammad ibn Abd Allāh ibn Abd al-Muttalib. They say that these Ismā‘īlīs were infallible imams. Indeed, they may say that they are superior to the prophets, and they may say that they are gods to be worshipped. in Syria; he led the people of that region astray, and remnants of his following remain among them to this day, professing the divinity of al-Hākim. He led them out of Islam, so they do not recognize the obligation of the five daily prayers, fasting the month of Ramadan, or pilgrimage to the Sacred House, nor do they acknowledge the prohibition of what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, such as carrion, blood, pork, wine, and other things. These people initially invite anyone who responds to their call to embrace Shiism, observe what the Rāfidīs deem obligatory, and regard as forbidden what they forbid.

They then lead him, step by step, until they finally bring him to abandon Islam altogether and to believe that the aim is to learn their secrets—the knowledge through which the soul attains perfection, as the heretical philosophers maintain. Whoever acquires this knowledge has reached the ultimate goal: the acts of worship incumbent upon ordinary people, such as the five daily prayers, fasting Ramadan, and pilgrimage to the House, are no longer obligatory for him, and forbidden things that remain unlawful for others become lawful for him.

Thus, when these people exalt the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and say that his knowledge was perfect, they place him in the same category as their heretical leaders, claiming that he presented the common people with teachings contrary to those he concealed for the elite. Elsewhere we have explained the falsity of their claims in a discussion beyond the scope of the present occasion.

The point here is that those who deny Allah’s being above creation and His attributes known through revelation, such as the author of al-Lumʿa and others like him, make claims about the Messenger similar to theirs: what he openly taught was not the actual truth, because he could not disclose that truth to the common people. translated_text:
they say this about the Messenger himself, what, then, do they say about his followers “among the early generations of the Muslim community”—the Companions and the Successors?

Anyone whose fundamental position concerning the Messenger and the earliest forerunners among the Emigrants and the Helpers is of this kind is opposing them, not agreeing with them. This is especially so if he openly professes the denial which, in his view, the Messenger and his closest Companions concealed rather than proclaimed: in this respect too, he would be opposing them. This approach is adopted by most of those who negate the divine attributes, such as Ibn Rushd the Younger and others. A substantial amount of this also appears in the writings of Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī. Ibn ʿAqīl and others like him sometimes say this as well. However, when Ibn ʿAqīl departed from the Sunnah early in his life, his predominant tendency was toward Jahmism and Muʿtazilism. His later position was different, for he came to embrace the pure Sunnah.

Abū Hāmid inclined toward philosophy, but presented it in the guise of Sufism and Islamic expressions. For this reason, Muslim scholars refuted him, including even his closest disciple, Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī, who said:

“Our shaykh, Abū Hāmid, became deeply immersed in the philosophers’ thought, then tried to break free of them, but could not.”

He has also been reported to have professed doctrines of the Bātiniyya (esotericists), and corroboration of these reports can be found in his books. The scholars mentioned earlier refuted him.

Section

The objector then said:

Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī said in his refutation of the Hanbalīs:

“They have affirmed for Allah, glorified be He, an eye, a form, a right and a left, a face in addition to His essence, a forehead, a chest, two hands, two legs, fingers, a little finger, a thigh, a shin, a foot, a side, a waist, a back and a front, ascending, descending, hurrying, and 'ujb. They have indeed completed the whole bodily form, yet they say: ‘This is to be understood in its apparent sense, but these are not bodily organs.’ People like these should not be addressed, for they defy reason, and it is as though they were speaking to children.”

I say:

This statement must be examined from several perspectives:

First: exposing the partisanship marked by ignorance and injustice that it contains, before discussing the substantive scholarly question.

Second: showing that it is a refutation entirely devoid of argument or evidence.

Third: showing the weakness of its transmitted material and its reasoning.

As for the “first” point: Abū al-Faraj did not compose the work from which his words were quoted

فِي الرَّدِّ عَلَى الْحَنَابِلَةِ كَمَا ذَكَرَ هَذَا وَإِنَّمَا رَدَّ بِهِ - فِيمَا ادَّعَاهُ - عَلَى بَعْضِهِمْ. وَقَصْدَ أَبا عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ حَامِدٍ وَالْقَاضِي أَبا يَعْلَى وَشَيْخِهِ أَبا الْحَسَنِ بْنِ الزَّاغُونِي وَمَنْ تَبِعَهُمْ؛ وَإِلَّا فَجِنْسُ الْحَنَابِلَةِ لَمْ يَتَعَرَّضْ أَبُو الْفَرَجِ لِلرَّدِّ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا حَكَى عَنْهُمْ مَا أَنْكَرَهُ؛ بَلْ هُوَ يَحْتَجُّ فِي مُخَالَفَتِهِ لِهَؤُلَاءِ بِكَلَامِ كَثِيرٍ مِنْ الْحَنْبَلِيَّةِ كَمَا يَذْكُرُهُ مِنْ كَلَامِ التَّمِيمِيِّينَ. مِثْلَ رِزْقِ اللَّهِ التَّمِيمِيِّ وَأَبِي الوفا بْنِ عَقِيلٍ.
 وَرِزْقُ اللَّهِ كَانَ يَمِيلُ إلَى طَرِيقَةِ سَلَفِهِ كَجَدِّهِ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ التَّمِيمِيِّ وَعَمِّهِ أَبِي الْفَضْلِ التَّمِيمِيِّ وَالشَّرِيفِ أَبِي عَلِيِّ بْنِ أَبِي مُوسَى هُوَ صَاحِبُ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ التَّمِيمِيِّ وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ عَنْهُ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
" لَقَدْ خري الْقَاضِي أَبُو يَعْلَى عَلَى الْحَنَابِلَةِ خرية لَا يَغْسِلُهَا الْمَاءُ "
 وَسَنَتَكَلَّمُ عَلَى هَذَا بِمَا يُيَسِّرُهُ اللَّهُ مُتَحَرِّينَ لِلْكَلَامِ بِعِلْمِ وَعَدْلٍ.
 وَلَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إلَّا بِاَللَّهِ:
 فَمَا زَالَ فِي الْحَنْبَلِيَّةِ مَنْ يَكُونُ مَيْلُهُ إلَى نَوْعٍ مِنْ الْإِثْبَاتِ الَّذِي يَنْفِيهِ طَائِفَةٌ أُخْرَى مِنْهُمْ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يُمْسِكُ عَنْ النَّفْيِ وَالْإِثْبَاتِ جَمِيعًا. فَفِيهِمْ جِنْسُ التَّنَازُعِ الْمَوْجُودِ فِي سَائِرِ الطَّوَائِفِ لَكِنَّ نِزَاعَهُمْ فِي مَسَائِلِ الدَّقِّ؛ وَأَمَّا الْأُصُولُ الْكِبَارُ فَهُمْ مُتَّفِقُونَ عَلَيْهَا وَلِهَذَا كَانُوا أَقَلَّ الطَّوَائِفِ تَنَازُعًا وَافْتِرَاقًا لِكَثْرَةِ اعْتِصَامِهِمْ بِالسُّنَّةِ وَالْآثَارِ لِأَنَّ لِلْإِمَامِ أَحْمَدَ فِي بَابِ أُصُولِ الدِّينِ مِنْ الْأَقْوَالِ الْمُبَيِّنَةِ لِمَا تَنَازَعَ فِيهِ النَّاسُ مَا لَيْسَ لِغَيْرِهِ. وَأَقْوَالُهُ مُؤَيَّدَةٌ بِالْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ وَاتِّبَاعِ سَبِيلِ السَّلَفِ الطَّيِّبِ. وَلِهَذَا كَانَ جَمِيعُ مَنْ يَنْتَحِلُ السُّنَّةَ مِنْ طَوَائِفِ الْأُمَّةِ - فُقَهَائِهَا وَمُتَكَلِّمَتِهَا وَصُوفِيَّتِهَا - يَنْتَحِلُونَهُ.
translated_text:
as a refutation of the Hanbalīs, as this objector stated. Rather, he intended it—as he claimed—to refute some of them, specifically Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Hāmid, Qādī Abū Ya‘lā, his teacher Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Zāghūnī, and their followers. Abū al-Faraj did not undertake to refute the Hanbalīs as a whole, nor did he attribute to them what he condemned. Indeed, in opposing these men, he cites the statements of many Hanbalīs as evidence, including members of the Tamīmī family, such as Rizq Allāh al-Tamīmī, and Abū al-Wafā’ ibn ‘Aqīl.

Rizq Allāh inclined toward the approach of his predecessors, such as his grandfather Abū al-Hasan al-Tamīmī and his uncle Abū al-Fadl al-Tamīmī. Al-Sharīf Abū ‘Alī ibn Abī Mūsā was a companion of Abū al-Hasan al-Tamīmī. It is reported of him that he said:

“Qādī Abū Ya‘lā has indeed shat on the Hanbalīs—filth that water cannot wash away.”

We shall discuss this as Allah enables us, striving to speak with knowledge and justice. There is no power nor strength except through Allah.

There have always been Hanbalīs who incline toward a form of affirmation that another group among them rejects, while others refrain from both negation and affirmation. Thus, they experience the same kind of disagreement found among all other groups. Their disagreements, however, concern subtle points; as for the major principles, they agree upon them. For this reason, they have had less disagreement and division than other groups, owing to their firm adherence to the Sunnah and transmitted reports. In matters concerning the foundations of religion, Imam Ahmad has statements clarifying disputed questions that no one else possesses. His statements are supported by the Quran and Sunnah and by following the path of the righteous predecessors. Hence, all groups within the Muslim community that profess adherence to the Sunnah—its jurists, speculative theologians, and Sufis—profess adherence to him.

ثُمَّ قَدْ يَتَنَازَعُ هَؤُلَاءِ فِي بَعْضِ الْمَسَائِلِ. فَإِنَّ هَذَا أَمْرٌ لَا بُدَّ مِنْهُ فِي الْعَالِمِ وَالنَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَدْ أَخْبَرَ بِأَنَّ هَذَا لَا بُدَّ مِنْ وُقُوعِهِ وَأَنَّهُ لَمَّا سَأَلَ رَبَّهُ أَنْ لَا يُلْقِي بَأْسَهُمْ بَيْنَهُمْ مُنِعَ ذَلِكَ. فَلَا بُدَّ فِي الطَّوَائِفِ الْمُنْتَسِبَةِ إلَى السُّنَّةِ وَالْجَمَاعَةِ مِنْ نَوْعِ تَنَازُعٍ لَكِنْ لَا بُدَّ فِيهِمْ مِنْ طَائِفَةٍ تَعْتَصِمُ بِالْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ كَمَا أَنَّهُ لَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَكُونَ بَيْنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ تَنَازُعٌ وَاخْتِلَافٌ لَكِنَّهُ لَا يَزَالُ فِي هَذِهِ الْأُمَّةِ طَائِفَةٌ قَائِمَةٌ بِالْحَقِّ لَا يَضُرُّهَا مَنْ خَالَفَهَا وَلَا مَنْ خَذَلَهَا حَتَّى تَقُومَ السَّاعَةُ.

 وَلَمْ يَذْكُرْ فِيهِ أَلْفَاظَهُ وَإِنَّمَا ذَكَرَ جُمَلَ الِاعْتِقَادِ بِلَفْظِ نَفْسِهِ وَجَعَلَ يَقُولُ:
 
" وَكَانَ أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ "
. وَهُوَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ مَنْ يُصَنِّفُ
translated_text:
Yet these people may disagree over certain questions, for this is inevitable in the world. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, foretold that this would inevitably occur, and that when he asked his Lord not to let them turn their violence against one another, his request was denied. Thus, some disagreement is inevitable among groups professing adherence to the Sunnah and the community. Nevertheless, there must be among them a group that holds firmly to the Quran and Sunnah. Likewise, although disputes and differences inevitably arise among Muslims, there will always remain within this nation a group upholding the truth, unharmed by those who oppose or abandon them, until the Hour comes.

Accordingly, since Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī and his followers professed adherence to the Sunnah and the community, he professed allegiance to Imam Ahmad, stating that he took him as his example and followed his path. The agreement and harmonious relations between his leading followers and many followers of Imam Ahmad are well known. Indeed, Abū Bakr ‘Abd al-‘Azīz cited Abū al-Hasan’s arguments in his discussions just as he cited those of his own fellow adherents, because he regarded him as one of their speculative theologians.

Among those most strongly inclined toward them were members of the Tamīmī family: Abū al-Hasan al-Tamīmī, his son, his grandson, and others like them. The affection and companionship between Abū al-Hasan al-Tamīmī and Qādī Abū Bakr ibn al-Bāqillānī were well known and widely recognized. For this reason, when the hadith scholar Abū Bakr al-Bayhaqī discussed Imam Ahmad’s creed in the book he compiled on his merits, he relied on what he transmitted from the statements of Abū al-Fadl ‘Abd al-Wāhid ibn Abī al-Hasan al-Tamīmī.

Abū al-Fadl also wrote a work on this subject, setting out Ahmad’s creed as he understood it. He did not reproduce Ahmad’s own words, but instead presented the broad statements of his creed in his own wording, repeatedly using the phrase, “And Abū ‘Abd Allāh was.” He is like someone who writes

كِتَابًا فِي الْفِقْهِ عَلَى رَأْيِ بَعْضِ الْأَئِمَّةِ وَيَذْكُرُ مَذْهَبَهُ بِحَسَبِ مَا فَهِمَهُ وَرَآهُ وَإِنْ كَانَ غَيْرُهُ بِمَذْهَبِ ذَلِكَ الْإِمَامِ أَعْلَمَ مِنْهُ بِأَلْفَاظِهِ وَأَفْهَمَ لِمَقَاصِدِهِ؛ فَإِنَّ النَّاسَ فِي نَقْلِ مَذَاهِبِ الْأَئِمَّةِ قَدْ يَكُونُونَ بِمَنْزِلَتِهِمْ فِي نَقْلِ الشَّرِيعَةِ.
 وَمِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ:
 أَنَّ أَحَدَهُمْ يَقُولُ: حُكْمُ اللَّهِ كَذَا أَوْ حُكْمُ الشَّرِيعَةِ كَذَا بِحَسَبِ مَا اعْتَقَدَهُ عَنْ صَاحِبِ الشَّرِيعَةِ؛ بِحَسَبِ مَا بَلَغَهُ وَفَهِمَهُ وَإِنْ كَانَ غَيْرُهُ أَعْلَمَ بِأَقْوَالِ صَاحِبِ الشَّرِيعَةِ وَأَعْمَالِهِ وَأَفْهَمَ لِمُرَادِهِ. فَهَذَا أَيْضًا مِنْ الْأُمُورِ الَّتِي يَكْثُرُ وُجُودُهَا فِي بَنِي آدَمَ. وَلِهَذَا قَدْ تَخْتَلِفُ الرِّوَايَةُ فِي النَّقْلِ عَنْ الْأَئِمَّةِ كَمَا يَخْتَلِفُ بَعْضُ أَهْلِ الْحَدِيثِ فِي النَّقْلِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَكِنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مَعْصُومٌ. فَلَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَصْدُرَ عَنْهُ خَبَرَانِ مُتَنَاقِضَانِ فِي الْحَقِيقَةِ. وَلَا أَمْرَانِ مُتَنَاقِضَانِ فِي الْحَقِيقَةِ إلَّا وَأَحَدُهُمَا نَاسِخٌ وَالْآخَرُ مَنْسُوخٌ. وَأَمَّا غَيْرُ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَلَيْسَ بِمَعْصُومِ. فَيَجُوزُ أَنْ يَكُونَ قَدْ قَالَ خَبَرَيْنِ مُتَنَاقِضَيْنِ. وَأَمْرَيْنِ مُتَنَاقِضَيْنِ وَلَمْ يَشْعُرْ بِالتَّنَاقُضِ. لَكِنْ إذَا كَانَ فِي الْمَنْقُولِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مَا يَحْتَاجُ إلَى تَمْيِيزٍ وَمَعْرِفَةٍ - وَقَدْ تَخْتَلِفُ الرِّوَايَاتُ حَتَّى يَكُونَ بَعْضُهَا أَرْجَحَ مِنْ بَعْضٍ وَالنَّاقِلُونَ لِشَرِيعَتِهِ بِالِاسْتِدْلَالِ بَيْنَهُمْ اخْتِلَافٌ كَثِيرٌ - لَمْ يُسْتَنْكَرْ وُقُوعُ نَحْوٍ مِنْ هَذَا فِي غَيْرِهِ؛ بَلْ هُوَ أَوْلَى بِذَلِكَ. لِأَنَّ اللَّهَ قَدْ ضَمِنَ حِفْظَ الذِّكْرِ الَّذِي أَنْزَلَهُ عَلَى رَسُولِهِ وَلَمْ يَضْمَنْ حِفْظَ مَا يُؤْثَرُ عَنْ غَيْرِهِ. لِأَنَّ مَا بَعَثَ اللَّهُ بِهِ رَسُولَهُ مِنْ الْكِتَابِ وَالْحِكْمَةِ هُوَ هُدَى اللَّهِ الَّذِي جَاءَ مِنْ عِنْدِ اللَّهِ وَبِهِ يُعْرَفُ سَبِيلُهُ وَهُوَ حُجَّتُهُ عَلَى عِبَادِهِ؛

فَلَوْ وَقَعَ فِيهِ ضَلَالٌ لَمْ يُبَيَّنْ لَسَقَطَتْ حُجَّةُ اللَّهِ فِي ذَلِكَ وَذَهَبَ هُدَاهُ وَعَمِيَتْ سَبِيلُهُ؛ إذْ لَيْسَ بَعْدَ هَذَا النَّبِيِّ نَبِيٌّ آخَرُ يُنْتَظَرُ لِيُبَيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ مَا اخْتَلَفُوا فِيهِ؛ بَلْ هَذَا الرَّسُولُ آخِرُ الرُّسُلِ. وَأُمَّتُهُ خَيْرُ الْأُمَمِ. وَلِهَذَا لَا يَزَالُ فِيهَا طَائِفَةٌ قَائِمَةٌ عَلَى الْحَقِّ بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ. لَا يَضُرُّهَا مَنْ خَالَفَهَا وَلَا مَنْ خَذَلَهَا. حَتَّى تَقُومَ السَّاعَةُ.
الْوَجْهُ الثَّانِي:
 أَنَّ أَبَا الْفَرَجِ نَفْسَهُ مُتَنَاقِضٌ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ: لَمْ يَثْبُتْ عَلَى قَدَمِ النَّفْيِ وَلَا عَلَى قَدَمِ الْإِثْبَاتِ؛ بَلْ لَهُ مِنْ الْكَلَامِ فِي الْإِثْبَاتِ نَظْمًا وَنَثْرًا مَا أَثْبَتَ بِهِ كَثِيرًا مِنْ الصِّفَاتِ الَّتِي أَنْكَرَهَا فِي هَذَا الْمُصَنَّفِ. فَهُوَ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ مِثْلُ كَثِيرٍ مِنْ الْخَائِضِينَ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ مِنْ أَنْوَاعِ النَّاسِ يُثْبِتُونَ تَارَةً وَيَنْفُونَ أُخْرَى فِي مَوَاضِعَ كَثِيرَةٍ مِنْ الصِّفَاتِ كَمَا هُوَ حَالُ أَبِي الْوَفَاءِ بْنِ عَقِيلٍ وَأَبِي حَامِدٍ الْغَزَالِيِّ.
الْوَجْهُ الثَّالِثُ:
 أَنَّ بَابَ الْإِثْبَاتِ لَيْسَ مُخْتَصًّا بِالْحَنْبَلِيَّةِ وَلَا فِيهِمْ مِنْ الْغُلُوِّ مَا لَيْسَ فِي غَيْرِهِمْ؛ بَلْ مَنْ اسْتَقْرَأَ مَذَاهِبَ النَّاسِ وَجَدَ فِي كُلِّ طَائِفَةٍ مِنْ الْغُلَاةِ فِي النَّفْيِ وَالْإِثْبَاتِ مَا لَا يُوجَدُ مِثْلُهُ فِي الْحَنْبَلِيَّةِ وَوَجَدَ مَنْ مَالَ مِنْهُمْ إلَى نَفْيٍ بَاطِلٍ أَوْ إثْبَاتٍ بَاطِلٍ
translated_text:
so if error were to enter it and go unexposed, Allah’s proof in that regard would be nullified, His guidance lost, and His path obscured; for no prophet is awaited after this Prophet to clarify for people the matters over which they have differed. Rather, this Messenger is the last of the messengers, and his community is the best of communities. Hence, by Allah’s permission, a group within it will always stand firm upon the truth, unharmed by those who oppose or abandon it, until the Hour comes.

The second point:

Abū al-Faraj himself is inconsistent on this subject: he has maintained neither a consistent position of denial nor one of affirmation. Indeed, in both verse and prose, he has affirmed many of the attributes he denies in this work. In this respect, he resembles many people of various backgrounds who engage in this subject, sometimes affirming and sometimes denying in numerous matters concerning the attributes. Such is also the case with Abū al-Wafā’ ibn ‘Aqīl and Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī.

The third point:

Affirmation is not exclusive to the Hanbalīs, nor do they exhibit forms of excess absent from other groups. Rather, anyone who surveys people’s doctrines will find in every group extremists in denial and affirmation whose like are not found among the Hanbalīs, and will find that any of them who inclines toward an erroneous denial or an erroneous affirmation

فَإِنَّهُ لَا يُسْرِفُ إسْرَافَ غَيْرِهِمْ مِنْ الْمَائِلِينَ إلَى النَّفْيِ وَالْإِثْبَاتِ؛ بَلْ تَجِدُ فِي الطَّوَائِفِ مِنْ زِيَادَةِ النَّفْيِ الْبَاطِلِ وَالْإِثْبَاتِ الْبَاطِلِ مَا لَا يُوجَدُ مِثْلُهُ فِي الْحَنْبَلِيَّةِ. وَإِنَّمَا وَقَعَ الِاعْتِدَاءُ فِي النَّفْيِ وَالْإِثْبَاتِ فِيهِمْ مِمَّا دَبَّ إلَيْهِمْ مِنْ غَيْرِهِمْ الَّذِينَ اعْتَدَوْا حُدُودَ اللَّهِ بِزِيَادَةِ فِي النَّفْيِ وَالْإِثْبَاتِ إذْ أَصْلُ السُّنَّةِ مَبْنَاهَا عَلَى الِاقْتِصَادِ وَالِاعْتِدَالِ دُونَ الْبَغْيِ وَالِاعْتِدَاءِ. وَكَانَ عِلْمُ 
" الْإِمَامِ أَحْمَدَ وَأَتْبَاعِهِ "
 لَهُ مِنْ الْكَمَالِ وَالتَّمَامِ عَلَى الْوَجْهِ الْمَشْهُورِ بَيْنَ الْخَاصِّ وَالْعَامِّ مِمَّنْ لَهُ بِالسُّنَّةِ وَأَهْلِهَا نَوْعُ إلْمَامٍ وَأَمَّا أَهْلُ الْجَهْلِ وَالضَّلَالِ: الَّذِينَ لَا يَعْرِفُونَ مَا بَعَثَ اللَّهُ بِهِ الرَّسُولَ وَلَا يُمَيِّزُونَ بَيْنَ صَحِيحِ الْمَنْقُولِ وَصَرِيحِ الْمَعْقُولِ وَبَيْنَ الرِّوَايَاتِ الْمَكْذُوبَةِ وَالْآرَاءِ الْمُضْطَرِبَةِ: فَأُولَئِكَ جَاهِلُونَ قَدْرَ الرَّسُولِ وَالسَّابِقِينَ الْأَوَّلِينَ مِنْ الْمُهَاجِرِينَ وَالْأَنْصَارِ الَّذِينَ نَطَقَ بِفَضْلِهِمْ الْقُرْآنُ فَهُمْ بِمَقَادِيرِ الْأَئِمَّةِ الْمُخَالِفِينَ لِهَؤُلَاءِ أَوْلَى أَنْ يَكُونُوا جَاهِلِينَ إذْ كَانُوا أَشْبَهَ بِمَنْ شَاقَّ الرَّسُولَ وَاتَّبَعَ غَيْرَ سَبِيلِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ وَالْإِيمَانِ وَهُمْ فِي هَذِهِ الْأَحْوَالِ إلَى الْكُفْرِ أَقْرَبُ مِنْهُمْ لِلْإِيمَانِ: تَجِدُ أَحَدَهُمْ يَتَكَلَّمُ فِي 
" أُصُولِ الدِّينِ وَفُرُوعِهِ "
 بِكَلَامِ مَنْ كَأَنَّهُ لَمْ يَنْشَأْ فِي دَارِ الْإِسْلَامِ وَلَا سَمِعَ مَا عَلَيْهِ أَهْلُ الْعِلْمِ وَالْإِيمَانِ وَلَا عَرَفَ حَالَ سَلَفِ هَذِهِ الْأُمَّةِ وَمَا أُوتُوهُ مِنْ كَمَالِ الْعُلُومِ النَّافِعَةِ وَالْأَعْمَالِ الصَّالِحَةِ وَلَا عَرَفَ مِمَّا بَعَثَ اللَّهُ بِهِ نَبِيَّهُ مَا يَدُلُّهُ عَلَى الْفَرْقِ بَيْنَ الْهُدَى وَالضَّلَالِ وَالْغَيِّ وَالرَّشَادِ.
translated_text:
does not go to the extremes of others who incline toward denial or affirmation. Indeed, among the various groups you will find excesses in erroneous denial and erroneous affirmation whose like are not found among the Hanbalīs. Such transgression in denial and affirmation arose among them only through influences that crept in from others who overstepped Allah’s limits through excessive denial and affirmation. For the Sunnah rests fundamentally upon moderation and balance, not wrongdoing and transgression.

The knowledge possessed by “Imam Ahmad and his followers” was marked by a completeness and comprehensiveness well known to specialists and ordinary people alike who have some familiarity with the Sunnah and its adherents. As for the ignorant and misguided—those who do not know what Allah sent the Messenger with, and cannot distinguish authentic transmitted evidence and clear rational evidence from fabricated reports and confused opinions—they are ignorant of the standing of the Messenger and the earliest forerunners among the Emigrants and Helpers, whose merit the Quran proclaims. They are therefore all the more likely to be ignorant of the standing of the imams who oppose such people, since they more closely resemble those who oppose the Messenger and follow a path other than that of the believers endowed with knowledge and faith. In these circumstances, they are closer to disbelief than to faith.

You find one of them speaking about “the fundamental principles and subsidiary matters of religion” as though he had neither grown up in a Muslim land nor heard the teachings upheld by the people of knowledge and faith; as though he knew nothing of this community’s early generations and the excellence they were granted in beneficial knowledge and righteous deeds, nor knew enough of what Allah sent His Prophet with to distinguish guidance from misguidance, and error from right direction.

وَتَجِدُ وَقِيعَةَ هَؤُلَاءِ فِي 
" أَئِمَّةِ السُّنَّةِ وَهُدَاةِ الْأُمَّةِ "
 مِنْ جِنْسِ وَقِيعَةِ الرَّافِضَةِ وَمَنْ مَعَهُمْ مِنْ الْمُنَافِقِينَ فِي أَبِي بَكْرٍ وَعُمَرَ؛ وَأَعْيَانِ الْمُهَاجِرِينَ وَالْأَنْصَارِ؛ وَوَقِيعَةَ الْيَهُودِ وَالنَّصَارَى وَمَنْ تَبِعَهُمْ مِنْ مُنَافِقِي هَذِهِ الْأُمَّةِ فِي رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَوَقِيعَةَ الصَّابِئَةِ وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ مِنْ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ فِي الْأَنْبِيَاءِ وَالْمُرْسَلِينَ وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ اللَّهُ فِي كِتَابِهِ مِنْ كَلَامِ الْكُفَّارِ وَالْمُنَافِقِينَ فِي الْأَنْبِيَاءِ وَالْمُرْسَلِينَ وَأَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ وَالْإِيمَانِ مَا فِيهِ عِبْرَةٌ لِلْمُعْتَبِرِ؛ وَبَيِّنَةٌ لِلْمُسْتَبْصِرِ؛ وَمَوْعِظَةٌ لِلْمُتَهَوِّكِ الْمُتَحَيِّرِ.
وَتَجِدُ عَامَّةَ أَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ وَمَنْ أَعْرَضَ عَنْ جَادَّةِ السَّلَفِ - إلَّا مَنْ عَصَمَ اللَّهُ - يُعَظِّمُونَ أَئِمَّةَ الِاتِّحَادِ بَعْدَ تَصْرِيحِهِمْ فِي كُتُبِهِمْ بِعِبَارَاتِ الِاتِّحَادِ وَيَتَكَلَّفُونَ لَهَا مَحَامِلَ غَيْرَ مَا قَصَدُوهُ.
 وَلَهُمْ فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ مِنْ الْإِجْلَالِ وَالتَّعْظِيمِ وَالشَّهَادَةِ بِالْإِمَامَةِ وَالْوِلَايَةِ لَهُمْ وَأَنَّهُمْ أَهْلُ الْحَقَائِقِ:
 مَا اللَّهُ بِهِ عَلِيمٌ.
 هَذَا ابْنُ عَرَبِيٍّ يُصَرِّحُ فِي فُصُوصِهِ:
 أَنَّ الْوِلَايَةَ أَعْظَمُ مِنْ النُّبُوَّةِ؛
 بَلْ أَكْمَلُ مِنْ الرِّسَالَةِ وَمِنْ كَلَامِهِ:
 مَقَامُ النُّبُوَّةِ فِي بَرْزَخٍ فُوَيْقَ الرَّسُولِ وَدُونَ الْوَلِيِّ وَبَعْضُ أَصْحَابِهِ يَتَأَوَّلُ ذَلِكَ بِأَنَّ وِلَايَةَ النَّبِيِّ أَفْضَلُ مِنْ نُبُوَّتِهِ وَكَذَلِكَ وِلَايَةُ الرَّسُولِ أَفْضَلُ مِنْ رِسَالَتِهِ أَوْ يَجْعَلُونَ وِلَايَتَهُ حَالَهُ مَعَ اللَّهِ وَرِسَالَتَهُ حَالَهُ مَعَ الْخَلْقِ وَهَذَا مِنْ بَلِيغِ الْجَهْلِ. فَإِنَّ الرَّسُولَ إذَا خَاطَبَ الْخَلْقَ وَبَلَّغَهُمْ الرِّسَالَةَ لَمْ يُفَارِقْ الْوِلَايَةَ بَلْ هُوَ وَلِيُّ
translated_text:
You also find that these people’s attacks on “the imams of the Sunnah and the guides of the community” resemble the attacks of the Rāfidīs and their hypocritical allies on Abū Bakr, Umar, and the leading Emigrants and Helpers; the attacks of the Jews, Christians, and their followers among this community’s hypocrites on the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; and the attacks of the Sabians and polytheists, philosophers and others, on the prophets and messengers. In His Book, Allah has recorded statements made by disbelievers and hypocrites against the prophets and messengers and the people of knowledge and faith. These contain lessons for those who reflect, clear evidence for those who seek insight, and admonition for those who are bewildered and confused.

You find that most speculative theologians and those who have turned away from the path of the early generations—except those whom Allah protects—venerate the leaders of monism even after these men have explicitly expressed monism in their books. They strain to interpret those statements in ways their authors never intended. Allah knows the extent of the reverence and veneration they hold for these men in their hearts, and how readily they attest to their standing as imams and saints, and as masters of spiritual realities.

Here is Ibn Arabī, explicitly declaring in his Fusūs (Bezels) that sainthood is greater than prophethood—indeed, more perfect than messengership. Among his words are:

“Prophethood occupies an intermediate station,
Just above the messenger, yet below the saint.”

Some of his followers interpret this to mean that a prophet’s sainthood is superior to his prophethood, and likewise that a messenger’s sainthood is superior to his messengership. Alternatively, they take his sainthood to be his state in relation to Allah, and his messengership to be his state in relation to creation. This is profound ignorance. For when the messenger addresses creation and conveys the message to them, he does not cease to possess sainthood; rather, he is a friend of

اللَّهِ فِي تِلْكَ الْحَالِ كَمَا هُوَ وَلِيُّ اللَّهِ فِي سَائِرِ أَحْوَالِهِ فَإِنَّهُ وَلِيُّ اللَّهِ لَيْسَ عَدُوًّا لَهُ فِي شَيْءٍ مِنْ أَحْوَالِهِ. وَلَيْسَ حَالُهُ فِي تَبْلِيغِ الرِّسَالَةِ دُونَ حَالِهِ إذَا صَلَّى وَدَعَا اللَّهَ وَنَاجَاهُ.
 وَأَيْضًا:
 فَمَا يَقُولُ هَذَا الْمُتَكَلِّفُ فِي قَوْلِ هَذَا الْمُعَظِّمِ: إنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَبِنَةٌ مِنْ فِضَّةٍ وَهُوَ لَبِنَتَانِ مِنْ ذَهَبٍ وَفِضَّةٍ وَيَزْعُمُ أَنَّ لَبِنَةَ مُحَمَّدٍ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ هِيَ الْعِلْمُ الظَّاهِرُ وَلَبِنَتَاهُ: الذَّهَبُ عِلْمُ الْبَاطِنِ وَالْفِضَّةُ عِلْمُ الظَّاهِرِ وَأَنَّهُ يَتَلَقَّى ذَلِكَ بِلَا وَاسِطَةٍ؛ وَيُصَرِّحُ فِي فُصُوصِهِ أَنَّ رُتْبَةَ الْوِلَايَةِ أَعْظَمُ مِنْ رُتْبَةِ النُّبُوَّةِ لِأَنَّ الْوَلِيَّ يَأْخُذُ بِلَا وَاسِطَةٍ وَالنَّبِيَّ بِوَاسِطَةِ فَالْفَضِيلَةُ الَّتِي زَعَمَ أَنَّهُ امْتَازَ بِهَا عَلَى النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَعْظَمُ عِنْدِهِ مِمَّا شَارَكَهُ فِيهِ.
 وَبِالْجُمْلَةِ:
 فَهُوَ لَمْ يَتْبَعْ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي شَيْءٍ فَإِنَّهُ أَخَذَ بِزَعْمِهِ عَنْ اللَّهِ مَا هُوَ مُتَابِعُهُ فِيهِ فِي الظَّاهِرِ كَمَا يُوَافِقُ الْمُجْتَهِدُ الْمُجْتَهِدَ وَالرَّسُولُ الرَّسُولَ فَلَيْسَ عِنْدَهُ مِنْ اتِّبَاعِ الرَّسُولِ وَالتَّلَقِّي عَنْهُ شَيْءٌ أَصْلًا لَا فِي الْحَقَائِقِ الْخَبَرِيَّةِ وَلَا فِي الْحَقَائِقِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ.
 وَأَيْضًا:
 فَإِنَّهُ لَمْ يَرْضَ أَنْ يَكُونَ مَعَهُ كَمُوسَى مَعَ عِيسَى وَكَالْعَالِمِ مَعَ الْعَالِمِ فِي الشَّرْعِ الَّذِي وَافَقَهُ فِيهِ بَلْ ادَّعَى أَنَّهُ يَأْخُذُ مَا أَقَرَّهُ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ الشَّرْعِ مِنْ اللَّهِ فِي الْبَاطِنِ فَيَكُونُ أَخْذُهُ لِلشَّرْعِ عَنْ اللَّهِ أَعْظَمَ مِنْ أَخْذِ الرَّسُولِ.
translated_text:
Allah in that state, just as he is a friend of Allah in all his other states. He is Allah’s friend, never His enemy in any state. Nor is his state when conveying the message inferior to his state when he prays, supplicates to Allah, and communes with Him.

Moreover, what does this man who strains to interpret his words make of this venerated man’s statement that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is a silver brick, whereas he himself is two bricks, one gold and one silver? He claims that Muhammad’s brick, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, represents outward knowledge, while his own two bricks represent inward knowledge—the gold—and outward knowledge—the silver—and that he receives this without an intermediary. In his Fusūs (Bezels), he explicitly states that the rank of sainthood is greater than the rank of prophethood because the saint receives without an intermediary, whereas the prophet receives through an intermediary. Thus, the distinction by which he claims superiority over the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is, in his estimation, greater than what he shares with him.

In short, he has not followed the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in anything. For he claims to have received from Allah even those things in which he outwardly follows him, just as one jurist exercising independent judgment may agree with another, or one messenger with another. In his view, therefore, he neither follows the Messenger nor receives anything from him at all, whether truths conveyed in revealed reports or truths concerning religious law.

Furthermore, he was not content for his relationship with the Messenger to resemble that of Moses with Jesus, or one scholar with another, regarding the religious law in which he agreed with him. Rather, he claimed that he receives inwardly from Allah the religious law that he acknowledges the Messenger to be correct in teaching. His reception of religious law from Allah would thus be greater than the Messenger’s reception of it.

وَأَمَّا مَا ادَّعَى امْتِيَازَهُ بِهِ عَنْهُ وَافْتِقَارَ الرَّسُولِ إلَيْهِ - وَهُوَ مَوْضِعُ اللَّبِنَةِ الذَّهَبِيَّةِ - فَزَعَمَ أَنَّهُ يَأْخُذُهُ عَنْ الْمَعْدِنِ الَّذِي يَأْخُذُ مِنْهُ الْمَلَكُ الَّذِي يُوحَى بِهِ إلَى الرَّسُولِ. فَهَذَا كَمَا تَرَى فِي حَالِ هَذَا الرَّجُلِ وَتَعْظِيمِ بَعْضِ الْمُتَأَخِّرِينَ لَهُ. وَصَرَّحَ الْغَزَالِيُّ بِأَنَّ قَتْلَ مَنْ ادَّعَى أَنَّ رُتْبَةَ الْوِلَايَةِ أَعْلَى مِنْ رُتْبَةِ النُّبُوَّةِ أَحَبُّ إلَيْهِ مِنْ قَتْلِ مِائَةِ كَافِرٍ لِأَنَّ ضَرَرَ هَذَا فِي الدِّينِ أَعْظَمُ. وَلَا نُطِيلُ الْكَلَامَ فِي هَذَا الْمَقَامِ لِأَنَّهُ لَيْسَ الْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا. وَأَيْضًا فَأَسْمَاءُ اللَّهِ وَأَسْمَاءُ صِفَاتِهِ عِنْدَهُمْ شَرْعِيَّةٌ سَمْعِيَّةٌ لَا تُطْلَقُ بِمُجَرَّدِ الرَّأْيِ فَهُمْ فِي الِامْتِنَاعِ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءِ أَحَقُّ بِالْعُذْرِ مِمَّنْ امْتَنَعَ مِنْ تَسْمِيَةِ صِفَاتِهِ أَعْرَاضًا.
 وَذَلِكَ أَنَّ الصِّفَاتِ الَّتِي لَنَا:
 مِنْهَا مَا هُوَ عَرَضٌ كَالْعِلْمِ وَالْقُدْرَةِ وَمِنْهَا مَا هُوَ جِسْمٌ وَجَوْهَرٌ قَائِمٌ بِنَفْسِهِ كَالْوَجْهِ وَالْيَدِ وَتَسْمِيَةُ هَذِهِ جَوَارِحَ وَأَعْضَاءَ أَخَصُّ مِنْ تَسْمِيَتِهَا أَجْسَامًا لِمَا فِي ذَلِكَ مِنْ مَعْنَى الِاكْتِسَابِ وَالِانْتِفَاعِ وَالتَّصَرُّفِ وَجَوَازِ التَّفْرِيقِ وَالْبَعْضِيَّةِ.
translated_text:
As for that in which he claimed to differ from the Messenger, and which he claimed the Messenger needed—represented by the golden brick—he alleged that he receives it from the very source from which the angel who conveys revelation to the Messenger receives it. Such, as you can see, is this man’s position, yet some later figures venerate him. Al-Ghazālī explicitly stated that killing someone who claims that the rank of sainthood is higher than the rank of prophethood is dearer to him than killing a hundred unbelievers, because the harm such a person does to religion is greater. We shall not dwell on this matter, since it is not our concern here.

Moreover, in their view, the names of Allah and the names of His attributes are established by religious law and transmitted revelation; they may not be applied on the basis of opinion alone. They therefore have greater grounds for being excused for refraining from using these names than those who refrain from calling His attributes “accidents.”

For some of our attributes are accidents, such as knowledge and power, while others are bodies and self-subsisting substances, such as the face and the hand. Calling these “limbs and organs” is more specific than calling them “bodies,” since the former terms imply acquisition, benefit, and action, as well as the possibility of being separated and of constituting parts.

translated_text:
The fourth point:

This question is not confined to these people. Rather, the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading authorities in jurisprudence, hadith, Sufism, and spiritual knowledge agreed on affirming this category of attributes, as did the leading speculative theologians of the Kullābī, Karrāmī, and Ashʿarī schools. All of them affirm for Allah the attributes of the face, the hand, and the like.

Al-Ashʿarī stated in his book al-Maqālāt (The Doctrinal Positions) that this is the position of the scholars of hadith, and declared that he himself held it. In summarizing the position of Ahl al-Sunnah and the scholars of hadith, he wrote:

“The position of Ahl al-Sunnah and the scholars of hadith, in summary, is to affirm such and such; that Allah rose over His Throne; and that He has two hands, without specifying how, as He says:

‘I created with My two hands,’

and as He says:

‘Rather, both His hands are outstretched’;

and that He has two eyes, without specifying how, as He says:

‘Sailing under Our eyes’;

and that He has a face, as He says:

‘And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.’”

We have already explained that all the leading authorities of these groups are among those who affirm the divine attributes. among the scholars of hadith, the Sufis, the Mālikīs, the Shāfiʿīs, the Hanafīs, and others like them. Indeed, this is also found among groups that do not profess adherence to the Sunnah and the community, to hadith, or to the way of the early generations, such as the Shīʿah and others. Among them, both affirmation and negation reach extremes not found among the aforementioned groups.

Likewise, these opposing positions of negation and affirmation are found among the followers of the two Scriptures—the Torah and the Gospel. The Sabians, including philosophers and others, likewise hold opposing positions on negation and affirmation. Some of them even affirm what many speculative theologians who affirm the divine attributes do not affirm. In general, however, affirmation predominates among the followers of the messengers: the believers, the Jews, the Christians, and the rightly guided Sabians. Negation generally predominates among those who do not follow the messengers: the polytheists and the Sabians who introduce religious innovations.

Elsewhere, outside this response, we have set out the position of the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading authorities, quoting their own words and those of the people from all the various groups who transmitted their position. This leaves no group with an exclusive claim to affirming the divine attributes.

One example is what the shaykh of the Two Holy Sanctuaries, Abū al-Hasan Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Malik al-Karajī, mentioned in his book, which he entitled “Chapters on the Fundamentals, Drawn from the Eminent Imams, to Confute Those Given to Innovation and Idle Talk.” He was one of the leading Shāfiʿī authorities. He said:

“Then I wished—and a request from some of the brothers coincided with my wish—to present a summary of their explicit statements, incorporating some of their own wording. Such a summary is easier to memorize and contains the essence of the book. So I sought the help of Him upon whom all reliance rests, and said:

“The explicit statements we have selected fall into two chapters: the first explains the sunnah and its merit; the second concerns shunning innovation and its adherents.

“As for the first chapter, know that the ‘sunnah’ is the way of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Following the sunnah means walking that path and conforming to it. It comprises ‘three categories’: sayings, deeds, and beliefs.

“Sayings include the transmitted formulas of remembrance and glorification of Allah. Deeds include the aforementioned sunnah practices of prayer, fasting, and charity, as well as approved ways of conduct and transmitted manners. These two categories comprise practices that are strongly encouraged and recommended, through which reward and recompense are earned. The third category is the sunnah concerning beliefs, which is one of the foundations of faith.”

He said:

“Now, with Allah’s help, I shall present a summary of what I have transmitted from them in scattered passages, adding material recorded in works on foundational belief that has not reached me from them at all. I shall arrange this material in a carefully prepared form, interweaving some of their explicit statements and using the briefest wording I can, so that it may be easy to memorize for anyone wishing to retain it. I therefore say: Let the follower of the sunnah know that the sunnah concerning beliefs falls into ‘three categories’: one concerns Allah’s names, essence, and attributes; another concerns the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his Companions, and his miracles; and another concerns the people of Islam in this life and the Hereafter.

translated_text:
As for the first category:

Let us believe that Allah has eternal, uncreated names and attributes, conveyed in His Book and reported by the Messenger to his Companions in narrations transmitted by trustworthy narrators and authenticated by reliable hadith critics. The clear Quran and sound, firmly established hadith attest to them.”

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—said:

“They are as follows: Allah Most High is the First, who has always existed, and the Last, who will never cease to exist; the One, the Eternal, the Self-Sufficient, the Generous, the All-Knowing, the Forbearing, the Most High, the Magnificent, the Exalted, the Glorious. His retribution is severe. He originates and restores, and does whatever He wills. He is the Strong, the All-Powerful, the Unassailable, the Helper:

‘There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.’

“And so too His other names and attributes: His Self, face, eye, foot, two hands, knowledge, looking, hearing, sight, will, volition, pleasure, anger, love, laughter, wonder, shyness, protective jealousy, dislike, wrath, grasping, spreading out, nearness, proximity, being above, highness, speech, greeting with peace, utterance, calling, manifestation, meeting, descent, ascent, and rising over the Throne; and that He Most High is in heaven, upon His Throne, distinct from His creation.

“Mālik said: ‘Allah is in heaven, and His knowledge is everywhere.’

“Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak said: ‘We know our Lord to be above His seven heavens, upon the Throne, distinct from His creation. We do not say, as the Jahmiyya say, that He is here’—and he pointed to the earth.

“Regarding ‘And He is with you wherever you are,’ Sufyān al-Thawrī said: ‘His knowledge.’

“Al-Shāfiʿī said: ‘He is upon His Throne in His heaven, drawing near to His creation however He wills.’

and He rises above His Seat. We believe in the Throne and the Seat, and in the verses and reports concerning them. Good words ascend to Him, and the angels and the Spirit ascend to Him. He created Adam with His two hands, created the Pen, the Garden of Eden, and the tree of Tūbā with His two hands, and wrote the Torah with His two hands. Both His hands are right hands.

Ibn Umar said:

‘Allah created four things with His two hands: Adam, the Throne, the Pen, and the Garden of Eden. To the rest of creation He said, “Be,” and it was.’

He speaks revelation however He wills. Āʾisha—may Allah be pleased with her—said:

‘In my own estimation, my affair was too insignificant for Allah to speak concerning me in revelation that would be recited.’

The Quran, in all its aspects, is the speech of Allah, revealed and uncreated. Not a single letter of it is created. It originated from Him and will return to Him. Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak said:

‘Whoever disbelieves in a single letter of the Quran has disbelieved. Whoever says, “I do not believe in this letter lām,” has disbelieved.’

The books revealed to the messengers—one hundred and four books—are the uncreated speech of Allah. Ahmad said:

‘What is in the Preserved Tablet, what is in the written copies of the Quran, and people’s recitation—however it is recited and however it is described—is the uncreated speech of Allah.’

Al-Bukhārī said:

‘I say: The Quran is in the written copy, and the Quran is in men’s hearts. Whoever says otherwise is to be called upon to repent; if he repents, so be it; otherwise, his course is that of disbelief.’”

His Book, and which His Prophet has made known to his community. No one among Allah’s creation against whom the proof has been established may reject them.” He later said:

“Examples include Allah—glorified is He—informing us that He is All-Hearing, All-Seeing; that He has two hands, as He says:

‘Rather, both His hands are outstretched.’

That He has a right hand, as He says:

‘And the heavens will be folded up in His right hand.’

That He has a Face, as He says:

‘Everything will perish except His Face.’

And:

‘And there will remain the Face of your Lord, full of majesty and honour.’

That He has a foot, as stated in the report:

‘Until the Lord places His foot in it’—meaning Hell.

‘He met Allah, who was laughing toward him.’

That He descends every night to the lowest heaven, as reported by the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him; and that He is not one-eyed, as the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said when mentioning the Dajjāl:

‘He is one-eyed, but your Lord is not one-eyed.’

That the believers will see their Lord on the Day of Resurrection with their own eyes, just as they see the moon when it is full; and that He has a finger, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

‘There is no heart except that it is between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful.’”

“My mercy has preceded My wrath.”’ And his saying:

And other such hadiths, whether they alarm us or not, and whether they have reached us or not. Our belief concerning them and the verses pertaining to the divine attributes is that we accept them without distorting them, specifying their manner, denying them, or reinterpreting them. We do not make them conform to reason or liken them to the attributes of created beings. We do not bring our own opinions and speculation to bear upon them, nor do we add to them or subtract from them. Rather, we believe in them and entrust knowledge of them to the One who knows them, as did the righteous predecessors, who are our example in every branch of knowledge.

It has been transmitted to us from Ishāq that he said:

‘We do not divert any attribute with which Allah has described Himself, or with which the Messenger has described Him, from what it is, either in speech or in intent. The Muslim is only required to convey these descriptions and to be certain in his heart that what Allah has described Himself with in the Quran are indeed His attributes. Neither a prophet sent by Allah nor an angel brought near to Him comprehends those attributes except through the names by which the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, has made them known to them. As for any descendant of Adam apprehending those attributes, no one can apprehend them—and so on to the end of the report.

translated_text:
—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best.”

And the Most High said:

“And do not argue with the People of the Scripture except in a way that is best.”

Even if the opponent of someone who speaks in this manner—whether the speaker is Abū al-Faraj or someone else—belonged to one of the sects most notorious for innovation, such as the Rāfidah, he ought to present evidence and avoid what serves no purpose when undertaking to refute them; let alone (1) when those disputing with him—as he claims—are acknowledged by everyone to be more knowledgeable than he is about fundamentals and subsidiary matters. Yet in his discourse and rebuttal he has presented no evidence whatsoever, whether scriptural or rational. Rather, he has relied on blindly following a group of speculative theologians opposed by a greater number of speculative theologians. He has followed them in what they claimed was rational evidence, just as this objector has done. Anyone who seeks to refute others through reason must set out a rational argument; otherwise, he merely refers people to unknown entities, such as the Rāfidah’s infallible imam and the Sufis’ ghawth.

As for his statement, “Such people are not to be spoken to,” we reply: Allah sent the messengers to all creation to call them to Him. Who among mankind, then, has Allah exempted from being addressed? Let alone those whom you and others know, whom Allah has favored in ways that need not be discussed here. If a foolish person wished to answer this critic with a rebuttal like his own, he would have no difficulty doing so.

Likewise, concerning his statement, “They defy reason,” we say:

Defiance of reason

translated_text:
lies either in their affirming what they have affirmed, or in their contradicting themselves by combining (1) the affirmation of these matters with the denial of bodily organs.

As for the first possibility, it is false. No one has ever said that the position of outright corporealists, who explicitly affirm corporeality and take it to extremes, defies reason; nor has anyone said that they are not to be addressed. Rather, those who refuted extreme corporealists—such as Hishām ibn al-Hakam and his followers—used only rational arguments requiring examination and inference. Their opponent, although wrong in much of what he says, has countered them with arguments comparable to their own. Their case against him was no clearer than his against them, for each group holds both truth and falsehood.

And if someone such as “Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī” relies solely, in denying these matters, on what speculative thinkers who advocate negation put forward, then those thinkers scarcely ever claim that any affirmation or denial amounts to defiance of reason. Even concerning those who deny the Creator—who are the most ignorant, misguided, and unbelieving of all people, and the most opposed to reason—most of those whose support Abū al-Faraj has enlisted do not claim that their position defies reason. Rather, they claim that its falsity can be known only through examination and inference. Although most of these advocates of negation among the speculative theologians maintain this view, it is not a satisfactory approach.

The point, however, is that these advocates of negation do not claim that knowledge of the falsity of

translated_text:
the position of those who affirm is self-evident, nor that their position defies reason. Although they denounce them for things that repel many people, they do so to enlist that aversion in opposing them and suppressing their position—not because people’s aversion to them establishes truth or falsehood, nor because their position defies reason or its falsity is known through rational necessity or immediate intuition. I know of no leading speculative thinker among the advocates of negation who makes such a claim about any of his opponent’s affirmative positions, however extreme they may be.

It is well known that mere aversion on the part of those who recoil, or approval on the part of those who agree, establishes neither the soundness nor the falsity of a position, unless it is grounded in guidance from Allah. Rather, appealing to this as evidence amounts to appealing to the pursuit of desires without guidance from Allah.

For a person to follow his desires is to accept the statements and actions he likes and reject those he dislikes, without guidance from Allah. The Most High says:

“And indeed, many lead others astray through their desires without knowledge.”

He also says:

“But if they do not respond to you, then know that they only follow their desires. And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah?”

The Most High said to David:

“And do not follow desire, lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah.”

The Most High also says:

“If they testify, do not testify with them. And do not follow the desires of those who deny Our signs and those who do not believe in the Hereafter and who set others equal to their Lord.”

The Most High also says:

“Say, ‘O People of the Scripture, do not exceed the bounds of truth in your religion, and do not follow the desires of a people who went astray before, led many astray, and strayed from the right path.’”

The Most High also says:

“The Jews will never be pleased with you
