 .
 وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ فِي الصَّحِيحِ:
 {أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَمَّا اسْتَشَارَ أَصْحَابَهُ فِي أَسَارَى بَدْرٍ وَأَشَارَ عَلَيْهِ أَبُو بَكْرٍ أَنْ يَأْخُذَ الْفِدْيَةَ مِنْهُمْ وَإِطْلَاقَهُمْ وَأَشَارَ عَلَيْهِ عُمَرُ بِضَرْبِ أَعْنَاقِهِمْ.
 قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ إنَّ اللَّهَ يُلِينُ قُلُوبَ رِجَالٍ فِيهِ حَتَّى تَكُونَ أَلْيَنَ مِنْ الْبَزِّ وَيُشَدِّدُ قُلُوبَ رِجَالٍ فِيهِ حَتَّى تَكُونَ أَشَدَّ مِنْ الصَّخْرِ وَإِنَّ مَثَلَك يَا أَبَا بَكْرٍ مَثْلُ إبْرَاهِيمَ الْخَلِيلِ إذْ قَالَ:
 {فَمَنْ تَبِعَنِي فَإِنَّهُ مِنِّي وَمَنْ
translated_text:
Mālik in al-Muwatta’ and elsewhere. Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, walked beside his mount to see him off. Yazīd said to him: “Successor to the Messenger of Allah, either you must ride or I must dismount.” He replied: “You will not dismount, and I will not ride. I seek reward for these steps in the cause of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.”

‘Amr ibn al-‘Ās was also one of the commanders, as was Abū ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrāh. Abū Bakr placed Khālid ibn al-Walīd over them because of his courage and effectiveness in jihad. When Abū Bakr died, ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb appointed Abū ‘Ubaydah commander over them all. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, was stern in Allah’s cause, so he appointed Abū ‘Ubaydah because he was gentle. Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was gentle, whereas Khālid was stern towards the disbelievers. Thus, the gentle man appointed the stern man, and the stern man appointed the gentle man, so that a balance would be maintained. Each did what was most beloved to Allah Most High in his particular circumstances.

Our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is the most perfect of all creation. He was stern towards the disbelievers and hypocrites, and Allah Most High described him in terms of the most perfect religious laws, just as Allah Most High said in describing his community:

“Firm against the disbelievers, compassionate among themselves.”

He also said of them:

“Humble towards the believers, mighty against the disbelievers, striving in the cause of Allah and fearing no blame from anyone.”

It is established in the Sahīh:

“When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, consulted his Companions about the captives of Badr, Abū Bakr advised him to accept ransom from them and release them, while ‘Umar advised him to have them beheaded. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: ‘Allah softens the hearts of some men for His sake until they become softer than cloth, and He makes the hearts of other men firm for His sake until they become harder than rock. Your likeness, Abū Bakr, is that of Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, when he said: “Whoever follows me is indeed of me, and whoever

original_footnote: (١) كذا بالأصل
translated_text:
disobeys me—You are indeed Forgiving, Merciful.” And that of Jesus son of Mary, when he said:

“If You punish them, they are Your servants; but if You forgive them, You are indeed the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

Your likeness, ‘Umar, is that of Noah, peace be upon him, when he said:

“My Lord, do not leave a single disbeliever on the earth.”

And that of Moses son of ‘Imrān, when he said:

“Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment.”’”

Throughout the Prophet’s lifetime, peace and blessings be upon him, the two were as the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, had described them. They were his two ministers from among the people of the earth. It is established in the Sahīh, on the authority of Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both:

“When the bier of ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, was set down and people came to offer the funeral prayer over him, Ibn ‘Abbās said: ‘I turned around and there was ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him. He said: “By Allah, there is no one on the face of the earth whose deeds I would rather meet Allah Most High with than those of this deceased man. By Allah, I hope that Allah will gather you with your two companions, for I often heard the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, say: ‘I entered with Abū Bakr and ‘Umar; I went out with Abū Bakr and ‘Umar; and I went with Abū Bakr and ‘Umar.’”’”

It is also established in the Sahīh:

“On the day of Uhud, most of the Muslims fled. Then there was Abū Sufyān—and the people were the object sought (1)—when he said: ‘Is Muhammad among the people? Is Muhammad among the people? Is Muhammad among the people?’

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: ‘Do not answer him.’ Then he said: ‘Is there among

الْقَوْمِ ابْنُ أَبِي قُحَافَةَ؟ أَفِي الْقَوْمِ ابْنُ أَبِي قُحَافَةَ؟ أَفِي الْقَوْمِ ابْنُ أَبِي قُحَافَةَ؟
 فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَا تُجِيبُوهُ فَقَالَ:
 أَفِي الْقَوْمِ ابْنُ الْخَطَّابِ؟ أَفِي الْقَوْمِ ابْنُ الْخَطَّابِ؟ أَفِي الْقَوْمِ ابْنُ الْخَطَّابِ؟
 فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَا تُجِيبُوهُ} الْحَدِيثُ بِطُولِهِ فَهَذَا أَبُو سُفْيَانَ قَائِدُ الْأَحْزَابِ لَمْ يَسْأَلْ إلَّا عَنْ هَؤُلَاءِ الثَّلَاثَةِ:
 عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَأَبِي بَكْرٍ وَعُمَرَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا لِعِلْمِهِ بِأَنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ هُمْ رُءُوسُ عَسْكَرِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ.
 وَقَالَ الرَّشِيدُ لِمَالِكِ بْنِ أَنَسٍ:
 أَخْبِرْنِي عَنْ مَنْزِلَةِ أَبِي بَكْرٍ وَعُمَرَ مِنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَقَالَ: مَنْزِلَتُهُمَا مِنْهُ فِي حَيَاتِهِ كَمَنْزِلَتِهِمَا بَعْدَ وَفَاتِهِ فَقَالَ: شَفَيْتَنِي يَا مَالِكُ فَلَمَّا تُوُفِّيَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَاسْتَخْلَفَ أَبَا بَكْرٍ جَعَلَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى فِيهِ مِنْ الشِّدَّةِ مَا لَمْ يَكُنْ فِيهِ قَبْلَ ذَلِكَ حَتَّى فَاقَ عُمَرَ فِي ذَلِكَ حَتَّى قَاتَلَ أَهْلَ الرِّدَّةِ بَعْدَ أَنْ جَهَّزَ جَيْشَ أُسَامَةَ وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ تَكْمِيلًا لَهُ لِكَمَالِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ الَّذِي صَارَ خَلِيفَةً لَهُ. وَلَمَّا اسْتَخْلَفَ عُمَرَ جَعَلَ اللَّهُ فِيهِ مِنْ الرَّأْفَةِ وَالرَّحْمَةِ مَا لَمْ يَكُنْ فِيهِ قَبْلَ ذَلِكَ تَكْمِيلًا لَهُ حَتَّى صَارَ أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَلِهَذَا اسْتَعْمَلَ هَذَا خَالِدًا؛ وَهَذَا أَبَا عُبَيْدَةَ. وَكَانَ يَزِيدُ بْنُ أَبِي سُفْيَانَ عَلَى الشَّامِ؛ إلَى أَنْ وُلِّيَ عُمَرُ؛ فَمَاتَ يَزِيدُ بْنُ أَبِي سُفْيَانَ؛ فَاسْتَعْمَلَ عُمَرُ مُعَاوِيَةَ مَكَانَ أَخِيهِ يَزِيدَ بْنِ أَبِي سُفْيَانَ وَبَقِيَ مُعَاوِيَةُ
translated_text:
the people Ibn Abī Quhāfah? Is Ibn Abī Quhāfah among the people? Is Ibn Abī Quhāfah among the people?’

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: ‘Do not answer him.’ He then asked: ‘Is Ibn al-Khattāb among the people? Is Ibn al-Khattāb among the people? Is Ibn al-Khattāb among the people?’

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: ‘Do not answer him.’” The hadith continues at length.

Thus Abū Sufyān, the leader of the confederates, asked only about these three: the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, Abū Bakr and ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, because he knew that they were the leaders of the Muslim army.

Al-Rashīd said to Mālik ibn Anas: “Tell me about the standing of Abū Bakr and ‘Umar in relation to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.” He replied: “Their position in relation to him during his lifetime was like their position after his death.” Al-Rashīd said: “You have set my mind at rest, Mālik.”

When the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, passed away and Abū Bakr was appointed his successor, Allah Most High endowed him with a firmness he had not possessed before, to the point that he surpassed ‘Umar in this respect. He fought the apostates after equipping Usāmah’s army. This perfected his character in keeping with the perfection of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, whose successor he had become.

When ‘Umar was appointed successor, Allah endowed him with a tenderness and mercy he had not possessed before, perfecting his character so that he became Commander of the Faithful. This is why the former appointed Khālid, while the latter appointed Abū ‘Ubaydah.

Yazīd ibn Abī Sufyān governed Syria until ‘Umar took office. Yazīd ibn Abī Sufyān then died, and ‘Umar appointed Mu‘āwiyah in place of his brother Yazīd ibn Abī Sufyān. And Mu‘āwiyah remained

translated_text:
in his governorship throughout ‘Umar’s caliphate. ‘Umar and his subjects praised him and his conduct toward them, supported him and loved him for the forbearance and justice they had witnessed in him. Indeed, none of them complained about him or alleged that he had wronged them.

Yazīd ibn Mu‘āwiyah was not one of the Companions of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him; he was born during ‘Uthmān’s caliphate. He was named Yazīd after his uncle, who was one of the Companions.

Mu‘āwiyah, his brother Yazīd, Suhayl ibn ‘Amr, al-Hārith ibn Hishām and others who embraced Islam at the conquest of Mecca participated with the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in the expedition of Hunayn. They were included in the words of Allah Most High:

“Then Allah sent down His tranquillity upon His Messenger and upon the believers and sent down soldiers whom you did not see and punished those who disbelieved. And that is the recompense of the disbelievers.”

They were among the believers upon whom Allah sent down His tranquillity alongside the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. They also participated in the expedition of al-Tā’if, when they besieged al-Tā’if and he bombarded it with a catapult. They also faced the Christians in Syria, and Allah revealed Sūrat Barā’ah during that expedition.

This was the Expedition of Hardship, in which ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān, may Allah be pleased with him, equipped the Army of Hardship with a thousand camels in the cause of Allah Most High. When these proved insufficient, he completed the provision with fifty more camels. The Prophet said:

“Nothing ‘Uthmān does after today will harm him.”

This was the last of the Prophet’s military expeditions, peace and blessings be upon him, and no fighting took place during it. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, personally took part in more than twenty military expeditions, and did not

fight except in nine expeditions: Badr, Uhud, Banū al-Mustaliq, the Trench, Dhū Qarad, and the expedition of al-Tā’if. The largest army the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, assembled was at Hunayn and al-Tā’if, numbering twelve thousand. The largest army to accompany the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, on an expedition was the army of Tabūk: it was so numerous that it could not be counted, but no fighting took place during that expedition.

Those mentioned above are included in the words of Allah Most High:

“Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest; they are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward. Yet Allah has promised the best reward to all.”

For these men who were granted amnesty and embraced Islam at the conquest were among those who spent and fought after the conquest, and Allah promised them the best reward. They spent at Hunayn and al-Tā’if and fought in both expeditions—may Allah be pleased with them.

They are also included among those with whom Allah is pleased, as He says:

“The foremost pioneers among the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in righteousness—Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him.”

The pioneers were those who embraced Islam before al-Hudaybiyah, such as those who pledged allegiance to him beneath the tree, concerning whom Allah revealed:

“Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you beneath the tree.”

They numbered more than fourteen hundred, and all of them are among the people of Paradise, as authentically reported from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, who said:

“No one who pledged allegiance beneath the tree will enter the Fire.”

Among them was Hātib ibn Abī Balta‘ah, and he had committed sins

It is also authentically reported:

Since I lacked that, I wanted to do them a favor so that they would protect my relatives in return.’ ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb said, ‘Let me strike off this hypocrite’s head.’ The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, replied, ‘He was present at Badr. For all you know, Allah may have said, “Do whatever you wish; I have forgiven you.”’”

This hadith shows that, by virtue of their early commitment, faith, and striving in His cause, Allah forgives these pioneers—such as those who were present at Badr and al-Hudaybiyah—grave sins for which no one is permitted to punish them, just as Hātib did not have to be punished for what he had done.

If, however, there was a sin, it has been established that Allah is pleased with these men and has forgiven them for what they did. Thus, whatever sins they committed—if any sin was indeed committed—will not harm them. Rather, if any of them committed a sin, Allah had erased it through one of the means by which He expiates sins. For example, he may have repented and Allah accepted his repentance; he may have had good deeds that erase evil deeds; or Allah may have expiated his sin through an affliction He visited upon him. For it is authentically reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“No fatigue, illness, worry, distress, sorrow, or harm befalls a believer without Allah thereby expiating some of his sins.”

As for those who came after these earliest pioneers—namely, those who embraced Islam after al-Hudaybiyah—they are included in the words of Allah Most High:

“To each Allah has promised the best reward.”

And in His words:

“And those who followed them in righteousness—Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him.”

Khālid ibn al-Walīd, ‘Amr ibn al-‘Ās, ‘Uthmān ibn Talhah al-Hajabī, and others embraced Islam before the conquest of Mecca. The people of Tā’if embraced Islam after those who had been set free, and they were the last people to embrace Islam. Among them was ‘Uthmān ibn Abī al-‘Ās al-Thaqafī, whom the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, appointed to govern the people of Tā’if. He was among the finest Companions, despite having embraced Islam late.

For a man may embrace Islam later yet be superior to some who embraced it before him. Such was the case with ‘Umar: it is said that his conversion brought the number to forty, yet Allah favoured him over many who had embraced Islam before him. ‘Uthmān, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa‘d, and ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Awf had embraced Islam before ‘Umar through Abū Bakr, yet ‘Umar surpassed them in merit.

The first free adult man to embrace Islam was Abū Bakr; the first free boy was ‘Alī; the first among the clients was Zayd ibn Hārithah; and the first woman was Khadījah, the Mother of the Believers. The scholars agree on this.

Allah Most High said:

The passage continues to His words:

“And those who believed, emigrated, and strove in the cause of Allah, and those who gave shelter and support—they are the true believers. For them are forgiveness and a generous provision.”

“And those who believed afterwards, emigrated, and strove alongside you—they are of you.”

This is general in scope.

He Most High also said:

“For the poor emigrants who were driven from their homes and their possessions, seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure, and supporting Allah and His Messenger—they are the truthful.”

This verse and the preceding one encompass all who come within their scope after the earliest forerunners, until the Day of Resurrection. How, then, could they exclude the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who believed in him and strove alongside him?

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“The emigrant is one who abandons what Allah has forbidden.”

Thus, whoever among those freed at the conquest of Mecca had embraced Islam and abandoned what Allah had forbidden fulfilled the meaning of this migration and was included in His words, Most High:

“And those who believed afterwards, emigrated, and strove alongside you—they are of you.”

Likewise, he was included in His words, Most High:

“To each Allah has promised the finest reward.”

He Most High also said:

“Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are firm against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure. Their mark is on their faces from the effect of prostration. That is their description in the Torah. He said this to Khālid and others like him who embraced Islam after al-Hudaybiyya, comparing them with the earliest forerunners. He was saying that if any of them spent gold equal to Mount Uhud, it would not equal one mudd given by any of those forerunners, nor even half a mudd. Those who embraced Islam after al-Hudaybiyya were included, with this standing, in His words, Most High:

“Not equal among you are those who spent before the conquest and fought. Those are greater in rank than those who spent afterwards and fought. Yet to each Allah has promised the finest reward.”

How, then, could he come after his Companions?

Companionship is a general term encompassing anyone who kept company with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, whether briefly or for a long time. Each person’s share of companionship, however, corresponds to its extent. Whoever kept his company for a year, a month, a day, or an hour, or saw him while being a believer, has a corresponding share of companionship. Thus, it is authentically reported in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“This son of mine is a leader, and through him Allah will reconcile two great groups of Muslims.”

Thus, one of the reasons the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, praised and commended his son al-Hasan was that Allah Most High reconciled two great groups of Muslims through him. This occurred when he handed authority over to Mu‘āwiya, after each had marched against the other with great armies. Since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, praised al-Hasan for bringing about reconciliation and abandoning fighting, this indicates that reconciling those two parties was more beloved to Allah Most High than their fighting. It therefore indicates that their fighting was not commanded. Had Mu‘āwiya been an unbeliever, appointing an unbeliever to authority and handing power over to him would not have been something Allah and His Messenger loved. Rather, the hadith indicates that Mu‘āwiya and his followers were believers, just as al-Hasan and his followers were believers, and that al-Hasan’s action was praiseworthy in the sight of Allah Most High, beloved and pleasing to Him and His Messenger.

This accords with what is established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the two Sahīh collections, in the hadith of Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī, that he said:

“A breakaway faction will emerge at a time of division among the people, and the one of the two parties with the greater claim to the truth will kill them.” In another wording: “Those closest to the truth will kill them.”

This authentic hadith is evidence that both warring parties—‘Alī and his followers, and Mu‘āwiya and his followers—had truth on their side, and that ‘Alī and his followers were closer to the truth than Mu‘āwiya and his followers. For it was ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib who fought the breakaway faction: the “Harūrī Kharijites,” who had been among ‘Alī’s supporters, then rebelled against him, declared him and those who supported him unbelievers, showed hostility towards him, and fought him and those with him. may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in authentic, widely transmitted hadiths—indeed, mass-transmitted ones—in which he said of them:

“Any one of you would consider his prayer insignificant compared with theirs, his fasting compared with theirs, and his recitation compared with theirs. They recite the Quran, but it does not pass beyond their throats. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for killing them brings a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection. Their distinguishing sign is that among them is a man with malformed hands and a quivering fleshy growth bearing a few hairs.”

These are the people who showed hostility towards ‘Alī and those who supported him. They considered it lawful to kill him and declared him an unbeliever. One of their leaders, “ ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Muljim al-Murādī,” killed him. When these enemies of ‘Alī—the renegade Kharijites—claimed that ‘Uthmān, ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, and those with them were unbelievers and apostates, the Muslims’ arguments against them included the mass-transmitted evidence of the Companions’ faith, together with what is established in the Book and the authentic Sunnah concerning Allah Most High’s praise and commendation of them, His pleasure with them, His declaration that they are among the people of Paradise, and other such texts. Whoever does not accept these proofs cannot establish the faith of ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib and others like him.

For if this enemy of ‘Alī were to tell a Rāfidī that ‘Alī was an unbeliever, or a sinful wrongdoer; that he fought for dominion, seeking leadership rather than serving the religion; that at the Battle of the Camel, Siffīn, and Harūrā’, he killed thousands upon thousands of “members of the faith” from the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; and that after the Prophet’s death, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he neither fought an unbeliever nor conquered a city, but instead fought those who face the qiblah—and were to make other such claims, fabricated by those enemies who hated ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him—

They would say to them:

The faith, migration, and jihad of Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, ‘Uthmān, Talhah, al-Zubayr, and others like them are established through mass-transmitted reports. These include his widely transmitted saying:

“Were I to take an intimate friend from among the people of the earth, I would take Abū Bakr as an intimate friend.”

And his saying:

“Among the nations before you were men who received divine inspiration. If there is anyone such as this in my community, it is ‘Umar.”

And his saying about ‘Uthmān:

“Should I not feel shy before someone before whom the angels feel shy?”

And his words to ‘Alī:

“I shall certainly give the banner to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love. Allah will grant victory through him.”

And his saying:

“Every prophet has devoted supporters, and my devoted supporter is al-Zubayr.”

There are other statements of this kind. A Rāfidī, however, cannot establish the case against those enemies who hate ‘Alī as Ahl al-Sunnah can, for they love them all.

translated_text:
Waqqās, ‘Ā’ishah, Sahl ibn Sa‘d al-Sā‘idī, and others like them, whom the Rāfidah impugn. If the reports of these men and women and others like them are weak, every reported virtue of ‘Alī is invalidated, and the Rāfidah have no proof. If their reports are authentic, then the virtues of ‘Alī are established, as are those of others whose virtues they narrated, such as Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, ‘Uthmān, and others.”

If the Rāfidī says, “‘Alī’s virtues are established among the Shia through mass-transmitted reports”—just as they say that his designation as imam is established through mass-transmitted reports—he is told:

“As for those ‘Shia’ who were not Companions, they neither saw the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor heard his words. Their reports have incomplete, disconnected chains of transmission; unless they trace them back to the Companions, they are not authentic. The Companions to whom the Rāfidah profess allegiance are only a small group—a little over ten, or roughly that number. Their transmission does not establish mass transmission, since collusion is possible among so few people. Yet the Rāfidah impugn the overwhelming majority of the Companions who transmitted accounts of their virtues. Moreover, if they consider lying and concealment possible on the part of the majority whom the Quran praises, then all the more readily may they consider these possible on the part of a small group.”

Furthermore, if the Rāfidī says, “Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, and ‘Uthmān sought leadership and kingship, and thus wronged others by assuming authority,” the reply to them is:

“These men did not fight any Muslim over authority. Rather, they fought the apostates and the disbelievers. They were the ones who shattered the power of Chosroes and Caesar, conquered the lands of Persia, established Islam, strengthened faith and its adherents, and humbled disbelief and its adherents.”

 الَّذِينَ يُقِيمُونَ الصَّلَاةَ وَيُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ وَيَحُجُّونَ الْبَيْتَ الْعَتِيقَ؛ وَيَصُومُونَ شَهْرَ رَمَضَانَ وَيَقْرَءُونَ الْقُرْآنَ أُلُوفًا مُؤَلَّفَةً؛ وَمَنْ لَمْ يُقَاتِلْ مُسْلِمًا؛ بَلْ أَعَزُّوا أَهْلَ الصَّلَاةِ وَالزَّكَاةِ وَنَصَرُوهُمْ وَآوَوْهُمْ أَوْ مَنْ قَتَلَ وَهُوَ فِي وِلَايَتِهِ لَمْ يُقَاتِلْ وَلَمْ يَدْفَعْ عَنْ نَفْسِهِ حَتَّى قُتِلَ فِي دَارِهِ وَبَيْنَ أَهْلِهِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ؟ فَإِنْ جَوَّزْت عَلَى مِثْلِ هَذَا أَنْ يَكُونَ ظَالِمًا لِلْمُلْكِ ظَالِمًا لِلْمُسْلِمِينَ بِوِلَايَتِهِ فَتَجْوِيزُ هَذَا عَلَى مَنْ قَاتَلَ عَلَى الْوِلَايَةِ وَقَتْلِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ عَلَيْهَا أَوْلَى وَأَحْرَى. وَبِهَذَا وَأَمْثَالِهِ يَتَبَيَّنُ أَنَّ الرَّافِضَةَ أُمَّةٌ لَيْسَ لَهَا عَقْلٌ صَرِيحٌ؛ وَلَا نَقْلٌ صَحِيحٌ وَلَا دِينٌ مَقْبُولٌ؛ وَلَا دُنْيَا مَنْصُورَةٌ بَلْ هُمْ مِنْ أَعْظَمِ الطَّوَائِفِ كَذِبًا وَجَهْلًا وَدِينُهُمْ يُدْخِلُ عَلَى الْمُسْلِمِينَ كُلَّ زِنْدِيقٍ وَمُرْتَدٍّ كَمَا دَخَلَ فِيهِمْ الْنُصَيْرِيَّة؛
translated_text:
‘Uthmān ranked below Abū Bakr and ‘Umar. Nevertheless, when they sought to kill him while he was in office, he neither fought the Muslims nor killed any Muslim to retain his authority.

If you allow that these men might have been unjust rulers and enemies of the Messenger, then the argument of the Nāsibī (one hostile to the Prophet’s family) against you is stronger still. If you malign these men and accuse them of injustice and hostility towards the Messenger and his followers, you thereby furnish the renegade Khārijite Nāsibīs with an argument against you. For they say:

“Who is more deserving of being accused of seeking leadership: someone who fought Muslims—not disbelievers—to retain his authority, initiating hostilities to make them obey him when they would not, and killing many thousands of ‘those who face the qiblah’—people who establish prayer, pay zakah, perform pilgrimage to the Ancient House, fast the month of Ramadan, and recite the Quran—or those who fought no Muslim, but instead strengthened, supported, and sheltered those who observed prayer and paid zakah? Or someone who was killed while in office, who neither fought nor defended himself, until he was killed in his own home among his family—may Allah be pleased with him?”

If you allow that someone like this might have exercised kingship unjustly and wronged the Muslims through his rule, then such an accusation is all the more applicable to someone who fought to retain authority and killed Muslims for its sake.

This and similar considerations make it clear that the Rāfidah are a community with neither sound reason, authentic transmitted evidence, acceptable religion, nor worldly success. Rather, they are among the most dishonest and ignorant sects. Their religion opens the way into the Muslim community for every heretic and apostate, as the Nusayriyyah have entered their ranks,

original_text: وَالْإسْماعيليَّةُ وَغَيْرُهُمْ فَإِنَّهُمْ يَعْمِدُونَ إلَى خِيَارِ الْأُمَّةِ يُعَادُونَهُمْ وَإِلَى أَعْدَاءِ اللَّهِ مِنْ الْيَهُودِ وَالنَّصَارَى وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ يُوَالُونَهُمْ وَيَعْمِدُونَ إلَى الصِّدْقِ الظَّاهِرِ الْمُتَوَاتِرِ يَدْفَعُونَهُ وَإِلَى الْكَذِبِ الْمُخْتَلَقِ الَّذِي يُعْلَمُ فَسَادُهُ يُقِيمُونَهُ؛ فَهُمْ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهِمْ الشَّعْبِيُّ - وَكَانَ مِنْ أَعْلَمِ النَّاسِ بِهِمْ - لَوْ كَانُوا مِنْ الْبَهَائِمِ لَكَانُوا حُمْرًا وَلَوْ كَانُوا مِنْ الطَّيْرِ لَكَانُوا رَخَمًا. وَلِهَذَا كَانُوا أَبْهَتْ النَّاسِ وَأَشَدَّهُمْ فِرْيَةً مِثْلَ مَا يَذْكُرُونَ عَنْ مُعَاوِيَةَ. فَإِنَّ مُعَاوِيَةَ ثَبَتَ بِالتَّوَاتُرِ أَنَّهُ أَمَرَهُ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَمَا أَمَرَ غَيْرَهُ وَجَاهَدَ مَعَهُ وَكَانَ أَمِينًا عِنْدَهُ يَكْتُبُ لَهُ الْوَحْيَ وَمَا اتَّهَمَهُ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي كِتَابَةِ الْوَحْيِ. وَوَلَّاهُ عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ الَّذِي كَانَ مِنْ أَخْبَرِ النَّاسِ بِالرِّجَالِ وَقَدْ ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ الْحَقَّ عَلَى لِسَانِهِ وَقَلْبِهِ وَلَمْ يَتَّهِمْهُ فِي وِلَايَتِهِ. وَقَدْ وَلَّى رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَبَاهُ أَبَا سُفْيَانَ إلَى أَنْ مَاتَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَهُوَ عَلَى وِلَايَتِهِ فَمُعَاوِيَةُ خَيْرٌ مِنْ أَبِيهِ وَأَحْسَنُ إسْلَامًا مِنْ أَبِيهِ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَإِذَا كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَلَّى أَبَاهُ فَلَأَنْ تَجُوزُ وِلَايَتُهُ بِطَرِيقِ الْأَوْلَى وَالْأَحْرَى؛ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ مِنْ أَهْلِ الرِّدَّةِ قَطُّ وَلَا نَسَبَهُ أَحَدٌ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ إلَى الرِّدَّةِ فَاَلَّذِينَ يَنْسُبُونَ هَؤُلَاءِ إلَى الرِّدَّةِ هُمْ الَّذِينَ يَنْسُبُونَ أَبَا بَكْرٍ وَعُمَرَ وَعُثْمَانَ وَعَامَّةَ أَهْلِ بَدْرِ وَأَهْلِ بَيْعَةِ الرِّضْوَانِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ مِنْ السَّابِقِينَ الْأَوَّلِينَ مِنْ الْمُهَاجِرِينَ وَالْأَنْصَارِ وَاَلَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوهُمْ بِإِحْسَانِ إلَى مَا لَا يَلِيقُ بِهِمْ.
translated_text:
and the Ismā‘īliyyah and others. They deliberately turn against the best of the Muslim community, while allying themselves with Allah’s enemies among the Jews, Christians, and polytheists. They reject manifest truth established through mass transmission, while upholding fabricated lies whose falsehood is known. They are as al-Sha‘bī—who knew them exceptionally well—described them:

“Were they beasts, they would be donkeys; were they birds, they would be vultures.”

Thus, they are among the most shameless slanderers and fabricators, as illustrated by what they relate about Mu‘āwiyah. It is established through mass transmission that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, assigned Mu‘āwiyah duties as he did others, and that Mu‘āwiyah fought alongside him. The Prophet trusted him to write down revelation for him and never suspected him of dishonesty in doing so.

‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb appointed him to office. ‘Umar was exceptionally discerning in his judgment of men, and Allah had established truth upon his tongue and in his heart; he did not suspect Mu‘āwiyah of dishonesty in his administration. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had also appointed his father, Abū Sufyān, to office, and he remained in that position until the Prophet died. By the Muslims’ agreement, Mu‘āwiyah was better than his father and more upright in his Islam. If the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, appointed his father, then Mu‘āwiyah’s appointment was all the more permissible and appropriate.

He was never an apostate, nor did any scholar ever accuse him of apostasy. Those who accuse such men of apostasy are the very people who attribute unworthy things to Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, ‘Uthmān, the great majority of those who fought at Badr and those who gave the Pledge of Divine Pleasure, and the other earliest pioneers among the Emigrants and the Helpers, as well as those who followed them in righteousness.

original_text:
وَاَلَّذِينَ نَسَبُوا هَؤُلَاءِ إلَى الرِّدَّةِ يَقُولُ بَعْضُهُمْ:
 إنَّهُ مَاتَ وَوَجْهُهُ إلَى الشَّرْقِ وَالصَّلِيبُ عَلَى وَجْهِهِ وَهَذَا مِمَّا يَعْلَمُ كُلُّ عَاقِلٍ أَنَّهُ مِنْ أَعْظَمِ الْكَذِبِ وَالْفِرْيَةِ عَلَيْهِ. وَلَوْ قَالَ قَائِلٌ هَذَا فِيمَنْ هُوَ دُونَ مُعَاوِيَةَ مِنْ مُلُوكِ بَنِي أُمَيَّةَ وَبَنِيَّ الْعَبَّاسِ كَعَبْدِ الْمَلِكِ بْنِ مَرْوَانَ وَأَوْلَادِهِ وَأَبِي جَعْفَرٍ الْمَنْصُورِ وَوَلَدَيْهِ - الْمُلَقَّبَيْنِ بِالْمَهْدِيِّ وَالْهَادِي - وَالرَّشِيدِ وَأَمْثَالِهِمْ مِنْ الَّذِينَ تَوَلَّوْا الْخِلَافَةَ وَأَمْرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ؛ فَمَنْ نَسَبَ وَاحِدًا مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ إلَى الرِّدَّةِ وَإِلَى أَنَّهُ مَاتَ عَلَى دِينِ النَّصَارَى لَعَلِمَ كُلُّ عَاقِلٍ أَنَّهُ مِنْ أَعْظَمِ النَّاسِ فِرْيَةً فَكَيْفَ يُقَالُ مِثْلُ هَذَا فِي مُعَاوِيَةَ وَأَمْثَالِهِ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ.
 بَلْ يَزِيدُ ابْنُهُ مَعَ مَا أَحْدَثَ مِنْ الْأَحْدَاثِ مَنْ قَالَ فِيهِ:
 إنَّهُ كَافِرٌ مُرْتَدٌّ فَقَدْ افْتَرَى عَلَيْهِ. بَلْ كَانَ مَلِكًا مِنْ مُلُوكِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ كَسَائِرِ مُلُوكِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَأَكْثَرُ الْمُلُوكِ لَهُمْ حَسَنَاتٌ وَلَهُمْ سَيِّئَاتٌ وَحَسَنَاتُهُمْ عَظِيمَةٌ وَسَيِّئَاتُهُمْ عَظِيمَةٌ فَالطَّاعِنُ فِي وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمْ دُونَ نُظَرَائِهِ إمَّا جَاهِلٌ وَإِمَّا ظَالِمٌ. وَهَؤُلَاءِ لَهُمْ مَا لِسَائِرِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ مِنْهُمْ مَنْ تَكُونُ حَسَنَاتُهُ أَكْثَرَ مِنْ سَيِّئَاتِهِ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ قَدْ تَابَ مِنْ سَيِّئَاتِهِ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ كَفَّرَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ قَدْ يُدْخِلُهُ الْجَنَّةَ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ قَدْ يُعَاقِبُهُ لِسَيِّئَاتِهِ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ قَدْ يَتَقَبَّلُ اللَّهُ فِيهِ شَفَاعَةَ نَبِيٍّ أَوْ غَيْرِهِ مِنْ الشُّفَعَاءِ فَالشَّهَادَةُ لِوَاحِدِ مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ بِالنَّارِ هُوَ مِنْ أَقْوَالِ أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ وَالضَّلَالِ.
translated_text:
Some of those who accuse these men of apostasy say: “He died facing east, with a cross upon his face.” Any reasonable person knows that this is among the most outrageous lies and slanders against him. Were someone to say this about Umayyad and Abbasid rulers of lesser standing than Mu‘āwiyah—such as ‘Abd al-Malik ibn Marwān and his sons, Abū Ja‘far al-Mansūr and his two sons, known as al-Mahdī and al-Hādī, al-Rashīd, and others who assumed the caliphate and governed the believers—any reasonable person would recognize someone who accused one of them of apostasy and of dying as a Christian as among the greatest fabricators. How, then, can such a thing be said about Mu‘āwiyah and other Companions like him?

Indeed, even his son Yazīd, despite the wrongs he committed, has been slandered by anyone who calls him an unbeliever and an apostate. Rather, he was a Muslim king, like other Muslim kings. Most kings have both good deeds and bad deeds: their good deeds are great, and their bad deeds are grave. Anyone who singles out one of them for condemnation while overlooking his counterparts is either ignorant or unjust.

The same considerations apply to them as to other Muslims. Some have more good deeds than bad; some have repented of their bad deeds; some have had their sins expiated by Allah; some He may admit to Paradise; some He may punish for their bad deeds; and for some Allah may accept the intercession of a prophet or another intercessor. Thus, declaring that any particular one of these men is destined for Hell is among the claims of the people of innovation and misguidance.

translated_text:
Likewise, deliberately singling out any one of them for a curse is not among the deeds of the righteous and virtuous.

It is authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah has cursed wine, the one who presses it, the one who has it pressed, the one who carries it, the one who serves it, the one who drinks it, the one who sells it, the one who buys it, and the one who consumes its proceeds.”

It is also authentically reported:

“During the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, there was a man called Himār who frequently drank wine. Whenever he was brought before the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he would flog him. On one occasion, he was brought before him to be flogged, and a man said, ‘May Allah curse him! How often he is brought before the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace!’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘Do not curse him, for he loves Allah and His Messenger.’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, thus cursed wine drinkers in general, but forbade cursing an individual believer.

Likewise, we affirm what Allah Most High has said:

“Indeed, those who unjustly consume the property of orphans are only filling their bellies with fire.”

Yet no one should declare that a particular individual is destined for Hell, for he may repent, or Allah may forgive him through good deeds that erase sins, afflictions that expiate them, accepted intercession, or Allah’s pardon, or otherwise.

The same applies to an individual king or anyone else: even if he has committed injustice, that does not warrant our cursing him and declaring him destined for Hell. Whoever engages in this is among the people of innovation and misguidance. said:

“The first army to campaign against Constantinople will be forgiven.”

The first army to campaign against it was commanded by “Yazīd ibn Mu‘āwiya.” Abū Ayyūb al-Ansārī was among those who accompanied him on the campaign. He died there, and his grave remains there to this day.

For this reason, the moderate imams of the early generations would say concerning Yazīd and others like him: “We neither revile them nor love them”—meaning that we do not love the injustice they committed. A single person may combine good deeds and bad deeds, obedience and disobedience, righteousness, wickedness, and evil. Allah rewards him for his good deeds and punishes him for his bad deeds if He wills, or forgives him. He loves the good that person has done and hates the evil he has done. As for those whose sins are minor, even the Mu‘tazilah agree that Allah forgives them.

As for someone who commits a major sin, the early generations of the Muslim community, its imams, and all other Sunni Muslims do not declare him destined for Hell. Rather, they acknowledge that Allah may forgive him, as He Most High says:

“Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but forgives anything less than that for whomever He wills.”

This applies to someone who has not associated partners with Allah, for He made such forgiveness conditional upon His will. As for His words, Most High:

“Say, ‘O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of Allah’s mercy. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.’”

This applies to someone who has repented; hence He stated it without qualification and included all sins.

The Khawārij and the Mu‘tazilah say that someone who commits a major sin will remain in Hell forever. Furthermore, they

As for the claim that “Mu‘āwiya’s faith was hypocrisy,” this too is a fabricated lie. No Muslim scholar accused Mu‘āwiya of hypocrisy; rather, the scholars agree on the soundness of his Islam. Some of them withheld judgment concerning the soundness of his father Abū Sufyān’s Islam. As for Mu‘āwiya and his brother Yazīd, however, they did not dispute the soundness of their Islam, just as they did not dispute that of ‘Ikrima ibn Abī Jahl, Suhayl ibn ‘Amr, Safwān ibn Umayya, and others who embraced Islam at the conquest of Mecca.

How could a man govern the Muslims for forty years, first as a deputy and then as a ruler in his own right—leading them in the five daily prayers, delivering sermons and exhorting them, enjoining good and forbidding evil, enforcing the prescribed punishments among them, distributing among them their revenues acquired without fighting, their war booty, and their alms, and leading them on pilgrimage—yet conceal his hypocrisy from them all? Among them were many eminent Companions.

More telling still is that—praise be to Allah—not one of the Umayyad or Abbasid caliphs who exercised general authority was accused of heresy and hypocrisy. None of the Umayyads was accused of heresy and hypocrisy. Although one of them might be accused of some form of religious innovation or injustice, none of them was accused by the scholars of heresy and hypocrisy.

Many people disputed ‘Alī’s caliphate, saying: “His time was a time of civil strife, and the community was not united during his rule.” One group said: “It is valid to appoint two caliphs: he was a caliph, and Mu‘āwiya was a caliph, because the community neither agreed upon him nor united under his caliphate.”

The correct position, upheld by the leading scholars, is that ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, was one of the rightly guided caliphs, as established by this hadith. During his rule, ‘Alī called himself Commander of the Faithful, and the Companions addressed him by that title. Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal said:

“Whoever does not count ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, as the fourth caliph is more astray than his family’s donkey.”

Nevertheless, each caliph has his own rank. No one equals Abū Bakr and ‘Umar, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Follow the two who come after me: Abū Bakr and ‘Umar.”

There was no disagreement among ‘Alī’s supporters who accompanied him concerning the precedence of Abū Bakr and ‘Umar. It is established through numerous reports that ‘Alī said: “If any man is brought before me who considers me superior to Abū Bakr and ‘Umar, I will flog him with the prescribed punishment for slander.”

Their disagreement concerned only ‘Uthmān and ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with them both. However, ‘Uthmān’s precedence over ‘Alī was established by the agreement of the early Muslims to pledge allegiance to (‘Uthmān willingly, without coercion, after ‘Umar entrusted the choice of his successor to a council of six: ‘Uthmān, ‘Alī, Talha, al-Zubayr, Sa‘d

translated_text:
We have slain many of their elders … and balanced it against Badr, so the score is even.”

They say other things of this kind as well. Such a view comes easily to the Rāfida, who declare Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, and ‘Uthmān unbelievers; declaring Yazīd an unbeliever is far easier still.

Those at the other extreme think that he was a righteous man and a just ruler, and that he was among the “Companions” born during the Prophet’s lifetime, whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, carried in his arms and blessed. Some of them even consider him superior to Abū Bakr and ‘Umar, while others go so far as to regard him as a prophet. They falsely attribute to “Shaykh ‘Adī” or to Hasan, who was killed, the claim that seventy friends of Allah had their faces turned away from the direction of prayer because they withheld judgment concerning Yazīd. This is the view of extremists among the ‘Adawiyya, the Kurds, and other misguided people like them.

Shaykh ‘Adī belonged to the Umayyads and was a righteous, devout, and virtuous man. Nothing is recorded from him indicating that he called them to anything other than the Sunnah upheld by others, such as Shaykh “Abū al-Faraj” al-Maqdisī, whose creed agreed with his. Yet they added lies and misguidance to the Sunnah: fabricated hadiths, false likening of Allah to His creation, excessive veneration of Shaykh ‘Adī and Yazīd, and excessive condemnation of the Rāfida, claiming that their repentance would not be accepted, along with other things.

Both views are plainly false to anyone possessing even the slightest reason and knowledge of these matters and the lives of earlier generations. Accordingly, neither view is attributed to any scholar known for adherence to the Sunnah, nor to any sensible person possessing sound judgment and experience.

translated_text:
The third view is that he was one of the Muslim kings, with both good deeds and bad. He was not born until the caliphate of ‘Uthmān, and he was not an unbeliever. Nevertheless, it was because of him that al-Husayn was killed and the people of al-Harra suffered what they suffered. He was neither a Companion nor one of Allah’s righteous friends. This is the view generally held by people of sound judgment and knowledge who adhere to the Sunnah and the community.

They then divided into (three groups: one cursed him, another loved him, and a third neither reviled nor loved him. This last position is explicitly reported from Imam Ahmad and is followed by the moderate among his followers and other Muslims.

Sālih ibn Ahmad said:
“I said to my father, ‘Some people say that they love Yazīd.’ He replied, ‘My son, could anyone who believes in Allah and the Last Day love Yazīd?’
“I asked, ‘Father, why, then, do you not curse him?’
“He replied, ‘My son, when have you ever seen your father curse anyone?’”

Muhannā said:
“I asked Ahmad about Yazīd ibn Mu‘āwiya ibn Abī Sufyān. He replied, ‘He is the one who did what he did to Medina.’
“I asked, ‘What did he do?’
“He replied, ‘He killed some of the Companions of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and did other things.’
“I asked, ‘What else did he do?’
“He replied, ‘He plundered it.’
“I asked, ‘Should hadith be transmitted on his authority?’
“He replied, ‘No hadith should be transmitted on his authority.’”

This is also related by Judge Abū Ya‘lā and others.

It has reached me that, when Abū Muhammad al-Maqdisī was asked about Yazīd, he said, “He is neither to be reviled nor loved.” It has also reached me that our grandfather, Abū ‘Abd Allāh Ibn Taymiyya, was asked about Yazīd and replied, “Neither detract nor add.” This is the fairest and best of the views concerning him and others like him.

translated_text:
As for refraining from reviling and cursing him, this rests either on the view that the sinfulness warranting his being cursed has not been established, or on the view that a particular sinner should not be singled out for cursing, because doing so is either forbidden or discouraged.

It is authentically reported in Sahīh al-Bukhārī, on the authority of ‘Umar, in the account of “Himār,” who repeatedly drank wine and was flogged for it, that when one of the Companions cursed him, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Do not curse him, for he loves Allah and His Messenger.”

He also said:

“Cursing a believer is like killing him.”

This is reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim. Yet it is also authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, cursed wine and those who drink it. Thus, the Prophet cursed wine-drinkers in general, while forbidding, in an authentic hadith, the cursing of this particular individual.

Similarly, the scriptural threats of punishment apply generally to those who devour orphans’ wealth, adulterers, and thieves. We do not, on the basis of these general texts, declare any particular individual to be among the people of the Fire, since a stronger countervailing factor may prevent the threatened consequence from following: repentance, good deeds that erase sins, afflictions that expiate them, accepted intercession, or something else, as we have explained elsewhere. These, then, are three grounds for refraining from cursing him.

Some of those who curse him hold that refraining from doing so is like refraining from other permissible forms of unnecessary speech—not that cursing him is discouraged.

As for refraining from loving him, this is because special love is reserved for the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous, and he is not one of them. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A person will be with those whom he loves.”

Anyone who believes in Allah and the Last Day would not choose to be with Yazīd or with other kings like him who are not just.

There are “two grounds” for refraining from loving him. The first is that he performed no righteous deeds that would warrant loving him, and thus remained merely one of the kings who wielded power. Loving particular individuals of this kind is not religiously prescribed. This ground, together with the position of those who do not consider his sinfulness established, rests on believing that he acted on an interpretation.

The second is that his conduct, including the affairs of al-Husayn and the people of al-Harra, involved deeds indicating his injustice and sinfulness.

As for the scholars who cursed him, such as Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī, Ilkiyā al-Harrāsī, and others, they did so because of the deeds he committed that permitted his being cursed. They may argue that he was a flagrant sinner and that every flagrant sinner may be cursed. Or they may hold that someone who commits a sin may be cursed even without being judged a flagrant sinner, just as the opposing sides at Siffīn cursed one another in the supplication during prayer. Thus, ‘Alī and his companions cursed particular men from Syria in their prayer supplications, and the Syrians likewise cursed their opponents. Yet when the combatants act on a defensible interpretation—both those in the right and those in rebellion—none of them is thereby deemed a flagrant sinner.

He may also be cursed specifically for his grave sins, even if other flagrant sinners are not cursed, just as the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, cursed certain categories of sinners and particular individuals, without cursing them all. These, then, are (three grounds for cursing him.

The first is that he was a Muslim entrusted with governing the community during the time of the Companions, and those of them who remained followed him. He possessed praiseworthy qualities and acted on an interpretation in the matters for which he is condemned, including the affair of al-Harra. Thus, they say that he exercised independent judgment but was mistaken. They also say that the people of al-Harra were the first to break their pledge of allegiance to him, and that Ibn ‘Umar and others condemned them for this. As for the killing of al-Husayn, he neither ordered it nor approved of it. Rather, he showed grief over his killing and condemned those who killed him. The head was not brought to him; it was brought only to Ibn Ziyād.

(The second ground is that it is established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī, on the authority of Ibn ‘Umar, that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The first army to attack Constantinople will be forgiven.”

The commander of the first army to attack it was Yazīd.

“The sound conclusion” is that both these positions allow scope for independent judgment. Cursing those who commit sins is a matter open to independent judgment, as is loving those who perform both good and evil deeds. Indeed, in our view, there is no contradiction in a person deserving both praise and blame, both reward and punishment. Likewise, there is no contradiction in offering the funeral prayer for him and supplicating for him, while also cursing and reviling him, each on account of a different aspect of his conduct.

For Ahl al-Sunnah agree that flagrant sinners among the Muslims—even if they enter the Fire or deserve to enter it—must eventually enter Paradise. Thus, they receive both reward and punishment. The Khawārij and the Mu‘tazila, however, deny this. They hold that whoever deserves reward does not deserve punishment, and whoever deserves punishment does not deserve reward. This is a well-known issue, and its detailed exposition belongs elsewhere.

As for the permissibility of supplicating both for a man and against him, this issue is discussed in detail in connection with funeral rites. The funeral prayer is offered for deceased Muslims, righteous and sinful alike, even if a sinful person is also cursed individually or as one of a class. Nevertheless, the first position is more balanced and just. This was the answer I gave Būlāy, the Mongol commander, when they came to Damascus during the great upheaval. I had discussions with him and others, and among his questions he asked me:

“What do you say about Yazīd?”

I replied: “We neither revile him nor love him. He was not a righteous man whom we should love, and we do not single out any Muslim for reviling.”

He said: “Do you not curse him, then? Was he not an oppressor? Did he not kill al-Husayn?”

I replied: “When oppressors such as al-Hajjāj ibn Yūsuf and others like him are mentioned, we say what Allah says in the Quran:

‘Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers.’

“We do not like to curse anyone individually. Some scholars have cursed him, and this is a position that allows scope for independent judgment. Nevertheless, the position I have stated is preferable to us and better. As for anyone who killed ‘al-Husayn’, helped to kill him, or approved of it, upon him is the curse of Allah, the angels, and all mankind. Allah accepts neither sarf nor ʿadl from him.”

He said: “Do you not love the Prophet’s household, then?”

I replied: “Loving them is, in our view, a binding obligation for which one is rewarded. translated_text:
He was asked:

About a group united in various forms of corruption. Among them is someone who says that religion became corrupt before “this”—namely, when the caliphate was taken from ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib. Those who took office in his place were not qualified to govern, so their appointment was invalid. Consequently, no contract concluded by Muslims thereafter was valid, whether a marriage contract or any other. Everyone who married after that event therefore has an invalid marriage; likewise, all contracts, appointments to office, and other such matters are invalid.

The person making this claim also alleges that Allah is a cross, with each letter of the Divine Name at the end of one of the cross’s lines. He asserts to people that the Jews and Christians follow the truth, as do the Magians and others.

He replied—may Allah Most High have mercy on him:

This ignorant man resembles, in his ignorance, the Rāfidah, who tell lies and whose superstitions deceive only ignorant people unfamiliar with the foundations of Islam, such as those mentioned in this question. It was stated that they say religion became corrupt when the caliphate was taken from ‘Alī, and that was

Such a man is among the worst heretics, of the same kind as the Qarmatian esotericists, such as the Nusayrīs, the Ismāʿīlīs, and their followers.

This is why his statements are contradictory. Someone who endorses the religions of the Jews, Christians, and Magians, yet attacks the faith of the rightly guided Caliphs, who were themselves guided aright, and of the earliest pioneers among the Emigrants and Helpers, can only be among the most ignorant of people and those most deeply steeped in unbelief. If he were among the believers who know that this community is the best community brought forth for mankind, and that its best generation is the first, followed by the next, and then the next, he would not endorse the religion of the disbelievers while attacking the faith of the Emigrants and Helpers.

The refutation of this and similar claims is set out at length elsewhere. In our refutation of the Rāfidah, we have discussed this matter at greater length than space here permits. No one who believes that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah would make such a statement. We therefore answer someone who acknowledges that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah by explaining to him what the Messenger brought that dispels his misconception. As for someone who attacks his prophethood, we address him from another angle: each situation calls for its own manner of discourse.

الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، هَذِهِ الْأُمُورُ الْمَذْكُورَةُ كَذِبٌ مُخْتَلَقٌ بِاتِّفَاقِ أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ وَالْإِيمَانِ
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“Do the scholars regard the following claims as authentic: that ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, fought the jinn in the well; that he stretched out his hand on the day of Khaybar and the army crossed over it; that he charged the Confederates, who divided into seventeen groups before him, with a man behind each group striking with a sword and saying, ‘I am ʿAlī’; and that he had a sword called Dhū al-Faqār which could lengthen and shorten?

“That he struck Marhab with it while Marhab had a marble basin on his head, splitting it, him, and his horse with a single blow that continued into the ground, while a voice called out in the air, ‘There is no sword but Dhū al-Faqār, and no valiant man but ʿAlī’; that he launched toward the fortress of al-Ghurāb in a catapult; that he was sent secretly to every prophet and openly alongside the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; and that he would charge armies of fifty thousand, twenty thousand, and thirty thousand single-handedly?

“That when Marhab came out from Khaybar to face him, he struck him once, cleaving him lengthwise and his horse crosswise, and the sword penetrated two or three cubits into the ground; and that he grasped the ring of Khaybar’s gate and shook it, causing the town to shake and battlements to fall from the wall? Is any of this authentic?”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. These accounts are fabricated lies, by the unanimous agreement of the people of knowledge and faith.

translated_text:
Neither Alī nor any other Companion fought the jinn, nor did any human fight the jinn, whether in the well of Dhāt al-Alam or elsewhere.

The hadith reporting that he fought the jinn is a fabrication and a lie, by the unanimous agreement of the knowledgeable scholars. During the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, Alī never fought an army of fifty thousand or thirty thousand, let alone charged such an army single-handedly. The campaigns he attended with the Messenger of Allah and in which he fought numbered nine: Badr, Uhud, the Trench, Khaybar, the conquest of Mecca, the battle of Hunayn, and others.

The polytheists were most numerous at the Battle of the Confederates, also known as the Battle of the Trench. They were besieging Medina, but neither they nor the Muslims fought with their entire forces. Only a few Muslims and a few disbelievers fought one another. It was during this battle that Alī killed Amr ibn Abd Wudd al-Āmirī. Whenever Alī fought in single combat, he faced only one opponent, never two.

As for Marhab at Khaybar, it is established in the Sahih that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I shall give the banner to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love. Allah will grant victory at his hands.”

He gave it to Alī. The fighting at Khaybar lasted several days, and some of its fortresses were conquered at the hands of Alī, may Allah be pleased with him. A report relates that he killed Marhab, while another relates that Muhammad ibn Maslama killed him. Perhaps there were two men named Marhab. He killed him in the usual manner: he did not cleave his entire body in two, nor did he cleave the horse, nor did there descend

He did not stretch out his hand for the army to cross over it; the wall of Khaybar did not shake when the gate was torn off, nor did any of its battlements fall. Khaybar was not a city, but rather a collection of scattered fortresses whose inhabitants had farmland.

What is reported, however, is that he did not tear off the fortress gate until the Muslims had crossed it. Nor did he ever launch anything from a catapult. Many lies have been added to most of these accounts of campaigns involving Alī and others, like the fabrications told in the tales of Antara and other heroes.

Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, took part in only three wars after the death of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: the Battle of the Camel, Siffīn, and the war against the people of Nahrawān. Allah knows best.

سُئِلَ:
عَمَّنْ قَالَ:
 إنَّ عَلِيًّا قَاتَلَ الْجِنَّ فِي الْبِئْرِ؟ وَأَنَّهُ حَمَلَ عَلَى اثْنَيْ عَشَرَ أَلْفًا وَهَزَمَهُمْ؟ .
فَأَجَابَ:
لَمْ يَحْمِلْ أَحَدٌ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَحْدَهُ لَا فِي اثْنَيْ عَشَرَ أَلْفًا وَلَا فِي عَشَرَةِ آلَافٍ لَا عَلِيٌّ وَلَا غَيْرُهُ؛ بَلْ أَكْثَرُ عَدَدٍ اجْتَمَعَ عَلَى النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ هَمّ الْأَحْزَابُ الَّذِينَ حَاصَرُوهُ بِالْخَنْدَقِ وَكَانُوا قَرِيبًا مِنْ هَذِهِ الْعُدَّةِ وَقَتَلَ عَلِيٌّ رَجُلًا مِنْ الْأَحْزَابِ اسْمُهُ 
" عَمْرُو بْنُ عَبْدِ وُدٍّ الْعَامِرِيُّ "
. وَلَمْ يُقَاتِلْ أَحَدٌ مِنْ الْإِنْسِ لِلْجِنِّ لَا عَلِيٌّ وَلَا غَيْرُهُ بَلْ عَلِيٌّ كَانَ أَجَلَّ قَدْرًا مِنْ ذَلِكَ وَالْجِنُّ الَّذِينَ يَتَّبِعُونَ الصَّحَابَةَ يُقَاتِلُونَ كُفَّارَ الْجِنِّ لَا يَحْتَاجُونَ فِي ذَلِكَ إلَى قِتَالِ الصَّحَابَةِ مَعَهُمْ.
translated_text:
He was asked about someone who said that Alī fought the jinn in the well, and that he charged twelve thousand men and defeated them.

He replied:

No Companion ever charged twelve thousand or ten thousand men single-handedly—neither Alī nor anyone else. Rather, the largest force assembled against the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was the Confederates who besieged him at the Trench. They numbered approximately that many, and Alī killed a man from among them named “Amr ibn Abd Wudd al-Āmirī”.

No human has fought the jinn—neither Alī nor anyone else. Indeed, Alī was of too high a standing for that. The jinn who follow the Companions fight the disbelieving jinn; they do not need the Companions to fight alongside them.

original_text:
سُئِلَ:
عَنْ 
" 
{فَاطِمَةَ أَنَّهَا أَتَتْ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَقَالَتْ: يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ إنَّ عَلِيًّا يَقُومُ اللَّيَالِيَ كُلَّهَا إلَّا لَيْلَةَ الْجُمْعَةِ فَإِنَّهُ يُصَلِّي الْوِتْرَ ثُمَّ يَنَامُ إلَى أَنْ يَطْلُعَ الْفَجْرُ فَقَالَ: إنَّ اللَّهَ يَرْفَعُ رُوحَ عَلِيٍّ كُلَّ لَيْلَةِ جُمْعَةٍ تُسَبِّحُ فِي السَّمَاءِ إلَى طُلُوعِ الْفَجْرِ}
 "
 فَهَلْ ذَلِكَ صَحِيحٌ أَمْ لَا؟
 وَهَلْ هَذَا صَحِيحٌ عَنْ عَلِيٍّ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 اسْأَلُونِي عَنْ طُرُقِ السَّمَاءِ فَإِنِّي أَعْرِفُ بِهَا مِنْ طُرُقِ الْأَرْضِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
 وَأَمَّا الْحَدِيثُ الْمَذْكُورُ عَنْ عَلِيٍّ فَكَذِبٌ؛ مَا رَوَاهُ أَحَدٌ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ.
 وَأَمَّا قَوْلُهُ:
 اسْأَلُونِي عَنْ طُرُقِ السَّمَاءِ فَإِنَّهُ قَالَهُ وَلَمْ يُرِدْ بِذَلِكَ طَرِيقًا لِلْهُدَى؛ وَإِنَّمَا يُرِيدُ بِمِثْلِ هَذَا الْكَلَامِ الْأَعْمَالَ الصَّالِحَةَ الَّتِي يَتَقَرَّبُ بِهَا وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
He was asked about the following report:

“Fātimah came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, Alī prays throughout every night except the night before Friday, when he offers the witr prayer and then sleeps until dawn.’ He replied, ‘Allah raises Alī’s soul every night before Friday, and it glorifies Him in heaven until dawn.’”

Is this authentic? And is it authentically reported that Alī said, “Ask me about the paths of heaven, for I know them better than the paths of the earth”?

He replied:

As for the report mentioned concerning Alī, it is a lie; no scholar has narrated it.

As for his saying, “Ask me about the paths of heaven,” he did say it, but he did not mean by this a path to guidance. Rather, by such words he meant righteous deeds through which one draws near to Allah. And Allah knows best.

original_text:
سُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ قَالَ عَنْ 
" عَلِيِّ "
 بْنِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ - إنَّهُ لَيْسَ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْبَيْتِ وَلَا تَجُوزُ الصَّلَاةُ عَلَيْهِ وَالصَّلَاةُ عَلَيْهِ بِدْعَةٌ
فَأَجَابَ:
أَمَّا كَوْنُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْبَيْتِ فَهَذَا مِمَّا لَا خِلَافَ فِيهِ بَيْنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَهُوَ أَظْهَرُ عِنْدَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ مِنْ أَنْ يَحْتَاجَ إلَى دَلِيلٍ؛ بَلْ هُوَ أَفْضَلُ أَهْلِ الْبَيْتِ وَأَفْضَلُ بَنِي هَاشِمٍ بَعْدَ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ 
{عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ أَدَارَ كِسَاءَهُ عَلَى عَلِيٍّ وَفَاطِمَةَ وَحَسَنٍ وَحُسَيْنٍ فَقَالَ: اللَّهُمَّ هَؤُلَاءِ أَهْلُ بَيْتِي فَأَذْهِبْ عَنْهُمْ الرِّجْسَ وَطَهِّرْهُمْ تَطْهِيرًا}
 ". وَأَمَّا الصَّلَاةُ عَلَيْهِ مُنْفَرِدًا فَهَذَا يَنْبَنِي عَلَى أَنَّهُ هَلْ يُصَلَّى عَلَى غَيْرِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مُنْفَرِدًا؟
 مِثْلَ أَنْ يَقُولَ:
 اللَّهُمَّ صَلِّ عَلَى عُمَرَ أَوْ عَلِيٍّ. وَقَدْ تَنَازَعَ الْعُلَمَاءُ فِي ذَلِكَ.
 فَذَهَبَ مَالِكٌ وَالشَّافِعِيُّ وَطَائِفَةٌ مِنْ الْحَنَابِلَةِ:
 إلَى أَنَّهُ لَا يُصَلَّى عَلَى غَيْرِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مُنْفَرِدًا كَمَا رُوِيَ عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: لَا أَعْلَمُ الصَّلَاةَ تَنْبَغِي عَلَى أَحَدٍ إلَّا عَلَى النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about a man who said of Alī ibn Abī Tālib—may Allah be pleased with him—that he was not a member of the Prophet’s household, that invoking blessings upon him was impermissible, and that doing so was a religious innovation.

He replied:

There is no disagreement among Muslims that Alī ibn Abī Tālib belongs to the Prophet’s household. This is so evident to Muslims that it requires no proof. Indeed, after the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he is the best member of the household and the best of Banū Hāshim. It is authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, wrapped his cloak around Alī, Fātimah, Hasan, and Husayn, saying:

“O Allah, these are the members of my household. Remove impurity from them and purify them thoroughly.”

As for invoking blessings upon him individually, this depends on whether blessings may be invoked individually upon someone other than the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—for example, by saying, “O Allah, bless Umar,” or “O Allah, bless Alī.” Scholars have differed on this matter.

Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and a group of Hanbalī scholars held that blessings should not be invoked individually upon anyone other than the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This accords with the report that Ibn Abbās said: “I do not know of anyone upon whom it is fitting to invoke blessings except the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

original_text:
وَذَهَبَ الْإِمَامُ أَحْمَد وَأَكْثَرُ أَصْحَابِهِ إلَى أَنَّهُ لَا بَأْسَ بِذَلِكَ؛
 لِأَنَّ عَلِيَّ بْنَ أَبِي طَالِبٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ لِعُمَرِ بْنِ الْخَطَّابِ:
 صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْك. وَهَذَا الْقَوْلُ أَصَحُّ وَأَوْلَى.
 وَلَكِنَّ إفْرَادَ وَاحِدٍ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَالْقُرَابَةِ كَعَلِيِّ أَوْ غَيْرِهِ بِالصَّلَاةِ عَلَيْهِ دُونَ غَيْرِهِ مُضَاهَاةً لِلنَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِحَيْثُ يُجْعَلُ ذَلِكَ شِعَارًا مَعْرُوفًا بِاسْمِهِ:
 هَذَا هُوَ الْبِدْعَةُ.
translated_text:
Imam Ahmad and most of his followers held that there was no harm in doing so, because Alī ibn Abī Tālib—may Allah be pleased with him—said to Umar ibn al-Khattāb, “May Allah bless you.” This view is more correct and preferable.

However, singling out one of the Companions or the Prophet’s relatives, such as Alī or anyone else, for invocations of blessings to the exclusion of others, in imitation of the way blessings are invoked upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, so that this becomes a recognized hallmark associated with his name—this is the religious innovation.

سُئِلَ شَيْخُ الْإِسْلَامِ - قَدَّسَ اللَّهُ رُوحَهُ -:
هَلْ صَحَّ عِنْدَ أَحَدٍ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ وَالْحَدِيثِ أَوْ مَنْ يُقْتَدَى بِهِ فِي دِينِ الْإِسْلَامِ أَنَّ أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ 
" عَلِيَّ بْنَ أَبِي طَالِبٍ "
 - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ -
 قَالَ:
 إذَا أَنَا مُتّ فَأَرْكِبُونِي فَوْقَ نَاقَتِي وَسَيِّبُونِي فَأَيْنَمَا بَرَكَتْ ادْفِنُونِي. فَسَارَتْ وَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ أَحَدٌ قَبْرَهُ؟ فَهَلْ صَحَّ ذَلِكَ أَمْ لَا؟ وَهَلْ عَرَفَ أَحَدٌ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ أَيْنَ دُفِنَ أَمْ لَا؟ وَمَا كَانَ سَبَبُ قَتْلِهِ؟ وَفِي أَيِّ وَقْتٍ كَانَ؟ وَمَنْ قَتَلَهُ؟ . وَمَنْ قَتَلَ الْحُسَيْنَ؟ وَمَا كَانَ سَبَبُ قَتْلِهِ؟ وَهَلْ صَحَّ أَنَّ أَهْلَ بَيْتِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ سُبُوا؟ وَأَنَّهُمْ أُرْكِبُوا عَلَى الْإِبِلِ عُرَاةً وَلَمْ يَكُنْ عَلَيْهِمْ مَا يَسْتُرُهُمْ فَخَلَقَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى لِلْإِبِلِ الَّتِي كَانُوا عَلَيْهَا سَنَامَيْنِ اسْتَتَرُوا بِهَا. وَأَنَّ الْحُسَيْنَ لَمَّا قُطِعَ رَأْسُهُ دَارُوا بِهِ فِي جَمِيعِ الْبِلَادِ وَأَنَّهُ حُمِلَ إلَى دِمَشْقَ وَحُمِلَ إلَى مِصْرَ وَدُفِنَ بِهَا؟ وَأَنَّ يَزِيدَ بْنَ مُعَاوِيَةَ هُوَ الَّذِي فَعَلَ هَذَا بِأَهْلِ الْبَيْتِ فَهَلْ صَحَّ ذَلِكَ أَمْ لَا؟ . وَهَلْ قَائِلُ هَذِهِ الْمَقَالَاتِ مُبْتَدِعٌ بِهَا فِي دِينِ اللَّهِ؟ وَمَا الَّذِي يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ إذَا
translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked:

Has any scholar or hadith scholar, or anyone regarded as an authority in the religion of Islam, established as authentic the report that the Commander of the Faithful, Alī ibn Abī Tālib—may Allah be pleased with him—said, “When I die, place me on my she-camel and let her go. Wherever she kneels, bury me,” and that she then went off and no one knew where his grave was? Is this authentic or not? Has any scholar known where he was buried or not? Why was he killed? When did this happen? Who killed him?

Who killed al-Husayn, and why was he killed? Is it authentic that the family of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, were taken captive; that they were made to ride camels naked, with nothing to cover them, so Allah Most High created two humps for the camels they were riding, behind which they concealed themselves; and that, when al-Husayn’s head was severed, it was paraded throughout all the lands, taken to Damascus, then taken to Egypt and buried there? And that Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah was the one who did this to the Prophet’s family—is this authentic or not?

Is someone who makes these assertions thereby an innovator in Allah’s religion? And what is required of him if

" الْخَوَارِجُ "

he relates this among the people? If someone objects to these claims, is he considered to be enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, or not? Give us your ruling—may you be rewarded—and provide us with a clear and thorough explanation.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. As for the claim that the Commander of the Faithful, “Alī ibn Abī Tālib”—may Allah be pleased with him—instructed that, upon his death, he should be placed on his mount, that it should be let loose, and that he should be buried wherever it knelt, and that this was done to him: this is a fabricated lie, by agreement of the scholars. Alī gave no such instructions, nor was anything of the kind done to him. No one known for learning and integrity has mentioned this; it is related only by those who transmit accounts from certain liars.

It is not permissible to do this to any deceased Muslim, nor is it permissible for anyone to leave instructions to this effect. Rather, this is an indignity inflicted on the deceased, and there is no benefit in it. If the purpose is to conceal the location of his grave, then once the she-camel kneels, a grave must still be dug for him and he must be buried in it. A grave could therefore be dug and he could be buried in it without this disgraceful treatment: leaving his dead body on the back of an animal roaming through the wilderness.

The scholars have differed over “the location of his grave.” The generally accepted account among scholars is that he was buried in the governor’s palace in Kufa, and that his grave was concealed so that the “Khārijites,” who declared him an unbeliever and regarded killing him as lawful, would not exhume him. Indeed, the man who killed him was one of the Khārijites, namely Abd al-Rahmān

ibn Muljam al-Murādī. He and two others had pledged to kill Alī, Mu‘āwiya, and Amr ibn al-Ās, for they declared all of them unbelievers, as well as anyone who did not conform to their whims. Reports condemning them have been transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through numerous independent chains. Muslim included the hadith concerning them in his Sahīh through ten chains of transmission, and al-Bukhārī through several chains; the compilers of the Sunan and Musnad collections transmitted it through still more.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said concerning them:

“Any of you would consider his prayer insignificant compared with theirs, his fasting compared with theirs, and his recitation compared with theirs. They recite the Quran, but it does not pass beyond their throats. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. If I encounter them, I will surely kill them as ‘Ād were killed”—and in another version—“Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will have a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection. They kill the followers of Islam.”

The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, agreed that they should be fought. It was Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, however, who personally fought them and ordered that they be fought. As related in the two Sahīh collections, Abū Sa‘īd reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A faction will break away at a time when the people are divided. They will be killed by the one of the two parties that is closer to the truth.”

Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, killed them at al-Nahrawān. They had previously gathered at a place called “Harūrā’,” which is why they are called the Harūriyya. Ibn Abbās was sent to them and debated with them until approximately half of them abandoned their position. The remainder then killed “Abd Allāh ibn Khabbāb” and raided the Muslims’ grazing herds, so orders were given

He related to them the Prophet’s command, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to fight them, and described their identifying sign: among them would be a man with underdeveloped hands, one hand incomplete, and something like a quivering lump of flesh on his breast. When they were killed, the man matching this description was found among them.

When the three Khārijites agreed to kill the three rulers of the Muslims, Abd al-Rahmān ibn Muljam killed “Alī,” may Allah be pleased with him, on Friday, the seventeenth of Ramadan, in the year 40 AH. He lay in wait for him and struck him when he came out for the dawn prayer.

The established practice was that the caliphs and their deputies—the governors who ruled the Muslims—would lead the Muslims in the five daily prayers, the Friday prayer, the prayers of the two Eids, the prayer for rain, the eclipse prayer, and other prayers such as funeral prayers. Thus, the military commander was also the imam who led the prayer.

As for the man who intended to kill “Mu‘āwiya,” they reported that he wounded him. The physician said, “You can be treated, but you will no longer be able to have children.” It is said that from that time onward Mu‘āwiya had an enclosure installed in the mosque. The governors followed his example so that they and their entourages could pray inside it, fearing that someone might attack the Commander of the Faithful and kill him. Nevertheless, impermissible things were done within these enclosures, and some disapproved of praying in enclosures of this kind.

As for the man who intended to kill “Amr ibn al-Ās,” Amr had appointed a man—named Khārija—to take his place that day. The Khārijite mistook him for Amr and killed him. When he discovered his mistake, he said, “I intended Amr, but Allah intended Khārija.” This became a proverb.

translated_text:
It is said that they concealed the graves of “Alī,” “Mu‘āwiya,” and “Amr” out of fear that the Khārijites would attack them. For this reason, they buried Mu‘āwiya inside the southern wall of the congregational mosque, in the governor’s palace known as al-Khadrā’. This is what ordinary people call the grave of “Hūd.” Yet the scholars agree that Hūd never came to Damascus. Rather, his grave is in Yemen, where he was sent as a prophet; it is also said to be in Mecca, to which he migrated. No one has said that it is in Damascus.

As for the “Mu‘āwiya” buried outside “Bāb al-Saghīr,” he is Mu‘āwiya ibn Yazīd, who ruled for about forty days and was known for asceticism and religious devotion. Alī was buried there, but the traces of his grave disappeared, which is why its location is not apparent. As for the shrine at Najaf, those with knowledge agree that it is not Alī’s grave. Rather, it has been said to be the grave of al-Mughīra ibn Shu‘ba. For more than three hundred years, no one identified it as Alī’s grave or visited it, despite the large numbers of Muslims—members of the Prophet’s household, Shia, and others—and their rule in Kufa. It was only made into a shrine during the reign of the non-Arab Banū Buwayh, more than three hundred years after Alī’s death. They related a story claiming that al-Rashīd used to visit that place, along with other accounts that establish no proof.

As for the question about members of the Prophet’s household being taken captive and made to ride camels until the camels grew two humps—these being the bukht camels—so that they could conceal themselves in this way, this is among the most disgraceful and obvious lies. It is among the fabrications of the heretics

"

. فَالنَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ شَبَّهَ أَصْحَابَ الْعَصَائِبِ الْكِبَارِ الَّتِي سَتَكُونُ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهِ بِأَسْنِمَةِ الْبَخَاتِيِّ فَلَوْلَا أَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يَعْرِفُونَهَا لَمْ يَفْهَمُوا وَهَذِهِ الْعَصَائِبُ قَدْ
translated_text:
and the hypocrites, whose purpose is to malign Islam and its adherents, including the Prophet’s household and others. Anyone who hears such a story, how widely it circulates, and the falsehoods it contains may think or say: “The accounts transmitted to us of the miracles of the prophets and the wonders granted to Allah’s righteous servants are of this same kind.” Then, if it were established that the community had taken its own Prophet’s household captive, this would constitute an attack on the best community brought forth for mankind whose gravity Allah alone knows. Every rational person knows that bukht camels had already been created and existed before Allah sent the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and before the Prophet’s household existed, just as other camels, sheep, cattle, horses, mules, and goats existed.

This fabrication is merely like their lie that Alī—may Allah be pleased with him—put out his hand at Khaybar, and a mule stepped on it, whereupon he said to it: “May Allah put an end to your offspring!” Every rational person knows that mules have never had offspring. Moreover, they had no mule with them at Khaybar; indeed, the Muslims had no mules at all. The first mule they acquired was the one that al-Muqawqis—the ruler of Egypt—gave to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. It remained with him until his death.

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“There are two kinds of people from my community who will be among the inhabitants of the Fire whom I have not yet seen: women who are clothed, straying and leading others astray, with things upon their heads resembling the humps of bukht camels. They will neither enter Paradise nor smell its fragrance. And men carrying whips like cattle’s tails, with which they beat Allah’s servants.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, thus likened those wearing the large head-wraps that would appear after his death to the humps of bukht camels. Had his listeners not already known these camels, they would not have understood. These head-wraps have
